| `"laptop"` | under 1900 pt wide | 0.75 | 0.667 |
| `"widescreen"` | every other screen | 0.5 | 0.5 |
| `"ultrawide"` | 3000 pt wide or more, or 2.1:1 | 0.333 | 0.5 |
| `"super_ultrawide"` | 3:1 or wider | 0.25 | 0.5 |
| `"portrait"` | taller than wide | 0.75 | 0.5 |

The defaults are the two right-hand columns.

**Example:**

```lua
maximize.set_share("height", 0.6, "widescreen")
```

sections.heading: maximize.set_anchor
parts:
### maximize.set_anchor

**Expects:** `"center"` or `"in_place"`, and optionally a screen
shape, as [`maximize.set_share`](#maximizeset_share) takes.

**Does:** sets where a Maximize Height or Width grows from on a
screen of that shape: `"center"` centres it on the screen,
`"in_place"` on the window's own slot, moved back inside the
screen where it would cross an edge. A wider share in place covers
part of a neighbour. Without a shape it sets every shape. Default
`"in_place"` on `"ultrawide"` and `"super_ultrawide"`, `"center"`
elsewhere. A full Maximize ignores it.

**Example:**

```lua
maximize.set_anchor("center", "ultrawide")
```

sections.heading: maximize.set_share_override
parts:
### maximize.set_share_override

**Expects:** a Space id, an axis, `"height"` or `"width"`, and a
share from 0.1 to 1, or `nil` to clear that axis.

**Does:** sets that Space's own share for the axis, over the row
[`maximize.set_share`](#maximizeset_share) stores for its screen
shape. The other axis keeps its screen's row. A binding's own share
still wins. A window already maximized keeps the shape it was
pressed with. Settings ▸ Spaces sets it in the Space's
**Customize…** editor, as **Maximize Height** and **Maximize
Width**; [`get_settings`](#get_settings) with the Space folds it in.

**Example:**

```lua
maximize.set_share_override("editor", "height", 2 / 3)
```

sections.heading: maximize.set_anchor_override
parts:
### maximize.set_anchor_override

**Expects:** a Space id and `"center"` or `"in_place"`, or `nil` to
clear it.

**Does:** sets where a Maximize Height or Width grows from in that
Space, over the row [`maximize.set_anchor`](#maximizeset_anchor)
stores for its screen shape. A window already maximized keeps the
shape it was pressed with. The **Customize…** editor's row is
**Maximize from**.

**Example:**

```lua
maximize.set_anchor_override("editor", "center")
```

sections.heading: maximize.set_follow_focus
parts:
### maximize.set_follow_focus

**Expects:** `true` or `false` (default `false`). Settings ▸ Layout
Defaults ▸ Maximize ▸ Maximize follows focus.

**Does:** with `true`, a Maximize made after the call moves to the
tiled window focus lands on instead of ending, in every shape. Only
the focused window fills; every other window keeps its place, so a
focus key moves by the layout's own slots: in a 2×2 grid with
bottom-left maximized, focus up fills top-left. Each step resizes two
windows, the one arriving and the one left, save a full Maximize on a
Monocle Space, where every window already fills the screen and a
step only raises one. A Maximize already on
screen keeps the switch it was made with. A float taking focus, a
swap, a resize or a layout change behave as for any Maximize.

**Example:**

```lua
maximize.set_follow_focus(true)
```

sections.heading: toggle_tiling
parts:
### toggle_tiling

**Expects:** nothing, or a Space id.

**Does:** turns tiling off for the active Space, or the Space
named, and back on with the next call. With tiling off, KiwiDesk
stops arranging that Space's windows and leaves them where they
are, as a Floating Space does, without gathering them; a drag
moves a window without reordering the Space. Turning tiling back
on puts each window back in its place, adds windows opened in
the meantime at the end and drops the ones closed. Bars, rings
and every shortcut keep working, unless
[`tiling.set_off_hides_borders`](#tilingset_off_hides_borders) or
[`tiling.set_off_hides_bars`](#tilingset_off_hides_bars) hides
them. The Space Bar marks the Space with a pause symbol, and the
quick menu's "Tiling Off for This Space" row shows the state. It
lasts until KiwiDesk quits; a restart in place keeps it. Bound to
`⌃⌥T` by default.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+t", function()
    KiwiDesk.toggle_tiling()
end)
```

sections.heading: set_tiling
parts:
### set_tiling

**Expects:** a boolean, then optionally a Space id.

**Does:** turns tiling on (`true`) or off (`false`) for the
active Space, or the Space named, as
[`toggle_tiling`](#toggle_tiling) does, without reading the state
first.

**Example:**

```lua
-- Space 3 holds a screen share: leave its windows alone.
KiwiDesk.set_tiling(false, 3)
```

sections.heading: set_tiling_start_global
parts:
### set_tiling_start_global

**Expects:** a boolean.

**Does:** sets whether a Space starts with tiling on where neither
the profile ([`tiling.set_start`](#tilingset_start)) nor the Space
says. Default `true`. A Space whose tiling a toggle set keeps that
choice; every other Space follows the new value at once.
App-wide, for this session only; it never reaches a file. The
stored value is the "Spaces start with tiling on" row's All
profiles value, under Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Size & float.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.set_tiling_start_global(false)
```

sections.heading: tiling.set_start
parts:
### tiling.set_start

**Expects:** a boolean or `nil`, then optionally a Space id.

**Does:** sets whether this profile's Spaces start with tiling
on, or with a Space id whether that Space does. A Space's value
wins over the profile's, and the profile's over
[`set_tiling_start_global`](#set_tiling_start_global); `nil`
removes the value, so the level above decides. The profile's
value is the "Spaces start with tiling on" row's own entry for that
profile; the Space form has no row. A Space whose
tiling a toggle set keeps that choice; every other Space follows a
new value at once.

**Example:**

```lua
tiling.set_start(false, "Share")
```

sections.heading: tiling.set_off_hides_borders
parts:
### tiling.set_off_hides_borders

**Expects:** a boolean.

**Does:** sets whether a Space with tiling off hides its focus
border, for every profile without its own value — the All profiles
value of Settings' "Hide the focus border while tiling is off"
row under Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Size & float. Default `false`. A
profile's own value wins. For this session only. Sticky and
floating marks stay.

**Example:**

```lua
tiling.set_off_hides_borders(true)
```

sections.heading: tiling.set_off_hides_bars
parts:
### tiling.set_off_hides_bars

**Expects:** a boolean.

**Does:** sets whether a Space with tiling off hides the bars on
its screen, for every profile without its own value — the All
profiles value of Settings' "Hide the bars while tiling is off"
row under Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Size & float. Default `false`. A
profile's own value wins. For this session only. Every bar and the Pocket then act as if set to Hidden on that
Space: gone at rest, and a bar's shortcut still shows it. Where the
Space Bar is hidden, the menu-bar item shows the Space with the
pause symbol.

**Example:**

```lua
tiling.set_off_hides_bars(true)
```

sections.heading: pocket
parts:
### pocket

**Expects:** nothing, or a window id.

**Does:** keeps pocket windows one key away. Mark one
with [`toggle_pocket_window`](#toggle_pocket_window); each
`pocket` call takes the next step:

- **Nothing marked:** marks the focused window and pockets it, a
  focused-window command like `make_floating`. It is parked
  off-screen — not minimized — belongs to no Space and is drawn on
  no bar, and focus moves on within the Space. A tiled window takes
  the frame [`set_float_placement`](#set_float_placement)'s
  `"center"` gives a window turned floating; under `"keep"`, or
  already floating, it keeps its size. Fails
  on a window in native full screen and on a transient panel or
  popup.
- **Pocketed:** takes it out onto the active Space's screen,
  floating and focused, at the frame it last had on that screen,
  else centred at its own size. A take-out never resizes it.
- **Out:** puts it back in the pocket, focused or not. If it had
  the focus, the focus goes back to the window it came out over
  where that is still on the Space, else to the Space's focused
  window.

While the window's app is hidden, taking it out or putting it back
fails with `the pocket window's app is hidden or relaunching` until
the app is shown again.

An app that quit while hidden empties the pocket at the next call. A
`move_to_space` or `swap` naming the pocketed window's id is
refused.

`pocket` also takes a window id, as the bar menus' Pocket Window
does: that window goes in, marked first, as
[`toggle_pocket_window`](#toggle_pocket_window) would mark it.

The pocket holds every marked window, in the order each last went in,
and a call puts away before it takes out: while a marked window is
out, it puts back the focused one, else the one focused last. Only
with every marked window in does it take one out, the one put in last.

Out of the pocket the window floats on every Space, as a
[global sticky](#make_sticky) window does, and a move to another
Space is refused with the same pill.

[`move_to_desktop`](#move_to_desktop) refuses it too.

It comes along when you switch
macOS Desktops whatever
[`sticky.set_desktop_reach`](#stickyset_desktop_reach) says, in
either state, where KiwiDesk can drive Desktops. Move and resize it
like any float: the frame it has when you put it back is kept for
the screen that frame sits on, and it comes out at that frame on
that screen.

Out of the pocket it wears the pocket mark inside its top-right
corner, whatever [`sticky.set_mark`](#stickyset_mark) and
[`floating.set_mark`](#floatingset_mark) say, and no mark while it
is presenting; [`pocket.set_color`](#pocketset_color)
colors it. Its Space Bar glyph wears the pocket
badge at the glyph's bottom-right corner, beside the floating badge,
and no sticky badge;
[`space_bar.set_sticky_badge(false)`](#space_barset_sticky_badge)
hides it with the others.

macOS focusing a pocketed window — `⌘-Tab` to its app, a Dock
click, a notification — takes it out as a call would, and so do
[`focus_window`](#focus_window) with its id and picking it with
Return or **⇧Return** under **Pocket** in KiwiHub's
[window switcher](#kiwihubshow).

Closing the window, minimizing it, quitting its app or unmarking it
empties the pocket; hiding the app keeps it. While the window is in the pocket
or out of it, `make_tiled`, `toggle_floating`, every
`make_*sticky` and `toggle_*sticky` verb and
`override_sticky_reach` are refused, with a pill: "Pocket windows
always float" or "Pocket windows are always sticky";
`make_floating` succeeds and changes nothing. While it is out,
KiwiVision keeps it and the window it came out over clear, and a
lens's focus keys skip neither. [`get_state`](#get_state) names
the window's state in its `pocket` field.

Quitting KiwiDesk files a pocketed window into the active Space as
a float, laid out with the others, and leaves a window that is out
where it is, as a float. An update's relaunch and
`kiwidesk service restart` keep it in the pocket. Bound to `⌃⌥P`
by default
([#2446](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2446)).

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+p", function()
    KiwiDesk.pocket()
end)
```

sections.heading: toggle_pocket_window
parts:
### toggle_pocket_window

**Expects:** nothing.

**Does:** marks the focused window as the [pocket](#pocket) window,
or unmarks it, a focused-window command like `make_floating`.
Marking floats it at once at the frame
[`set_float_placement`](#set_float_placement) gives a window turned
floating (a window already floating keeps its frame), and leaves it
out of the pocket: on every Space, wearing the pocket
mark. Unmarking tiles it on the active Space, as
[`make_tiled`](#make_tiled) does; a window detection floats stays
floating.
A window a float rule floats is tiled too, as `make_tiled` tiles
it.

A
pocketed window is never the focused one, so take it out
with [`pocket`](#pocket) before unmarking it. Fails on a window in
native full screen and on a transient panel or popup. Bound to
`⌃⌥⇧P` by default
([#2675](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2675)).

A call on another window marks it too, beside the others.

`toggle_pocket_window` also takes a window id, as the bar menus'
Remove from Pocket does: it marks or unmarks that window instead of
the focused one, and unmarks a pocketed window without taking it
out first.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+shift+p", function()
    KiwiDesk.toggle_pocket_window()
end)
```

sections.heading: pocket_app
parts:
### pocket_app

**Expects:** an app's bundle id.

**Does:** an app's own Pocket key. The first call opens a new
window of the app, launching it if it is not running, and that
window arrives out of the [pocket](#pocket): floating, on every
Space, focused. A running app gets its File ▸ New Window, also
when its windows are all on another Desktop; one with no window on
this Desktop, minimized ones included, and no New Window is
reopened, and one showing a window without a New Window fails with
a pill. Each later call puts it away or takes it out,
as `pocket` does for the other pocket windows. Its app rule's
"Open in a Space" does not apply to it.

The window is tied to the app while a shortcut's whole body is
the one call `KiwiDesk.pocket_app("<bundle id>")`, its argument in
double quotes, and no Pocket verb but that shortcut moves it:
`pocket` steps past it, and `pocket` naming it or
[`toggle_pocket_window`](#toggle_pocket_window) on it fails with
a pill naming its key. Remove the shortcut
and the window becomes an ordinary window again, on the Space you
are on; a profile that leaves the shortcut out keeps the tie, and
the key works again when you switch back. Closing the window or
quitting the app frees the key, and the next call opens a fresh
window. If the app is hidden, the call shows it again. Settings ▸
Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Pocket writes this shortcut: one row per
app, added with **Give an app its own Pocket key…**.

Called with no such shortcut — from the CLI, say — the window it
opens is an ordinary pocket window. Fails
with `app not found: <id>` for an app macOS cannot find.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+t", function()
    KiwiDesk.pocket_app("com.mitchellh.ghostty")
end)
```

sections.heading: override_sticky_reach
parts:
### override_sticky_reach

**Expects:** one of `on`, `off`, `auto`.

**Does:** pins the focused window's Desktop reach against the
global `sticky.set_desktop_reach` toggle — `on` keeps this
window following you across macOS Desktops even with the toggle
off, `off` leaves it on the Desktop it lives on even with the
toggle on, and `auto` clears the pin so the toggle rules again.
Session state: the pin does not survive the window closing.
Without the window-management bridge the pin is recorded but
nothing is carried.

**Example:**

```lua
-- The player follows me everywhere, whatever the toggle says.
KiwiDesk.override_sticky_reach("on")
```

sections.heading: sticky.set_mark
parts:
### sticky.set_mark

**Expects:** boolean (default `true`).

**Does:** shows or hides the on-window sticky mark — the small
glyph at a sticky window's top-right corner, and the carrier
for sticky's refusal pills (home-space, move-blocked), which
go silent with it. Off while the Space Bar is not shown leaves sticky state with no mark at all; neither
this setting nor the Settings app's toggle refuses that.

**Example:**

```lua
sticky.set_mark(false)
```

sections.heading: sticky.set_color
parts:
### sticky.set_color

**Expects:** a hex color string `#RRGGBB` or `#RRGGBBAA`, or an
empty string `""` for **Automatic** (default `""`).

**Does:** tints the sticky mark — the on-window mark and the
Space Bar sticky badge read this one value.
`""` is Automatic: the badge keeps the count-badge fill and the
mark is a neutral glyph on glass that flips black/white with
light and dark mode. Any non-empty value must parse as a hex
color.

**Example:**

```lua
sticky.set_color("#3D6FE8")  -- a blue sticky mark
sticky.set_color("")          -- back to Automatic
```

The color paints the sticky glyph itself, on the mark and on the
Space Bar badge: the mark stays clear glass, or a neutral plate
with Liquid Glass off, and the badge keeps the count-badge disc.
`""` keeps the label ink.

sections.heading: sticky.set_desktop_reach
parts:
### sticky.set_desktop_reach

**Expects:** boolean (default `true`).

**Does:** extends the sticky promise across **macOS Desktops**:
on, every sticky window of either scope is carried along when
its screen switches Desktop, and is already there when you
arrive. A single window can be pinned the other way with
`override_sticky_reach`. Off, a sticky window stays on the
Desktop it lives on and follows only KiwiDesk's own Spaces
there. Inert on a macOS without the window-management bridge.

**Example:**

```lua
sticky.set_desktop_reach(false)
```

sections.heading: sticky.set_liquid_glass
parts:
### sticky.set_liquid_glass

**Expects:** a boolean (default `true`).

**Does:** draws the on-window sticky mark as frosted, untinted
macOS 26 Liquid Glass; [`sticky.set_color`](#stickyset_color)
colors the glyph. Off, below macOS 26, or under Reduce
transparency, the glyph sits on a neutral plate. Settings writes this
through the one **Liquid Glass** switch
([kiwishelf.set_liquid_glass](#kiwishelfset_liquid_glass)).

The floating mark draws the same way, its glyph colored by
[`floating.set_color`](#floatingset_color). The mark wears the same
key-window rim as the bars.

**Example:**

```lua
sticky.set_liquid_glass(false)
```

sections.heading: floating.set_mark
parts:
### floating.set_mark

**Expects:** boolean (default `true`).

**Does:** shows or hides the on-window floating mark — the
`macwindow.on.rectangle` glyph at the top-right corner of a
floating window, including one in a floating-mode space: one
floated by `make_floating` or `toggle_floating`, by a
`float_rules` entry, or by KiwiDesk's own detection. A window
that floats only because its space is in floating mode gets no
mark. A window that is also
sticky carries both glyphs on one plate, the sticky one
outermost; on a window too narrow for both, the floating glyph
is left out. The mark draws as Liquid Glass under
[`sticky.set_liquid_glass`](#stickyset_liquid_glass).

**Example:**

```lua
floating.set_mark(false)
```

sections.heading: floating.set_color
parts:
### floating.set_color

**Expects:** a hex color string `#RRGGBB` or `#RRGGBBAA`, or an
empty string `""` for **Automatic** (default `""`).

**Does:** tints the floating mark — the on-window mark and the
Space Bar floating badge read this one value, as
[`sticky.set_color`](#stickyset_color) describes for sticky. On
a window that is both sticky and floating, each glyph takes its
own color and the glass stays untinted. `""`
is Automatic; any non-empty value must parse as a hex color.

**Example:**

```lua
floating.set_color("#8E5DE0")
```

sections.heading: Retired pocket verbs
parts:
### Retired pocket verbs

`pocket.set_capacity` is retired →
[`kiwishelf.set_pocket_visibility`](#kiwishelfset_pocket_visibility).
A call in `init.lua` is reported in Config Issues, naming the
replacement; over the CLI it fails with `pocket.set_capacity was
retired — use kiwishelf.set_pocket_visibility`. An `init.lua` that
never called it showed the pocket as `"one"` did and now takes
`"always"`; add `kiwishelf.set_pocket_visibility("hidden")` to keep
it out of sight.

sections.heading: pocket.toggle_list
parts:
### pocket.toggle_list

**Expects:** nothing.

**Does:** opens the [pocket](#pocket)'s list on the active Space's
screen, or closes the one open. The pocket comes up at
[`kiwishelf.set_pocket_edge`](#kiwishelfset_pocket_edge) and
[`kiwishelf.set_pocket_position`](#kiwishelfset_pocket_position) and
the list grows out of it, under any
[`kiwishelf.set_pocket_visibility`](#kiwishelfset_pocket_visibility),
and no bar shows or moves. The list is the one a click on the pocket opens, with
[`pocket_app`](#pocket_app)'s windows under **Pocket Keys**, its first
window row selected: the up and down arrows move, Return takes that
window out, and Esc closes the list, as does any other key. An empty
pocket shows how a window goes in. It refuses with a pill while
KiwiShelf stands down for a window filling the screen. Bound to `⌃⌥⌘P`
by default.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("control+option+command+p", function()
    pocket.toggle_list()
end)
```

sections.heading: pocket.set_color
parts:
### pocket.set_color

**Expects:** a hex color string `#RRGGBB` or `#RRGGBBAA`, or an
empty string `""` for **Automatic** (default `""`).

**Does:** fills the pocket of the [pocket](#pocket) mark and of
the Space Bar pocket badge, opaque, an alpha ignored; the kiwis
stay green and lose their outline. The pocket's outline takes the
color too, and the dashed stitch a legible auto-contrast black or
white, as [`sticky.set_color`](#stickyset_color)'s glyph does.
Each bundled palette sets its own pocket color. Neither the
mark's plate nor the badge's disc takes the color: the disc keeps
the count-badge fill. `""` is Automatic: the mark's pocket and
its outline take the label color, black in light mode and white in
dark, and the badge's pocket the disc's auto-contrast ink. Any
non-empty value must parse as a hex color.

Under Automatic too, the kiwis draw no outline.

**Example:**

```lua
pocket.set_color("#E8A33D")  -- an amber pocket
pocket.set_color("")          -- back to Automatic
```

sections.heading: Launching Apps
parts: ## Launching Apps

sections.heading: focus_or_spawn
parts:
### focus_or_spawn

Renamed from `pull_or_spawn`, which is now refused with a Config
Issue naming this verb. A shortcut made in Settings is updated for
you; a call in your `init.lua` needs the new name.

**Expects:** an app bundle identifier (e.g. `com.apple.safari`).
See [Finding a bundle identifier](#finding-a-bundle-identifier).

**Does:** if the app is already running, focuses its window; if
not, launches a new instance. Matching and launching are keyed
on the bundle id, so it finds apps anywhere on disk (Finder,
apps outside `/Applications`) regardless of system language.

Pressing again while one of the app's windows is focused
advances to the app's **next** window — space order (the order
spaces were created, as the Space Bar lists them), then slot
order within a space, wrapping around. With a single window a
repeat press changes nothing. The ring includes the app's
windows on other macOS Desktops, each at the rank it holds in
its Space's row; cycling onto one switches to that Desktop and
focuses it. That switch needs the Desktop bridge — without it
the ring is the windows KiwiDesk currently tracks, see
[Accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md).

If the app has **nothing on screen** — typically every window
minimized — the shortcut restores exactly one and brings the app
forward: the window you minimized most recently; when KiwiDesk
was not running to see the minimize there is no such record and
the app's own window order decides. While any window is still
visible, minimized windows are left alone. A window up on
another macOS Desktop counts: the shortcut switches to that
Desktop and focuses it instead of un-parking anything, and the
restore runs only when nothing is up anywhere. Without the
Desktop bridge, or where the per-Desktop window list cannot be
read, other Desktops are not consulted — see
[Accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md).

A first press focuses the app window you used **most recently**
among the ones KiwiDesk is tracking — its windows on the
Desktops on screen — switching to its Space. Right after
KiwiDesk starts, before you have used any of them, it takes the
app's own focused window, else the first in the cycle order
above. A window on another Desktop is reached only when the app
has none on the Desktops on screen, as described above.

If the app is running with **no window at all** — you closed
its last one and it stayed open, as Safari does — the shortcut
asks it for a new window, the same as clicking it in the Dock.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+return", function()
    KiwiDesk.focus_or_spawn("com.apple.safari")
end)
```

sections.heading: spawn_new
parts:
### spawn_new

**Expects:** an app bundle identifier (e.g. `com.apple.Terminal`).
See [Finding a bundle identifier](#finding-a-bundle-identifier).

**Does:** always launches a new instance of the app, even if one
is already running. Matching is keyed on the bundle id, like
`focus_or_spawn`.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+return", function()
    KiwiDesk.spawn_new("com.apple.Terminal")
end)
```

Both launch verbs are also reachable from the Settings app, from
the per-row menu of an Open applications shortcut: *Open or Focus*
(`focus_or_spawn`, the default) or *Open New* (`spawn_new`).

sections.heading: open_in_background
parts:
### open_in_background

**Expects:** an app bundle identifier (e.g. `com.apple.Notes`)
and, optionally, a Space id and a macOS Desktop number. See
[Finding a bundle identifier](#finding-a-bundle-identifier).

**Does:** opens an app without taking the focus from the window
you are in, the way `open -g` does. If the app is not running, it
is launched; if it is running with no window, it is asked for
one, as a Dock click would; if it has a window anywhere, up,
minimized or on another Desktop, nothing happens. Its new window
tiles into the Space you are in, or into its
[app rule](#app_rules)'s Space without taking you there, and the
layout makes room for it.

With a Space named, the app's windows go into that Space instead,
ahead of its app rule, and KiwiDesk switches nothing: you stay
where you are and find them there. A Space that does not exist is
refused, and so is the call when the app already has a window,
since nothing would move.

With a Desktop named, each window the app opens is sent to that
Desktop as soon as it appears, as
[`move_to_desktop`](#move_to_desktop) would send it, and a Space
named with it is the Space it joins there. You stay on the Desktop
you are on. Like `move_to_desktop`, this needs the Desktop bridge.
Without it, for a Desktop that does not exist or one a screen is
already showing (name its Space instead), or for a Space that lays
out on another screen, the call is refused before anything opens.
A move only the window itself can turn down, such as one onto
another screen that macOS refuses, is noted in the log, and the
window stays where it opened. A full-screen window, or one your
Pocket key claims, is not sent. To name
a Desktop without a Space, pass `nil` for the Space (`""` on the
command line).

A click on the app, or [`focus_or_spawn`](#focus_or_spawn) naming
it, ends the Space or Desktop it was sent to, so a window you open
of it yourself lands where you are.

Some apps, Electron ones among them, bring themselves forward on
launch anyway. KiwiDesk hands the focus back to the window it was
taken from, once per app, within 10 seconds of the call. If the
app takes the focus a second time, it keeps it. A click on the app
or its Dock icon keeps the focus there; a switch to the app by
keyboard (⌘Tab) within those 10 seconds is handed back once too.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+m", function()
    KiwiDesk.open_in_background("com.apple.Music")
end)
-- Mail opens in Space 3, out of the way.
KiwiDesk.open_in_background("com.apple.mail", "3")
-- Music opens on Desktop 2, which you are not looking at.
KiwiDesk.open_in_background("com.apple.Music", nil, 2)
```

sections.heading: gather
parts:
### gather

**Expects:** an app bundle identifier (e.g. `com.apple.Notes`).
See [Finding a bundle identifier](#finding-a-bundle-identifier).

**Does:** moves every window of the app into the Space you are
on, in the order the Space Bar lists them, after the windows
already there. Floating windows stay floating and sticky windows
stay sticky; a window in native full screen keeps its own Space.
Windows up on another macOS Desktop of the same screen are moved
onto the Desktop you are looking at, without switching to theirs;
another screen's Desktops are left alone, unless "Displays have
separate Spaces" is off and every screen shares them. That needs the
Desktop bridge; without it they stay where they are. It never
launches the app: with no window to move, it does nothing and
reports an error.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+shift+return", function()
    KiwiDesk.gather("com.apple.Notes")
end)
```

It is the third choice, *Gather Windows*, in the **Action** menu
of an Open applications shortcut in Settings.

sections.heading: move_here
parts:
### move_here

**Expects:** an app bundle identifier (e.g. `com.apple.Notes`),
then optionally a piece of window title. See [Finding a bundle
identifier](#finding-a-bundle-identifier).

**Does:** moves one window of the app into the Space you are on
and focuses it: the open window you focused most recently that is
not here yet — in another Space, or up on another macOS Desktop —
and only once none is left, a minimized one. Press it again for
the next. The app's other windows stay where they are; to move
them all, use [gather](#gather).

With a title, only windows whose title contains it count,
ignoring case and accents, so `"Inbox"` keeps finding Mail's
window as its message count changes.

- A window in native full screen is skipped, and so is a window
  on another Desktop when the Desktop bridge is absent. When
  nothing else is left, a refusal says the window can't be moved
  here.
- Every matching window already here, or a title no window has,
  shows a refusal on the focused window and moves nothing. A
  sticky window shown here counts as here.
- A hidden app is unhidden, and the window it brings back
  focused moves here — with a title, only if it matches.
- An app with no window at all is opened, the same as
  [focus_or_spawn](#focus_or_spawn).

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+shift+n", function()
    KiwiDesk.move_here("com.apple.Notes")
end)
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+shift+i", function()
    KiwiDesk.move_here("com.apple.mail", "Inbox")
end)
```

sections.heading: User Interface
parts: ## User Interface

sections.heading: kiwihub.show
parts:
### kiwihub.show

**Expects:** a side: `"windows"`, `"shortcuts"` or `"view"`.

**Does:** opens **KiwiHub** on that side, switches to it from
another side, or closes KiwiHub when it already shows that side.
Over the CLI it is `kiwidesk kiwihub.show windows`; any other side
is refused, naming the sides it takes.

The `"shortcuts"` side is the read-only **shortcuts panel** — a
live glance at the active layer's bindings.

- Typing narrows the list by name, the matched letters in bold.
- **↑** **↓** and **Page Up** / **Page Down** scroll the list;
  **Return** runs nothing.
- **⌘,** or **Edit in Settings…** opens Shortcuts.

The `"windows"` side is the **window switcher**, its field at
Spotlight's height on the screen under the pointer. It lists every
window KiwiDesk knows except the one you are in — open windows
first, most recently used first, including those up on another
macOS Desktop, then minimized windows, then one row per hidden
app. Typing narrows the list by app name, then by title. While a
[KiwiVision lens](#kiwivisiondefine_lens) is on, the rows of the
lens's apps come first and every other app's follow under **Other
apps**, while you type too. Moving the mouse over a row selects it.

A window in the [pocket](#pocket) is listed after the hidden apps,
under **Pocket**.

- **Return** goes to the selected window, switching Space or
  Desktop as needed; on a minimized window it brings it back, on a
  hidden app it unhides it.
- **⇧Return** moves the window into the Space you are on instead,
  as [move_here](#move_here) does.
- **⌘1** … **⌘9** pick one of the first nine results.

A window in native full screen is listed, and **Return** shows it
on its own full-screen Space
([#2939](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2939)).
One already full screen on a Space no screen showed when KiwiDesk
started is listed by its app's name
([#2949](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2949)), and
picking it brings the app forward
([accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md)).

**⌥Return** (or **⇧⌥Return**, or an ⌥-click) swaps the selected
window with yours, as [swap_here](#swap_here) does, and **⌥⌘1** …
**⌥⌘9** (or **⇧⌥⌘1** …) swap one of the first nine. Yours is
the window focused on
the screen KiwiHub opened on, else the focused window. A hidden app
and a pocketed window are refused, and so, until #2884, are a
minimized window and one on another macOS Desktop. A refused swap
or Move here keeps KiwiHub open, with the refusal sound where that
is on.

**↑** on the first row selects the last, and **↓** on the last
selects the first. Holding the key down stops at the end instead,
so the list never runs past it; press again to go round. **Page
Up** and **Page Down** stop at the ends.

Under the field sits the **app strip**, shown while you type or
while it is off **All**; KiwiHub opens on the list alone. It holds
**All** first, then one tile per app with a window in the list, the
app you are in first, then most recently used, with a count on an
app with two windows or more. **←** and **→** move along it and a
click picks a tile; the list then holds that app's windows alone,
its most recent window selected. Typing puts the strip back on
**All** and dims each app with no match; **←** and **→** then step
through the apps with a match, never the text, and narrow the
matches to that app. [kiwihub.show_last_app](#kiwihubshow_last_app)
opens this side with the strip on the app of the window you used
last.

With nothing typed, the window you are in sits greyed at the top
of **All** and of its app's tile, marked **Current window**. It is
never a row you pick: the arrows, the digits and search skip it.

A modifier still held from the shortcut that opened KiwiHub, or
from a step of `kiwihub.show_last_app`, counts for nothing until
you let it go: **Return** under the **⌥** of **⌥⇥** jumps.

The `"view"` side is the **view picker**, three lines in one
panel, the current item on each marked ✓. The menu bar's **Open
KiwiHub…** row opens it too, its bound combo shown beside that
row.

- **Layout** — a tile per layout for the Space shown on the screen
  under the pointer, greyed where there is none; Return applies it
  like `set_mode` for that Space.
- **Profile** — one per saved profile; one that cannot load is
  greyed. Return loads it like `load_profile`. The line ends in
  **Save as New Profile…**: Return turns the search field into a
  name field, and Return again saves the current arrangement under
  that name like `save_profile`, which hands it the connected
  screen setup; a taken name saves beside it rather than over it. Esc
  goes back to picking, and ⌘1–9 and ↓ skip the chip.
- **KiwiVision** — Default, which turns
  [KiwiVision](#kiwivisiontoggle) on with no lens, then one item
  per lens, which turns that lens on. Picking the item already on
  turns KiwiVision off. A lens with no apps is left out until it
  has some, and one the live profile leaves out is greyed "Not in
  Studio". The line ends in **New Lens…**, which opens Settings ▸
  KiwiVision ready to name a lens; ⌘1–9 and ↓ skip it, and a
  Lua-owned setup greys it.

Keys on this side:

- **←** and **→**, or moving the mouse over an item, move along a
  line; **↑** and **↓** move between lines and keep the position,
  clamped to a shorter line. A line longer than the panel scrolls
  sideways.

- Typing narrows all three lines, dimming the rest, and selects
  the first match.
- **Return** applies the selected item and closes KiwiHub.
  **⌘1** … **⌘9** apply the line's items by position, counted
  among the matches while you type; holding **⌘** shows the
  numbers.
- **⌘,** opens the Settings page of the line the selection is on;
  **⌘S** keeps the layouts in the profile, as Keep in a Space's
  Layout menu does.

Past the end of a line, **←** and **→** go round to its other end,
and past the last line **↓** comes back to the first, **↑** the
other way. Holding the key down stops at the end instead.

The `"desktops"` side is the **Desktop overview**, the fourth side,
after View: one row per screen, left to right, each screen's
Desktops as columns, and in each column the screen's Spaces with
their windows. A window on a Desktop no screen shows is listed in the
Space it returns to, or under **Not in a Space yet**, which nothing
can be moved into. The menu bar's **Show Desktop overview** row
opens it too. The side is seeded on **⌃⌥O**, and **Shortcuts ▸
Built-in ▸ Show & hide ▸ KiwiHub** lists the row to rebind or clear.
While KiwiHub has the keyboard, a modifier tap whose Shortcuts row
opens one of its sides works as that side's shortcut, so a ⌘⌘ set
to the overview closes it; a tap bound in `init.lua`, and every
other modifier tap, does nothing there, or while another KiwiDesk
panel has the keyboard.

- **↑** **↓** **←** **→** choose a Space; **Return** goes there,
  **⇧Return** moves your window there, **⌃Return** moves it and
  follows; **⌘1**–**⌘9** go to that Desktop of the row and
  **⇧⌘1**–**⇧⌘9** move your window there.
- **⌘↓** opens the Space to choose a window, **⌘↑** goes back.
  Inside, **Return** jumps to the window, **⇧Return** moves it to
  the Space KiwiHub's screen shows and **⌥Return** swaps it with
  yours there.
- **⌘Return** picks the window up, or puts it back; picked
  windows ride along while you choose another Space, and
  **Return** drops them there, **⌃Return** drops them and follows
  the first, **⌘1**–**⌘9** drop them on that Desktop's shown
  Space. A window on a Desktop no screen shows, a pocketed one and
  a full-screen one cannot be picked up.
- A click does what **Return** does on what you clicked: on a
  Space it goes there, on a window's icon it jumps to the window,
  on a Desktop's title it goes to that Desktop, and while windows
  ride along it drops them there. **⇧**-click moves, **⌥**-click
  swaps, **⌘**-click picks up. A double click acts once. Dragging
  an icon onto a Space moves it, and you stay.
- Typing finds windows by app and title; matches move to the
  front of their Space and the rest dim.
- **Escape** steps back: the picked windows, the open Space, the
  typing, then KiwiHub.

**Tab** reaches it from View, and **⇧Tab** from Windows.

On every side:

- **Tab** steps to the next side and **⇧Tab** to the one before —
  in the switch's order and wrapping — clearing the typing.
- **Escape** clears the typing, then closes KiwiHub; **⌘W**, a
  click elsewhere or another app taking the keyboard close it too.

The switch at the end of the field shows each side's own key,
read from your shortcuts.

Each key shows in place of its side's title: every side's while
you hold **⌘**, one side's while you point at it.

Seeded on **⌃⌥J** (windows), **⌃⌥K** (shortcuts, in every layer
you create too) and **⌃⌥L** (view), and offered under
**Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Show & hide ▸ KiwiHub**, where you can
rebind or clear
each per layer.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("alt+space", function()
    kiwihub.show("windows")
end)
```

sections.heading: kiwihub.show_last_app
parts:
### kiwihub.show_last_app

**Expects:** nothing.

**Does:** opens KiwiHub's window switcher with its app strip on
the app of the window you used last, that window selected — while
a [KiwiVision lens](#kiwivisiondefine_lens) is on too — so
**Return** goes back to it. It switches to the window switcher from
another side. Pressed again while the window switcher is up, it
steps the app strip to the next app, as **→** does, and the same
key with **⇧** steps back (**⇧⌥⇥** by default); **Esc** closes
KiwiHub.
It is bound to `⌥⇥` by default, listed under Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸
Show & hide ▸ KiwiHub as **Show window switcher for last app**.
Over the CLI it is `kiwidesk kiwihub.show_last_app`.

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+y", function()
    kiwihub.show_last_app()
end)
```

sections.heading: kiwihub.set_key
parts:
### kiwihub.set_key

**Expects:** a built-in KiwiHub key — `"up"`, `"down"`,
`"page_up"`, `"page_down"`, `"left"` or `"right"` — and a combo
string; no combo, or `""`, clears it.

**Does:** makes the combo a second key for that built-in key
while KiwiHub is open: `"down"` moves the selection down as **↓**
does, `"page_down"` a page as **Page Down** does. `"left"` and
`"right"` move only where **←** and **→** do;
elsewhere their combo types into the search field. The built-in
keys keep working, holding **⇧** with a combo moves as with the
arrows, and the combo does nothing outside KiwiHub. While the
field names a profile, every combo types. A KiwiDesk shortcut on
the same combo runs instead.

Refused, naming the reason: a combo it cannot read; one without
**ctrl** or **cmd**; one with **hyper**; **Return**, **Enter**,
**Escape**, **Tab**, an arrow or a page key under any modifier;
**cmd** with a digit or with **S**, **,**, **W**, **A**, **C**,
**V**, **X** or **Z**; and a combo already set for another key.

The combos for `"up"`, `"down"`, `"page_up"` and `"page_down"`
also scroll an open [key sequence](#define_sequence)'s panel, as
the arrows and page keys do, unless a step key takes the combo.

Four more keys name the Desktop overview's own presses:
`"open_space"` (**⌘↓**), `"leave_space"` (**⌘↑**), `"pick_up"`
(**⌘Return**) and `"follow"` (**⌃Return**); their combos act on
that side alone.

The keys are the Mac's, not a profile's. Lua-only: no Settings
row shows them.

**Example:**

```lua
kiwihub.set_key("down", "ctrl+n")
kiwihub.set_key("up", "ctrl+p")
kiwihub.set_key("page_down", "ctrl+d")
kiwihub.set_key("page_up", "ctrl+u")
```

sections.heading: Retired panel verbs
parts:
### Retired panel verbs

`show_shortcuts`, `show_jump_to_window` and `show_layout_picker`
are retired for [kiwihub.show](#kiwihubshow). A call in
`init.lua` is reported in Config Issues, naming `kiwihub.show`;
over the CLI it fails with `<verb> was retired — use
kiwihub.show`. A shortcut made in Settings is updated for you.

sections.heading: open_settings
parts:
### open_settings

**Expects:** nothing.

**Does:** opens the **Settings** window and brings it to the
front. It never closes the window: pressing the key with
Settings already open returns it to **Home**, the same as
opening Settings from the menu bar. Unsaved edits survive that;
only the place you were reading resets.

Seeded on **`⌃⌥,`** in the base layer and in every layer you
create in Settings.

Offered under **Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Show & hide ▸
KiwiDesk** ("Open Settings"), where you can rebind it per layer.

**Example:**

```lua
-- A second chord beside the seeded one.
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+shift+comma", function()
    KiwiDesk.open_settings()
end)
```

sections.heading: Keybindings
parts:
## Keybindings

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("cmd+alt+left", function()
    KiwiDesk.focus("left")
end)
KiwiDesk.bind("cmd+alt+f", function()
    KiwiDesk.make_floating()
end)
```

sections.heading: Modifiers and Keys
parts:
### Modifiers and Keys

**Modifiers:** `cmd`/`command`, `alt`/`opt`/`option`,
`ctrl`/`control`, `shift`.

`hyper` is KiwiDesk's own Hyper modifier, live once
[`set_hyper_key`](#set_hyper_key) names a key; it combines with
any of the others (`"hyper+cmd+ctrl+x"`). Held, a Hyper combo is
its chord without `hyper`, so an enabled macOS shortcut on that
chord (`hyper+cmd+space` is Spotlight's) still wins.

A side is `l` or `r` before a short name: `lcmd` / `rcmd`,
`lopt` / `ropt`, `lalt` / `ralt`, `lshift` / `rshift`, `lctrl` /
`rctrl` (`"rcmd+h"`). It counts only while
[`set_modifier_sides`](#set_modifier_sides) is on. Two spellings
of one modifier (`"lcmd+rcmd+h"`, `"cmd+rcmd+h"`) and a side with
`hyper` are unrecognized.

**A modifier tapped alone** binds like a chord. The modifier twice
is a double tap: `"cmd+cmd"` taps either ⌘ twice (the same key both
times), `"ropt+ropt"` the right ⌥ twice. One modifier alone is a
single tap: `"rcmd"` taps the right ⌘ once, `"cmd"` either ⌘ once.
Beside a sided tap of the same modifier, an either-side tap keeps
the other key. Three taps or more are unrecognized. A tap counts when
each press is shorter than 250 ms, the second follows within
300 ms, and no key or click comes between. Unlike a sided chord, a
tap keeps its side with `set_modifier_sides` off. A single tap on a
key that also has a double tap waits 300 ms before it fires. A tap
needs Accessibility; if macOS refuses it, a tap does not fire and
its row is flagged.

**Keys:** letters, digits, `left`, `right`, `up`, `down`,
`home`, `end`, `pageup`, `pagedown`, `space`,
`return`/`enter`, `tab`, `escape`/`esc`, `f1`–`f12`, and
punctuation.

**Punctuation aliases:** both the symbol and the word form work, so
`";"` and `"semicolon"` are the same key. Aliases:
- `comma`/`,`
- `period`/`.`
- `slash`/`/`
- `backslash`/`\`
- `minus`/`-`
- `equal`/`=`
- `leftbracket`/`[`
- `rightbracket`/`]`
- `grave`/`backtick`/`` ` ``
- `quote`/`apostrophe`/`'`
- `return`/`enter`
- `delete`/`backspace`
- `escape`/`esc`

**The numeric keypad.** Its ten digits are the **same key** as
their number-row twin — a binding written `control+option+4`
fires from either, and the two cannot be bound apart. Every
other keypad key is its own key: `keypadplus`, `keypadminus`,
`keypadmultiply`, `keypaddivide`, `keypaddecimal`,
`keypadequals`, `keypadenter`, `keypadclear`.
`keypad0`–`keypad9` are accepted as spellings of the plain
digits and resolve to them, so the recorder writes `4` whichever
of the two keys you press.

Keypad digits work whenever the keypad sends digits. Apple
keypads always do (a Clear key sits where PC keyboards put Num
Lock); a third-party PC keyboard with Num Lock **off** sends
navigation keys from the keypad instead, and no keypad shortcut
fires.

The Settings app's shortcut recorder writes the long forms
(`command`, `option`, `semicolon`, …), save for a modifier tap,
which it writes short (`cmd+cmd`, `rcmd`); every alias round-trips.

A combo is any set of modifiers plus **exactly one key**, or a
modifier tap (above).
Multi-key chords (`cmd+j+k`) are not expressible; a hand-written
combo that doesn't parse is never registered, and the Shortcuts
page flags the row with ⚠ *"isn't a recognized shortcut"*.

sections.heading: Shortcut Layers
parts:
### Shortcut Layers

Define vim-style layers; only the active layer's bindings
fire:

```lua
KiwiDesk.define_layer("resize", {
    ["h"]      = function() KiwiDesk.resize("x", -50) end,
    ["l"]      = function() KiwiDesk.resize("x", 50) end,
    ["j"]      = function() KiwiDesk.resize("y", -50) end,
    ["k"]      = function() KiwiDesk.resize("y", 50) end,
    ["escape"] = function() KiwiDesk.switch_layer("default") end,
})

KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+r", function()
    KiwiDesk.switch_layer("resize")
end)
```

sections.heading: switch_layer
parts:
#### switch_layer

**Expects:** a layer name: one `define_layer` declared, or
`"default"`.

**Does:** makes that layer the active one, so only its bindings
fire until the next switch. An unknown name changes nothing and
is logged.

sections.heading: resize
parts:
#### resize

**Expects:**

- An axis: `"x"` or `"y"`.
- A delta (points; positive = grow, negative = shrink).

**Does:** grows or shrinks the focused window. A **floating**
focused window resizes itself directly, in every layout mode:
`"x"` changes its width by the delta, `"y"` its height, floored
at its **effective minimum** — `min_window_size`, raised by a
larger minimum the app itself enforces once KiwiDesk has learned
it (#677). A window already smaller than that shrinks no
further.

On a floating window whose app holds its aspect ratio, such as mpv
or QuickTime Player, either axis scales both, and both stop at the
first floor or screen edge. KiwiDesk learns this from the first
press on that window; a first grow lands about a second late (#2973).

"Floating" here is the window's *effective* float (#1184): its
own float flag — set by a toggle, `make_floating`, a
`float_rules` entry or KiwiDesk's own detection — **or**
membership of a space set to the floating layout.

A floating window's `min_window_size` is Floating's
([`set_min_window_size`](#set_min_window_size)), whatever layout
its space uses: its width for `"x"`, its height for `"y"`.

The delta is split between **both** edges (#1091), so a float
grows and shrinks around its own centre. An edge already against
the boundary is *pinned* and the whole delta goes to the other
side; the boundary is the screen's visible bounds less any bar
strips on that space, so a float cannot be grown underneath a
bar, and when both edges are against it a grow refuses and
flashes a pill. Shrinking pins the same way.

The boundary is the screen's visible bounds, less a bar on the top
edge and the focus ring's reach: a float grows under a bottom or side
bar to the screen's edge, as a drag can take it (#3163).

A window whose app refuses the size stays where it is and `resize`
still reports success; one that takes part of the size moves only as
far as the size did. An app that keeps an axis or its ratio can show
the half step for a moment at a screen's right or bottom edge, or
off every screen
([#2981](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2981)).

Tiled windows resize in bsp, stack, scrolling, track and grid
layouts; monocle reports "not supported" and flashes a pill on
the focused window saying the layout has no resizing (#1255). In
a grid, `"x"` moves the edge the focused cell shares with the
column after it — or, for the last column, the one before — and
`"y"` does the same for rows, so the neighbour gives exactly what
the focused column takes and no other column moves (#763). A
mouse drag on a cell's inner edge moves that edge the same way.
The sizes are kept as [column and row weights](#gridset_column_weight)
in a session layer that
[`reset_layout_sizing`](#reset_layout_sizing) clears.

`set_refusal_sound(true)` adds the system alert sound
to that pill; only a hotkey fire sounds, so CLI and IPC callers
see the pill and read the error JSON without hearing anything.

A focused window in **native full screen** — floating or tiled,
whatever the space's layout — is refused ahead of both routes
(#1298): the press writes nothing, moves no other window, and
flashes a pill on the full-screen window saying full-screen
windows can't be resized; CLI and IPC callers read `the focused
window is fullscreen`.

A resize a size limit **truncates** (#933) — a shrink reaching
the focused window's effective minimum, a grow stopped where a
neighbor would drop below its own, or a grow reaching the
focused window's learned app maximum (scrolling, #1055; cued on
the resized window alone) — still applies the part that fits and
cues the refusal on the first truncated attempt. On a scrolling
space, a press the focused window's own learned bound blocks
outright (grow at its maximum, shrink at its minimum) refuses in
place: nothing applied, no neighbor moved, same bounce and pill
(#1057). The focus ring gives the rubber-band bounce of a
dead-end focus move (#436), and a pill names the reason on the
window that cannot shrink; on a refused grow the resized window
also names the reason while the blocking neighbor marks itself
at its minimum. Keyboard and mouse resizes share these clamps
and cues.

Along a run's scroll direction — a Stack zone, a Track track, an
auto-sized Grid's last track once the grid is full, a BSP chain —
a grow does not stop at a neighbour's minimum (#2709): the
neighbour it squeezes waits in the run, the grown window takes its
room, and the overflow mark's `+n` counts it. A mouse drag pushes
the neighbour on the side of the edge it moved; the keyboard
squeezes both sides and sends the last window in order. A window
alone in its run always fills it: any shrink gives up what the
next window needs at its minimum and that window comes back, the
one past the moved edge first (for the keyboard, the one after the
run), then the other end's once that side has none waiting. A next
window that cannot fit refuses the shrink. Beside a shown window a shrink widens that window, and a
waiting window comes back when you focus it or when every window
fits. The window keeps its length, like the stack and
track weights, while windows wait in its run, until
[`reset_layout_sizing`](#reset_layout_sizing), a layout change, or
the window moving between a Stack's zones clears it. Across the
run, in a Grid's last track while it draws its cells and in BSP's
halved splits a grow still stops at the neighbour's minimum.

The pill says *whose* minimum it was (#1261): "Minimum window
size reached" and "Neighboring window at its minimum size" mean
the `min_window_size` bound, and lowering it helps; "This app
won't go smaller" and "Neighboring app won't go smaller" mean
the app's own learned floor, which no setting moves.

The neighbour pair names the neighbour's app: "Neighboring
Safari window is at the minimum window size" is the
`min_window_size` bound, "Neighboring Safari window won't go
smaller" the app's own floor. Where the app's name is unknown the
nameless sentences above stay.

In **bsp**, the window that cannot shrink is often not the one
you are resizing (#1259). A window holding the whole height —
the first window, when the layout splits side by side — cannot
change height; that press moves the split *between its
neighbours*, and when one of them reaches its minimum the pill
goes on that neighbour while the focused window reads
"Neighboring window at its minimum size". Where the arrangement
has no split on that axis — two windows side by side, asked for
height — the press says so on the first try ("This zone divides
widths, not heights"); the stored ratio still records what a
later split on that axis will open at. Where the group an axis
divides holds only ONE member, the press says so instead
(#1258): "Nothing to divide here — try the other axis" where
the other axis does divide, and "This zone has nothing to
divide" where neither does. That covers a stack window alone in
its column, a stack space with an empty stack zone, a space
whose windows share one track, a window that fills its own
track, and a bsp space of one. In the stack and track cases the
press returns an error and CLI and IPC callers get the longer,
layout-specific text; the two ratio cases report success, since
the ratio is stored either way.

**Held, the chord glides (#1056, #1082).** A hotkey whose press
ran exactly one command, a successful `resize`, keeps applying
while you hold it: one step on the press, then, after your Mac's
own key-repeat delay, a continuous **glide** on the screen's
frame clock. Each frame moves a fraction of *that binding's own
delta*, at a speed in steps per second that starts gently and
ramps up over a second or two. The amount moved is the frame's
elapsed time × that speed, so the same hold travels the same
distance on a 60 Hz screen, a 120 Hz one, and a ProMotion panel
changing rate mid-hold.

The glide re-issues the **command your press ran**,
with a scaled delta — never the binding's Lua body, which runs
exactly once, on the press. Whether a binding glides is decided
by what its press **did**: a body that runs two commands, or a
verb that does not glide, fires once per press, and `focus`/`swap`
never glide. A body that rebuilds its own bindings (`bind` inside the
body) arms nothing.

While [`set_modifier_sides`](#set_modifier_sides) is on, a
shortcut whose keys a sided shortcut also uses — sided or not —
fires once per press.

A limit (#933/#1055) ends the run; scrolling's wordless out-of-screen
stop keeps gliding harmlessly until release.

[`move_floating`](#move_floating) glides the same way.

A hold reaching a limit stops with no pill, and a fresh press there
shows it (#3017).

Releasing the chord, switching layers, or arming a Settings
shortcut recorder ends the run immediately.

A glide writes each frame instantly, on every layout and on a
floating window alike, whatever `animations.set_on_window_resize`
says and under system **Reduce Motion** (#1082/#1090).

A glide along a run stops with the neighbour at its minimum and pushes
nothing; pressing again pushes one window
([#2709](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2709)).

A floating resize accumulates against what was last
*commanded* — the in-flight animation's target where one exists
(#129), and the glide's own record where none does — rather than
the lagging AX echo. That record is readable only by a glide
frame and is retired at the start of the next press. A fast run
of separate **presses** still re-reads the echo between them and
can come up short; see
[accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md).

What the `delta` adjusts depends on the layout:

- **bsp** — per-axis (#56): `"x"` nudges the side-by-side split
  ratio (`bsp.set_ratio_h`), `"y"` the stacked one
  (`bsp.set_ratio_v`). Focus-aware in direction (#122): a
  positive delta grows the *focused* window's region, so with a
  right/bottom window focused it lowers the shared ratio — the
  same side rule a mouse drag of that window's edge uses. All
  same-orientation splits share the one ratio; with no focused
  window the delta moves the left/top region. The write stops
  at the bound that keeps both regions at their effective
  minimums (per side, #933) within the area the layout fills
  (#383) — the screen minus any Space Bar strip.
- **stack** — focus-aware (#67). `"x"` moves the master/stack
  split *in the direction that grows the focused window*: with
  a master focused, a positive delta raises the master ratio;
  with a stack window focused, it lowers the ratio. The write
  stops at the bound that keeps both zones at their effective
  minimums (per zone, #933) within the area the layout fills
  (#44). `"y"` grows or shrinks the focused window's vertical
  share of its column via per-window weights — session-scoped,
  never saved to a profile, and reset when a window leaves the
  space or KiwiDesk quits. If the focused window is alone in
  its column, `"y"` reports an error.

  A bsp ratio or the master ratio that presses moved past an
  app's minimum before that minimum was learned heals back at
  the next layout pass, and a window arriving into a region
  narrower than its minimum gets the same move — the
  split-layout row of
  [accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md) has what
  remains.
- **scrolling** — adjusts the slot size in real points along
  the layout's own scroll axis (columns for horizontal, rows for
  vertical), whichever `axis` you pass — the `x`/`y` argument
  does not steer it.
- **track** — every resize has one target (#128). The axis
  **across** the tracks (`"x"` for columns, `"y"` for rows)
  grows or shrinks the focused window's whole *track*; the axis
  **along** them grows the focused window's *share within its
  track* — the same per-window weights as the stack's `"y"`
  path, with the same session-scoped lifetime and
  effective-minimum cap (#933). A single track cannot trade
  cross-axis area, and a window alone in its track has no share
  to grow; both report an error. In the track layout — and only
  there — session weights are also **healed** whenever the
  arrangement changes around them (#944): once another track
  opens or a member joins a track, the next layout pass shaves
  the largest weights just enough that every track and share
  can still hold `min_window_size`. Weights that still fit are
  never touched. A stack column's per-window weights keep only
  the write-time clamp (see the accepted limitations).

The area a layout fills, which every bound above is taken within, is the screen minus the [KiwiShelf](#kiwishelf) strip wherever a bar draws in that layout (#1517). **Where the ratio write lands (#458):** in a **session layer scoped to that space** — never the shared global, so resizing one space does not visibly resize every other space, and never a per-space override, authored or not, so what `bsp.set_ratio_h_override` or the Settings override editor set stays the number you wrote and [`reset_layout_sizing`](#reset_layout_sizing) can return to it. Session values behave like the stack's per-window weights: never saved to a profile, gone when KiwiDesk quits, reseeded from config on a real mode change, `reload_config`, `load_profile` (or any other explicit profile/preset/GUI apply), a Desktop switch or screen change that loads a *different* profile, and dropped for a field the moment you set it explicitly — its global (`bsp.set_ratio_h`, `stack.set_master_ratio`, `scroll.set_slot_size`) drops it on every space, its `_override` twin on that space — so an explicit write always shows. This covers the BSP split ratios, the stack master ratio, and the scrolling slot size — the three interactive-resize knobs — consistently. The session layer is kept per macOS Desktop and per profile live on it: a Space shown on two Desktops keeps its own sizes on each, switching profile keeps each profile's sizes for when it returns, and a Desktop where you have not resized it under the live profile uses the override, then the global. A screen connected since the last Desktop switch, or a Mac where KiwiDesk cannot read which Desktop is shown, shares one set of sizes across those Desktops ([accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md)). An in-place restart keeps every Desktop's sizes. What ends them: ```mermaid flowchart LR R["resize"] --> S[("sizes for this Space,
this Desktop, this profile")] S -->|"Desktop switch,
profile switch"| K["kept"] S -->|"load_profile"| A["cleared on the Desktops
shown now"] S -->|"Settings: saving a
stored profile"| B["that profile's,
cleared on every Desktop"] S -->|"reload_config,
a Settings save of Live"| C["all cleared"] S -->|"_override setter,
set_mode"| D["that Space's,
cleared everywhere"] S -->|"a global setter,
e.g. bsp.set_ratio_h"| F["that field,
cleared everywhere"] S -->|"reset_layout_sizing"| E["this Space here;
all: everything"] ``` **Example:** ```lua KiwiDesk.resize("x", -50) KiwiDesk.resize("y", 50) ``` A layer switch is also an event: `KiwiDesk.on("layer_change", function(from, to) … end)` hears every change of the active layer — `switch_layer`, or a profile switch returning you to `default` — and nothing for a switch to the layer already active ([Events](#events)). A config reload returns you to `default` too, but it also replaces every Lua callback, so only the CLI event stream hears that one.

sections.heading: Layer Icons
parts:
#### Layer Icons

An optional third argument to `define_layer` sets the layer's
icon — an SF Symbol name or a flat emoji. While the layer is
active, the KiwiDesk status item swaps to it, and the Space Bar
shows it as one item ahead of the Spaces; a layer without an
icon shows the first two characters of its name there,
uppercased. The default layer (`KiwiDesk.bind`) never takes an
icon — the status item shows the standard KiwiDesk glyph.

The icon also leads the layer's chip in Settings ▸ Shortcuts ▸
Layers and its Switch to row there and on KiwiHub's Shortcuts
side; a layer without one keeps the plain chip and the generic
layers symbol on its row.

Where a screen's Space Bar draws nothing at rest
([`space_bar.set_visibility`](#space_barset_visibility)), the
status item shows the Space that screen is showing instead
([User Guide ▸ Space Bar](user-guide.md#space-bar)), led by the layer's icon — or
the two-character cut of its name — the way the bar is.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.define_layer("resize", { --[[ bindings ]] },
    { icon = "arrow.left.and.right" })
KiwiDesk.define_layer("service", { --[[ bindings ]] },
    { icon = "⚙️" })
```

sections.heading: Describing a Shortcut
parts:
#### Describing a Shortcut

**Expects:** an optional third table on `KiwiDesk.bind`, or a
`{ fn = …, … }` table in place of a function in a `define_layer`
table, with any of:

- `desc` — what the shortcut does, in your words.
- `group` — the shortcut group it is listed in: a built-in
  group's token (`focus`, `move_windows`, `layout`, `size_float`,
  `kiwivision`, `kiwishelf`, `apps`) puts it there, whatever its
  case and the spaces around it; any other name makes a shortcut
  group of its own.
- `symbol` — an SF Symbol name for its row.

**Does:** KiwiHub's Shortcuts side lists the shortcut under its
description instead of its Lua, in its group, wearing its symbol.
A group of your own is listed after the built-in ones and before
Personal, under the name as written. Without a symbol a row wears
`</>`; a name that is not an SF Symbol shows `</>` too and is
listed in Config Issues, and the shortcut still works.

A shortcut whose action KiwiHub knows — `KiwiDesk.focus("left")` —
keeps its built-in name, group and symbol for each field it leaves
empty, and shows the ones it sets. An inactive or unavailable
shortcut stays in its own section whatever its group.
[`shortcut.list_groups`](#shortcutlist_groups) lists the names in
use.

A row in Settings ▸ Shortcuts ▸ Personal ▸ Lua bindings sets the
same three fields for a shortcut Settings made. A shortcut
`init.lua` binds is not listed there.

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.bind("ctrl+alt+shift+f", move_and_follow, {
  desc = "Move to the next Space and follow",
  group = "Move and follow",
  symbol = "arrow.right.square",
})
KiwiDesk.define_layer("resize", {
  ["h"] = { fn = shrink, desc = "Narrower", group = "size_float" },
})
```

sections.heading: Key Sequences
parts: ### Key Sequences

sections.heading: define_sequence
parts:
#### define_sequence

**Expects:**

- A leader: a combo (`"ctrl+alt+space"`) or a
  [modifier tap](#modifiers-and-keys) (`"cmd+cmd"`), never a Hyper
  chord.
- A table of step keys. Each value is a function, a
  `{ fn = …, name = …, desc = …, group = …, symbol = … }` table, or
  `{ name = "…", keys = { … } }`, a key that opens a further step,
  which may take a `symbol` for the panel (`folder` when absent).
  A step key is a combo; a modifier tap, a Hyper chord and a plain
  `escape` or `delete` are refused and logged.
- Optionally, a table with `name`, the leader's name, `layer`, the
  layer it belongs to (`"default"` when absent), and `desc`,
  `group` and `symbol`.

**Does:** pressing the leader opens step 1; each key then runs its
function or opens its next step. After 0.25 s a panel lists the
step's keys under the leader's name, the steps taken above them,
end keys under their `name` or `desc` in their shortcut group.
`escape` or the leader again cancels; `delete` goes back one step,
and at step 1 cancels; a click or a Space or Desktop switch
cancels. The panel opens where KiwiHub opens; past KiwiHub's
height its end keys scroll, with **↑** **↓** **Page Up** **Page
Down**, the scroll wheel, or a [`kiwihub.set_key`](#kiwihubset_key)
combo for one of those keys. A key the step does not hold leaves
the step open and plays the refusal sound while
[`set_refusal_sound`](#set_refusal_sound) is on, off by default
([#1871](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1871)).
macOS's own shortcuts still work while a sequence is open: a
screenshot, Zoom, Invert colours, contrast and Dock hiding leave the
panel up; Spotlight, Finder search, the app switcher, Force Quit,
Mission Control, Desktop switching and the next input source close
the sequence first. **⌘Q**, **⌘W**, **⌘M** and **⌘H** stay with the
sequence. A step key wins its chord over any of these, and an arrow
or page key recorded as a step key runs it rather than scrolling.

A step key matches its chord exactly, modifiers included: with
the leader's modifiers still held, `w` does not fire, and
`ctrl+alt+w` is a different key. The leader wins its chord: a
`KiwiDesk.bind` on the same chord in its layer is not registered
and is flagged. A second `define_sequence` on one leader replaces
the first. A leader on `ctrl+alt+space`, as in the example below,
takes that chord from macOS: the input source does not switch on it
while the sequence is bound. A leader works only through KiwiDesk's keyboard tap; if
macOS refuses the tap (Accessibility not granted), it does nothing
and is flagged. The CLI and an AI app build a sequence one key at a
time with [`shortcut.set_sequence_key`](#shortcutset_sequence_key);
`shortcut.remove_sequence` removes one. In Settings, Shortcuts ▸
Personal ▸ Key sequences records one.
Under Secure Input see
[Accepted Limitations](accepted-limitations.md).

**Example:**

```lua
KiwiDesk.define_sequence("ctrl+alt+space", {
  w = { name = "Windows", keys = {
    h = function() KiwiDesk.focus("left") end,
    l = function() KiwiDesk.focus("right") end,
  } },
  t = { fn = function() KiwiDesk.toggle_float() end,
        desc = "Float or tile" },
}, { name = "Leader" })
```

sections.heading: Config Cascade (Per-Profile Keybindings)
parts:
### Config Cascade (Per-Profile Keybindings)

Keybindings resolve through a two-level cascade, like tiling
(global settings ← profile):

> **The base config is the seed; the profile wins.** The base
> shortcuts (the app's `gui.json`, or your Lua-declared binds
> in a hand-written config) apply first. When the loaded
> profile carries a `"layers"` override, each of its rows
> shadows the base row with the same combo in the same layer;
> everything the profile does not mention stays active.
> Event hooks fire on their event — they are never a cascade
> layer.

The override is **sparse and soft**:

- A profile stores only the layers and rows that diverge; a
  profile without a `"layers"` key inherits the base shortcuts
  completely.
- Rebinding the same combo differently per profile stays
  possible. A base layer's icon a profile clears reverts to the
  base icon.
- Keybindings live in ONE home: the structured config (gui.json +
  profiles) when GUI-managed, or your `init.lua` otherwise —
  never merged. Hand-written binds that evade the managed-
  vocabulary detection are silently unregistered on every reload
  while GUI-managed.

A profile can also leave a base binding out: its layer entry
lists the combo under `"removed"`, and that base row is not
registered while the profile is loaded. That includes your
profile-switch shortcut — leave it in, or switch from the menu
bar.

Profiles re-resolve their bindings whenever they apply: on
`load_profile`, on a screen change, and on a Desktop binding
switch. Switching profiles also returns you to the default
layer.

sections.heading: Shortcut verbs
parts:
### Shortcut verbs

The `shortcut` table reads and writes the saved shortcuts of the
live profile from Lua, the CLI and an AI app, in the default layer. Shortcuts
load only from the saved files, so a write saves at once and the
key works straight away — the shortcut rows alone, never the rest
of the profile. A new shortcut goes into the shared base on the
loaded profile, as Settings ▸ Shortcuts starts one. With
`init.lua` owning the config, or no saved profile live, the verbs
refuse, save `shortcut.list_groups`, which reads the shortcuts in
effect.

sections.heading: shortcut.list
parts:
#### shortcut.list

**Expects:** nothing.

**Does:** returns the live `profile` and its `layers`, each with
its `name`, whether it is the `default`, and its `shortcuts` —
each `chord` and the `lua` it runs.

A shortcut that describes itself carries its `desc`, `group` and
`symbol` too ([Describing a Shortcut](#describing-a-shortcut)). It
reads the saved files, where
[`shortcut.list_groups`](#shortcutlist_groups) reads the shortcuts
in effect.

A [key sequence](#define_sequence) is listed by its leader's
`chord`, with an empty `lua`, its `label` and its `steps`: each
step key an entry of its own, a key that opens more keys carrying
its `label` and `steps` again.

sections.heading: shortcut.set
parts:
#### shortcut.set

**Expects:** a chord (`"ctrl+alt+h"`), a command's name, and that
command's arguments.

**Does:** binds the chord to one call of the command, built from
the arguments — strings, numbers and booleans. Only a command the
CLI could run is bound: never a destructive one, never `exec` or
another Lua-only verb, so the binding cannot run other Lua. A
chord another action holds, or a command already bound to another
chord, is refused; remove the old binding first.

sections.heading: shortcut.remove
parts:
#### shortcut.remove

**Expects:** a chord.

**Does:** unbinds it, from every profile holding it when it is a
shared shortcut. A chord with no shortcut is refused.

A chord that opens a key sequence is refused: remove it with
`shortcut.remove_sequence`.

**Example:**

```lua
shortcut.set("ctrl+alt+h", "focus", "left")
shortcut.remove("ctrl+alt+h")
```

sections.heading: shortcut.remove_sequence
parts:
#### shortcut.remove_sequence

**Expects:** the chord that opens a key sequence.

**Does:** removes that sequence from the default layer, with every
key under it, from every profile holding it when it is shared, and
saves at once. A chord that opens no sequence is refused.

**Example:**

```lua
shortcut.remove_sequence("ctrl+alt+space")
```

sections.heading: shortcut.set_sequence_key
parts:
#### shortcut.set_sequence_key

**Expects:** the leader chord, a path — the step keys after the
leader, as `"w,h"` or a list — a command's name, and that command's
arguments.

**Does:** binds the last key of the path to one call of the
command, built as [`shortcut.set`](#shortcutset) builds it, so it
never runs other Lua. A leader no sequence holds starts a sequence,
and a missing key on the way becomes a key that opens more keys. It
replaces nothing: a key already bound at that step, a path through
a key that runs a command, a leader chord another shortcut holds, a
Hyper leader and a step key the sequence cannot match are refused,
each with the reason.

sections.heading: shortcut.name_sequence_key
parts:
#### shortcut.name_sequence_key

**Expects:** the leader chord, a path (empty for the leader
itself), a name, and optionally an SF Symbol name.

**Does:** names the leader or the key that opens more keys, and
sets its icon when a symbol is given; an empty symbol clears it,
and a key with no icon shows `folder`. A key that runs a command is refused, and so is a symbol
that is no SF Symbol.

sections.heading: shortcut.remove_sequence_key
parts:
#### shortcut.remove_sequence_key

**Expects:** the leader chord and a path.

**Does:** removes the key at the end of the path, with every key
under it. An empty path is refused: `shortcut.remove_sequence`
removes a whole sequence.

**Example:**

```lua
shortcut.set_sequence_key("ctrl+alt+space", "w,h", "focus", "left")
shortcut.name_sequence_key("ctrl+alt+space", "w", "Windows", "macwindow")
shortcut.remove_sequence_key("ctrl+alt+space", "w,h")
```

sections.heading: shortcut.list_groups
parts:
#### shortcut.list_groups

**Expects:** nothing.

**Does:** returns `built_in`, the tokens of KiwiHub's built-in
groups, and `custom`, every shortcut group the installed shortcuts
make of their own, each once. It reads the
shortcuts in effect, so it answers with `init.lua` owning the
config too.

sections.heading: Events
parts:
## Events

Subscribe to state changes (see also the [recipes](recipes/index.md)):

```lua
KiwiDesk.on("space_change", function(space_id, mode)
    KiwiDesk.exec(
        "sketchybar --trigger space_change SPACE="
        .. space_id)
end)
```

| Event | Lua arguments |
|---|---|
| `space_change` | `space_id`, `mode` |
| `layout_change` | `space_id`, `mode` |
| `focus_change` | `window_id`, `app`, `bundle_id` |
| `monitor_change` | `monitor_count` |
| `desktop_change` | `desktop` (Desktop number now current on the screen that switched, counted across every screen), `monitor` (that screen's positional number; 1 is the main screen) |
| `window_created` | `window_id`, `app`, `space`, `reason`, `bundle_id` |
| `window_destroyed` | `window_id`, `app`, `space`, `reason`, `bundle_id`, `desktop` (the Desktop number holding a `vanished` window, counted across every screen, else `nil`) |
| `window_moved_to_space` | `window_id`, `app`, `from`, `to`, `bundle_id` |
| `layer_change` | `from`, `to` (layer names, `default` included; fires only when the layer actually changed) |

The window lifecycle events fire even when focus does not change
(a background window opening or closing). `space` is always the
space the window lives in — for `window_destroyed`, the one it
disappeared from, even when that space is not active. In the
CLI event stream the key is `space_id` (matching `space_change`)
and an unknown space is JSON `null`; the Lua callback receives
`""` instead.

Every window event also carries the owning app's `bundle_id` —
the identity key that app rules (`float_rules`, `app_rules`) and
`focus_or_spawn` match on; the display `app` name is
locale-dependent. It is the trailing Lua argument (skip it if
you don't need it), `""` for unbundled processes; in the CLI
event stream the key is `bundle_id`, JSON `null` when unknown.

When the number of screens changes, `monitor_change` fires once
the screens have stopped changing for a second (at most five
seconds after the first change), with the count they settled on. macOS briefly reports an in-between layout on
some changes, such as disconnecting an Apple Vision Pro, and the
profile is chosen only for the settled one.

`window_moved_to_space` fires on an explicit `move_to_space`
(with or without follow) when the target differs from the
window's current space. Bulk reassignments — profile loads,
session restore — stay silent. JSON keys: `from_space_id` (null
if unknown) and `to_space_id`.

The lifecycle events track the *visible window set*, not app
lifecycle: deminiaturizing surfaces as `window_created`, and
switching macOS Desktops makes every managed window on the old
Desktop vanish from the accessibility tree and reappear on
return. The `reason` argument says which kind of change fired:

- `window_created` — `"new"` (a genuinely new window),
  `"returned"` (back from another macOS Desktop, from an app that
  was unhidden, or from a session restore), `"restored"`
  (deminiaturized).
- `window_destroyed` — `"closed"` (a real close), `"minimized"`
  (it will come back as `"restored"`), `"hidden"` (its app was
  hidden, with cmd+H or by hiding itself as its last window
  closed; the window is untouched and comes back as
  `"returned"`), `"vanished"` (the window is on a macOS Desktop
  no screen is showing; it comes back as `"returned"`, and the
  sixth argument, `desktop`, names the Desktop holding it where
  the Desktop can be read — `nil` on a Mac without SkyLight).

`window_created` also reports `"existing"`: a window that was
already open when KiwiDesk began managing it — every window found
when KiwiDesk starts, and, where macOS reports windows opening, a
window it adopts later that macOS never reported opening, such as
one it lost track of and finds again.
`"restored"` wins over `"returned"`, which wins over `"existing"`;
`"new"` is everything else, KiwiDesk's own windows included. A
pocketed window that comes back after its app was hidden, or after
KiwiDesk restarted, is `"returned"`. Where KiwiDesk has to wait for
macOS to report the window opening, the event can follow the
window's `focus_change` by up to half a second; it always comes
before that window's `window_destroyed`. More reasons may be added,
so match the ones your callback handles.

A bar callback that only cares about real lifecycle filters in
one line:

```lua
KiwiDesk.on("window_destroyed",
    function(id, app, space, reason)
        if reason ~= "closed" then return end
        KiwiDesk.exec("sketchybar", {
            "--trigger", "window_closed",
        })
    end)
```

A fast app that folds its windows before the switch is noticed
still reports `"vanished"`. A window closed *while its macOS
Desktop is off-screen* is reported `"closed"` when KiwiDesk next
reads the Desktops — at the next Desktop switch, or within about
