under **Accent**, the unfocused one under **Window marks**, each
dimmed while the matching switch here is off.

**What gets no border.** Launcher and panel overlays (Spotlight,
Raycast, Alfred): never managed, never in a bar. Windows in
native (green-button) fullscreen: macOS moves such a window off
the Desktop, so the bars hide there, no layout pass or focus
raise targets it, and its space tiles as if it were away; it
keeps its slot and tiles back when it leaves fullscreen.

**The pills.** Focusing or swapping toward an edge with no window
there bounces the ring; the window never moves. A refused resize
bounces and shows a frosted pill:

- *Minimum window size reached* — the window can shrink no
  further than the configured minimum.
- *Neighboring window at its minimum size* — growing stopped
  where a neighbour would drop below its minimum; the neighbour
  marks itself.

  It also shows once, without a press, when a window arriving in
  a split cannot fit beside a neighbour already at its minimum.

- On a scrolling space, growing stops at a maximum the app
  enforces (System Settings will not grow past its own width).

Where windows that do not fit wait behind a `+n` overflow mark, a
grow along that line does not stop at the neighbour: the neighbour
joins the windows waiting and the `+n` counts it. Shrinking a window
alone on that line brings the next one back.

Where the limit is the **app's own** — a minimum or maximum the
app enforces, which KiwiDesk learns — the pill says so instead:
*This app won't go smaller*, *Neighboring app won't go smaller*,
*This app won't go bigger*. Lowering the configured minimum does
not move those.

The two neighbour pills name the neighbour's app, since that window
may be out of sight behind an overflow mark: *Neighboring Safari
window is at the minimum window size*, *Neighboring Safari window
won't go smaller*.

Running out of screen is a silent stop.

A held resize shortcut also stops silently at a limit. A fresh press
there shows the pill.

Floating windows join directional focus as a second tier: when
no tiled window lies in the pressed direction, focus reaches a
floating window that way.

sections.heading: Drag Visuals
parts:
### Drag Visuals

Releasing a dragged window over another's slot on the same
screen swaps the two. Dragging onto another screen moves it
there, live: once the cursor settles on the other screen, its
windows slide apart to open a slot, and pulling the cursor back
moves the window home. Releasing outside every slot on your own
screen snaps the window back. Floating windows show no overlay
and cannot be dropped onto a tiled slot; use *make tiled* first
([Accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md)).

A floating window dropped on another screen moves into the Space
that screen shows, and stays where you let go of it, clear of
the bars. A sticky window keeps its own Space.

A floating window keeps the size and place you give it. Only a bar
on the top edge moves one: down, at the same size, until its title
bar shows. A bar on the bottom or a side never moves it.

sections.heading: Sticky Windows
parts:
### Sticky Windows

A **sticky** window stays visible on every space. Two scopes
(stickiness is per window; there is no app-rule list):

- **Toggle sticky everywhere** — every space of every screen
  (pushpin mark).
- **Toggle sticky on this screen** — every space of its home
  screen, the one its home space is on (pushpin mark with a small
  screen). Moving it to a space on another screen re-homes it
  there.

**Toggle sticky everywhere** is a shortcut under Size & float.

**Toggle sticky on this screen** has no default key and no row
there; bind
[`toggle_display_sticky`](lua-reference.md#toggle_display_sticky)
in the Lua bindings drawer.

Moving a global sticky window anywhere, or a screen-sticky window
to another space on the same screen, is refused with a brief pill. On a single
screen the two are identical. The flag survives closing and
reopening the window and is independent of floating: a floating
sticky window keeps its frame everywhere; a tiled one tiles into
every space's layout near where it sits on its home space, keeps
a fully visible slot on a crowded space, and can be reordered or
mouse-resized only on its home space — elsewhere the gesture
snaps back and the mark expands into a pill naming the home
space. The same pill appears when you drag another window onto
its slot.

Where macOS supports it, sticky reaches across **macOS
Desktops**: switch Desktops and sticky windows come along with
the screen they are on. **Keep sticky windows visible across
Desktops** (beside the mark toggle) switches it and appears only on a macOS that can
drive Desktops; `override_sticky_reach` in Lua pins a single
window the other way. Mission Control shows a sticky window on
one Desktop at a time.

A global sticky window follows the space you focus onto its screen; when
that space is a floating-mode space on another screen, KiwiDesk
moves the window there at its last size, scaled to the screen.

The refusal pills ride the sticky **mark**: with **Show mark on
sticky windows** off, a refused move fails silently. The Space
Bar's badge shows *which* windows are sticky either way. (Lua:
`sticky.set_mark`, `space_bar.set_sticky_badge`,
[`sticky.set_color`](lua-reference.md#stickyset_color),
[`floating.set_color`](lua-reference.md#floatingset_color).)

sections.heading: KiwiShelf
parts:
## KiwiShelf

**Thickness** runs 20–80 pt on the **KiwiShelf** card; Lua
([`kiwishelf.set_thickness`](lua-reference.md#kiwishelfset_thickness))
takes any value from 20 up.

sections.heading: App Bar
parts:
### App Bar

The App Bar renders only in **Monocle** and **Scrolling**, and
its card has no on/off row.

The KiwiShelf card's **App Bar in Monocle** and **App Bar in
Scrolling** switches are its visibility.

Drag an item to reorder the windows.

Click a grouped item to list its windows; a row picks one.

Styling it differently per layout is
Lua-only: an `app_bar.*` field has a `monocle.set_app_bar_*` /
`scroll.set_app_bar_*` twin ([Per-layout App Bar
overrides](lua-reference.md#per-layout-app-bar-overrides)),
except the App Bar's edge, which every layout shares.

Whether the App Bar reserves its strip is global too
([`app_bar.set_reserve`](lua-reference.md#app_barset_reserve)).

The starter setup puts the App Bar on the bottom edge and
the Space Bar on top; set both to one edge to share one shelf.

Floating windows come last, past a thin line and the floating
symbol. They cannot be dragged; **Tile Window** on the item's
right-click menu tiles one.

**Liquid Glass** is one switch for both bars, the shortcuts
panel, the drag drop zone, and the sticky mark
(its own card in Settings); on macOS before 26 each draws its
flat look instead, the drop zone a blur.

It covers the floating mark too.

It covers the plates a Space switch slides too, and the Space,
Desktop and layout plates.

On by default, on every surface. While macOS's **Reduce
transparency** (System Settings ▸ Accessibility ▸ Display) is on,
each surface draws its look without glass — the bars their Boxed
or Plain shape with the Fill fully opaque, and no plate for a
fully transparent Fill — and the switch stays as you set it.

sections.heading: Space Bar
parts:
### Space Bar

One bar per screen, listing that screen's Spaces in profile
order. Click a Space to switch to it.

Click an app glyph to switch to its Space and focus that window.

Resting the pointer on a one-window glyph, or on an App Bar item
that cuts its title, shows that window's name beside the bar.

A glyph with a count badge, a `+n` badge and an App Bar group of
two or more windows are lists: click one to open its list beside
the bar, then click a row to switch to that window. The click on
the item switches nothing. A check marks the window that has the
focus.

An open list stays until you pick a row, click its item again,
press Escape or click elsewhere. The arrow keys walk its rows and
Return picks one.

A Space shown as its window count lists its windows when you rest
the pointer on it, since clicking it switches to that Space.

A list too long for the screen ends in **More windows**, which
opens a menu of every window. With VoiceOver, pressing the glyph
opens that menu.

A Space holding more apps than fit keeps its focused app in the
middle, with a `+n` on each side for the rest — at either end of
the row one more glyph fits instead.

A `+n` always stands for two glyphs or more: where only one would
be hidden, that glyph shows in its place.

While your pointer rests on
a Space it holds still, so a second click lands where the first
did; it re-centres once the pointer leaves. With **Windows in
other Spaces** set to *Window count*, a Space not on screen draws
no glyphs, so a click anywhere on it switches.

While a shortcut layer other than `default` is active, its icon
— or two letters of its name when it has none — leads the bar,
ahead of the Spaces ([Shortcut Layers](#shortcut-layers)).

Wherever a screen shows no Space Bar at rest, the menu bar icon
takes its place: the Space each screen is showing — its icon, or its name
where it has none — with the active layer's icon ahead of them,
and the KiwiDesk logo, or the layer's icon, back wherever the bar
shows at rest.

The bar shows the Desktop you are looking at: a window on a macOS
Desktop you are not looking at is not listed, and *Hide empty
Spaces* hides a Space holding only those. *Open or Focus* still
reaches such a window and switches Desktops to it.

A sticky window's glyph is listed under one Space only, the one
it *renders* on: a global sticky window under the Space you are
focused on, a screen-sticky window under the current Space of its
own screen.

| Mark | Where it sits | Means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Global sticky mark | On the window, top-right corner | **Global sticky** — every Space of every screen |
| Screen sticky mark | On the window, top-right corner | **Screen sticky** — every Space of its home screen |
| Floating mark | On the window, top-right corner — left of a sticky mark | A **floating** window |
| Badge, glyph's **top-left** | Space Bar | That window (or one in the group) is **sticky** |
| Badge, glyph's **bottom-left** | Space Bar | That window is **floating** |
| `+n` / count badge, glyph's **top-right** | Space Bar | How many windows a grouped glyph holds |

A window that floats only because its Space is in Floating
layout wears no floating mark. Glyphs wearing the floating badge
come last in their Space's row. The badges have no Settings
toggle; Lua hides them with `space_bar.set_sticky_badge(false)`.

A window out of the [pocket](lua-reference.md#pocket) wears the
**pocket mark** inside its top-right corner, in place of its
sticky and floating marks, and its glyph wears the **pocket badge**
on the bottom-right, beside the floating badge; that glyph comes
last in its row too.

**Drag a window onto a Space** to move it there:

- **Flick and drop** — release before the ring fills; the window
  jumps there and you stay.
- **Hold to place** — pause for the **Spring delay**; the view
  springs to that Space with the window in its live layout, so
  you can drop it exactly where you want. Move the cursor off
  the item before the ring completes to cancel. Under **Reduce
  Motion** the ring does not sweep: it stays away for the first
  half-second, then appears whole for the rest of the hold.

Dropping onto the Space a window is already on does nothing.

While dragging, hold over a bar's faded end to autoscroll a bar
that overflows.

sections.heading: Profiles
parts: ## Profiles

sections.heading: Which Profile Loads
parts:
### Which Profile Loads

The card at the top of the Profiles page answers for your
machine now — *"Right now: 2 screens →
Desk (it holds this screen setup)"* — naming which rung resolved
it; its **?** lists the rungs.

The rungs, in order:

1. A **Desktop binding** on the Desktop your main screen is on
   ([macOS Desktops](#macos-desktops-mission-control)), when
   a bound profile is saved for this many screens. With none
   the binding stands aside and the rungs below decide.
2. An **exact screen match** — these exact screens. It stops
   matching the moment you swap one out, unless you saved a set
   for the new hardware too.
3. The **default for this screen count**, whatever screens are
   plugged in. The first profile saved for a count becomes its
   default; **make default** moves it.
4. A **built-in Standard** for that screen count, or a line
   saying nothing matches.

A new hardware combination therefore uses the Standard and marks
the profile dirty until you Save on it; a profile saved for two
*different* screens sorts after your exact matches but before
one-screen profiles.

sections.heading: The Profile Banner
parts:
### The Profile Banner

The dropdown at the top of any section picks what your edits
target. Each profile is listed once: on top what is on screen —
the loaded profile, or the Standard or temporary layout in its
place — then every other profile, under a **For N screens**
heading per screen count when there is more than one.

- **The top row**: saving adopts your changes into the loaded
  profile.
- **Another profile, without switching**: Home becomes
  profile-scoped, the General card leaves the grid, and Save
  writes to that profile's JSON. Each App Rule and shortcut says
  which profiles it applies to.

Saving a profile that isn't loaded leaves the running layout
alone until it next loads, except for an App Rule or shortcut it
shares with the loaded profile ([Per-Profile Space
Assignments](#per-profile-space-assignments)). **Save a copy…**
while editing a stored profile duplicates it with your pending
edits, without touching the running layout.

The shared look is the other exception: saving a profile that
uses it changes it at once wherever it is worn, the running
layout included. A copy of such a profile whose look you changed
keeps that look as its own.

sections.heading: Saving
parts:
### Saving

**Save** writes to the current target and adds or refreshes the
connected screen setup; it is greyed when the connected screen
count differs from the profile's. A screen setup the profile has
no set for is itself an unsaved change, listed as a **Screens**
row. On a temporary layout or a built-in Standard the slot reads
**Save as New Profile…**.

Loading a profile saved for this many screens moves the connected
screen setup to it from any other profile, so the next time these
screens connect, it loads. Saving adds the connected screen setup
only when no other profile has it.

While management is **paused** (Accessibility off), KiwiDesk
detects no screens, so any save that captures the live screen
setup is unavailable. Shortcuts, app rules, float and ignore rules,
the space list and Desktop bindings carry no screen setup, so
**Save** still writes `gui.json` for them and keeps counting the
layout edits until you grant access.

The same holds before you press **Start Tiling** for the first
time: until then KiwiDesk detects no screens either.

Neither live save carries a keybinding override: to give a
profile its own shortcuts, pick it in the banner while it isn't
loaded and edit its Shortcuts page.

sections.heading: Built-in Standards & Presets
parts:
### Built-in Standards & Presets

One workflow layout per screen count is the *Standard* that
resolves silently when no saved profile matches; the starter
setup is derived from the screens you have ([Your first
run](#your-first-run)) and is offered for that count alone. Where
a preset does not name a layout for a space, the space takes the
layout its screen suits. Applying a preset saves it as a real,
editable profile; presets cannot be deleted.

Presets are picked on the setup tour's Spaces step, under **Start
with**; Profiles does not list them. Developer is the Standard at
every screen count. Over Spaces you changed, a preset replaces
only your Spaces and their layouts, and the step's **Revert** puts
them back while the tour is open.

sections.heading: App Rules
parts:
## App Rules

**The title match is case-sensitive**, and "Info" also catches
"Information"; the live window list under the chips shows what
the rule as written would float. Dialogs, sheets and
picture-in-picture windows float whatever a rule says, as do
windows of apps that remain accessory processes. For an app you
have not installed, `app_rules` in Lua takes bundle identifiers
([Finding a bundle
identifier](lua-reference.md#finding-a-bundle-identifier)).

Apps with **macOS native tabs** (Finder, Terminal, Ghostty) are
one tile per window that follows the active tab. Tabs cannot be
split into separate tiles.

sections.heading: Ignore Rules (Lua only)
parts:
### Ignore Rules (Lua only)

An ignore rule makes KiwiDesk treat every window of an app as
nonexistent — no space assignment, no window events — for HUDs,
menu-bar utilities, and apps that misbehave when AX-tracked.
There is no Settings control: add bundle ids to `ignore_rules =
{ ... }` in `init.lua`, or to the root `ignore_rules` array in
`gui.json` ([ignore_rules](lua-reference.md#ignore_rules)). An
ignore rule also opts a misbehaving tabbed app out.

sections.heading: Per-Profile Space Assignments
parts:
### Per-Profile Space Assignments

An App Rules row's **Applies to** menu picks the profiles its
rule reaches: **All profiles** keeps the rule in `gui.json`, and
otherwise a ticked profile whose value differs from the shared
one stores it in its own JSON. A new value reaches only the
ticked profiles; the others keep theirs, and the trash removes a
rule.
Removing a shared rule from one profile stores a `null` there.

A profile stores a sparse diff: `app_rules` maps apps to spaces,
while `float_rules` and `ignore_rules` are objects whose `true`
entries add rules and `null` entries remove inherited ones:

```json
{
  "app_rules": { "com.apple.mail": null },
  "float_rules": {
    "com.apple.systempreferences": null,
    "com.apple.finder:Get Info": true
  },
  "ignore_rules": {
    "eu.exelban.Stats": true,
    "com.example.inherited": null
  }
}
```

An absent entry inherits. Effective Ignore applies last as the
hard gate. Ignore has no GUI control; Settings preserves the
hidden object across saves, copies and renames.

sections.heading: Shortcuts
parts:
## Shortcuts

Every shortcut lives in a **layer**; only the active layer's
bindings fire. ("Layer", not "mode": *mode* names a space's
layout.)

> **Upgrading and every shortcut is gone?** See [The gui.json
> File](#the-guijson-file) for the `"modes"` → `"layers"` fix,
> before opening Settings.

sections.heading: Your first run
parts:
### Your first run

A fresh install seeds a setup chosen for the screens you have.
**Every screen opens in scrolling**, except the smallest, which
opens in monocle.

The slot is 85% of the screen; on an ultrawide or super
ultrawide it is 30%.

| Your screen | Gets, best first |
| --- | --- |
| Laptop (under 1900 pt wide) | scrolling · monocle |
| 2K / 4K desktop (1900–3000 pt) | grid · stack · bsp · scrolling |
| Ultrawide (3000 pt +, or 2.1:1 up to 3:1) | stack · track · grid |
| Super ultrawide (3:1 and wider, e.g. 32:9) | stack · track · grid |
| Portrait (taller than wide) | stack · grid · monocle |

Screens are measured in points, so a 5K 27" and a 1440p 27" get
the same answer. "Smallest" is read from width alone, so a 27"
beside an ultrawide opens in monocle.

The total is 3 spaces for one screen and 5 for two, three or
four, then one more per screen up to ten. Below four screens each
screen's share is proportional to its width; from four to nine,
the widest screen holds its first space and the floating one, and
every other screen one space; from ten, every screen holds one.
Away from an ultrawide, every setup with room for it gets exactly
one floating space, on the widest screen.

Only a screen holding two or more spaces opens as above. A screen
holding one opens in the first layout of its list here that no
other screen holds, or the one fewest screens hold once all are
taken: laptop monocle · scrolling, desktop grid · stack · bsp ·
scrolling, ultrawide stack · track · grid, portrait stack · grid ·
monocle.

Each layout is tuned for the screen it sits on, scrolling for
the widest screen that opens in it, and the minimum window size
follows the main screen — larger on an ultrawide or super
ultrawide main. A stack gets two mains side by side
on an ultrawide and three on a super ultrawide; on a portrait
screen its stack runs along the bottom. Scrolling on an
ultrawide or super ultrawide centres the focused window and
keeps a lone window at its slot size, and each scrolling space
scrolls the way its own screen faces — vertically on a portrait
screen.

With an ultrawide beside other screens, scrolling lives on the
ultrawide alone: every other screen holding two or more spaces
opens in monocle and ends in its own floating space, so a laptop
beside an ultrawide gets monocle · floating, and the ultrawide
scrolling · stack · floating. A screen holding one space takes its
list above, monocle in place of scrolling. From four screens the
widest ultrawide holds the two spaces and the only floating one.

While you are still on the starter setup, connecting or removing
a screen re-derives it and the `⌃⌥N` space shortcuts extend to
new spaces (up to ten).

It is saved as an ordinary profile named after your main screen
— **Ultrawide**, say, or **Widescreen + 1** across two screens —
and the same setup is always available as a preset of that name.

The tour offers the same setup as **Suggested** under **Start
with** on the Spaces step, in place of a preset of that name.

sections.heading: Default Shortcuts
parts:
### Default Shortcuts

| Action | Shortcut |
| --- | --- |
| Focus window left / down / up / right | `⌃⌥←` `⌃⌥↓` `⌃⌥↑` `⌃⌥→` |
| Go to space | `⌃⌥1` … `⌃⌥9`, then `⌃⌥0` for the tenth |
| Go to previous / next space | `⌃⌥⌘←` / `⌃⌥⌘→` |
| Go back / forward in space history | `⌥⌘Tab` / `⌥⌘⇧Tab` |
| Move to space | `⌃⌥⇧1` … `⌃⌥⇧9`, `⌃⌥⇧0` |
| Swap with window left / down / up / right | `⌃⌥⇧←` `⌃⌥⇧↓` `⌃⌥⇧↑` `⌃⌥⇧→` |
| Move to space and follow | `⌃⌥⌘1` … `⌃⌥⌘9`, `⌃⌥⌘0` |
| Grow / Shrink width | `⌥⌘2` / `⌥⌘1` |
| Grow / Shrink height | `⌥⌘5` / `⌥⌘4` |
| Toggle floating | `⌃⌥F` |
| Toggle sticky everywhere | `⌃⌥S` |
| Toggle KiwiVision | `⌃⌥V` |
| Next / previous layout | `⌃⌥C` / `⌃⌥⇧C` |
| Reset the space's sizes | `⌃⌥R` |
| Maximize the window | `⌃⌥M` |
| Pocket this window | `⌃⌥P` |
| Show / hide Space Bar, App Bar | `⌃⌥G`, `⌃⌥H` |
| Window switcher / view picker | `⌃⌥J` / `⌃⌥L` |
| Show shortcuts panel | `⌃⌥K` |

**Open Settings** ships on `⌃⌥,` as well.

`⌃⌥` moves your focus, `⇧` acts on the window — swaps it or
sends it to a space — and `⌘` steps through the spaces or sends
the window and follows. Resizing has its own layer, `⌥⌘`, which
also carries the space history on `Tab`, `⇧` stepping it the
other way as it does everywhere on macOS. A space past the tenth,
or one with a name, has no digit: the space steps and the history
reach it, and Shortcuts can give it a key of its own.

`⌃⌥C` moves the focused space to its next layout
([`cycle_mode`](lua-reference.md#cycle_mode)) and `⌃⌥⇧C` to the
previous one, `⇧` stepping back as it does on `Tab`. `⌃⌥J`, `⌃⌥K`
and `⌃⌥L` open **KiwiHub**
([`kiwihub.show`](lua-reference.md#kiwihubshow)), one panel whose
sides are listed together under Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Show & hide ▸
KiwiHub:
`⌃⌥J` the **window switcher**, `⌃⌥K` the **shortcuts panel**, where
typing searches your shortcuts, and `⌃⌥L` the **view picker**,
which switches the layout of the space under the pointer, the
profile and KiwiVision. `Tab` and `⇧Tab` step through its sides.

`⌥⇥` opens the window switcher on the app of the window you used
last, that window selected
([`kiwihub.show_last_app`](lua-reference.md#kiwihubshow_last_app)).

`⌃⌥O` opens KiwiHub's **Desktop overview**, and closes it again.
While KiwiHub has the keyboard, only a modifier tap set to one of
its sides works, as that side's shortcut does; while another
KiwiDesk panel has it, no modifier tap does.

`⌃⌥R` returns the focused space's sizes to what your profile set
([`reset_layout_sizing`](lua-reference.md#reset_layout_sizing)),
listed under Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Size & float.

`⌃⌥G` shows or hides the Space Bar and `⌃⌥H` the App Bar
([`space_bar.toggle_reveal`](lua-reference.md#space_bartoggle_reveal),
[`app_bar.toggle_reveal`](lua-reference.md#app_bartoggle_reveal)),
listed under Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Show & hide ▸ KiwiShelf.

`⌃⌥M` makes the focused window fill its screen and hides the bars
there, until you press it again or move focus to another tiled window
([`toggle_maximized`](lua-reference.md#toggle_maximized)), listed
under Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Size & float.

`⌃⌥⇧P` is **Toggle Pocket**, and `⌃⌥P` is **Pocket or take out**,
under Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Pocket
([`toggle_pocket_window`](lua-reference.md#toggle_pocket_window),
[`pocket`](lua-reference.md#pocket)). A pocketed window leaves
the screen and every bar, and comes out on the screen you are on,
floating on every Space. `⌘-Tab` to its app takes it out too, and
KiwiHub's window switcher lists it under **Pocket**.

`⌃⌥⇧⌘1` … `⌃⌥⇧⌘9`, `⌃⌥⇧⌘0` go to that macOS Desktop. Each
Desktop gets its key the first time KiwiDesk sees it, so a key you
delete stays deleted.

With **Shortcuts use** set to `✦`, these defaults sit on Hyper:
`✦` takes the place of `⌃⌥`, and Go to Desktop takes `✦⌥` + digit.
New spaces, new Desktops and later defaults land there too.

Each space digit is bound *by name* and follows a rename;
spaces past the tenth ship without a digit. The set is seeded
only while no shortcut is bound anywhere. An install that already
has shortcuts gets a later default once, at launch, where its
action has no shortcut and its key is free; **Restore…** on the
**Default shortcuts** row puts back the whole set, keeping the
shortcuts you added under **Open applications** and **Lua
bindings** except one sitting on a key a default needs; the
confirmation counts those.

**Restore…** puts the defaults back in the profile you are
editing. When another profile has changed them too, the
confirmation names it and asks whether to restore there as well.

sections.heading: Choosing Your Own Shortcuts
parts:
### Choosing Your Own Shortcuts

Three things can claim a chord, and they do not lose it the same
way:

- **macOS** wins outright: when a combo is one of its switched-on
  shortcuts, the row never fires.
- **KiwiDesk** wins against an app's menu shortcut; the app loses
  the accelerator but keeps the menu item. A shortcut with no
  menu behind it (`⌥⌘` arrows are next/previous tab in most
  browsers and terminals) costs the capability outright.

`⌃⌥` is the quiet corner macOS and most apps leave alone. `⌥`
alone types characters that vary by layout (`⌥L` is `¬` on a US
keyboard, `@` on a German one); adding `⌃` or `⌘` stops that.
Arrows and digits keep their place on every layout; letters do
not.

sections.heading: Conflict Detection
parts:
### Conflict Detection

The ⚠️ on a row means it duplicates another row in the same
layer or collides with a macOS shortcut. **Those two are the
whole of it**: KiwiDesk cannot see what other apps have bound, so
the safest test of a chord is to bind it and open the app you
would miss it in. A collision with a switched-off macOS shortcut
(Zoom, Invert Colors) keeps the ⚠️ but does not count toward the
banner. A collision with a shortcut every app carries (⌘W, ⌘Q,
⌘H, ⌘M) means your row works and every app loses that item while
it is bound.

It also marks a row whose keys other rows take on each side, so
it never runs.

The recorder **suspends your KiwiDesk shortcuts while it is
open**, so a combo already bound to a window action is recorded
instead of firing.

A recording, a clear or a deleted row takes effect when you
Save, like every other setting; Revert discards it.

sections.heading: Keyboard Modifiers & Keys
parts:
### Keyboard Modifiers & Keys

The spelling a stored combo uses (`gui.json`, Lua):

**Modifiers**: `cmd`/`command`, `alt`/`opt`/`option`,
`ctrl`/`control`, `shift`, and `hyper` (`✦`, live once a Hyper
key is set; see [`set_hyper_key`](lua-reference.md#set_hyper_key)).

**Keys**: letters (a–z), digits (0–9), arrows, `home`, `end`,
`pageup`, `pagedown`, `space`, `return`, `tab`, `escape`,
`f1`–`f12`, and punctuation by symbol or name:
`;`/`semicolon`, `,`/`comma`, `.`/`period`, `/`/`slash`,
`\`/`backslash`, `-`/`minus`, `=`/`equal`, `[`/`leftbracket`,
`]`/`rightbracket`, `` ` ``/`grave`/`backtick`,
`'`/`quote`/`apostrophe`.

The numeric keypad's digits are the same keys as the number row.
Its other keys are separate: `keypadplus`, `keypadminus`,
`keypadmultiply`, `keypaddivide`, `keypaddecimal`,
`keypadequals`, `keypadenter`, `keypadclear`. A third-party PC
keypad sends digits only while Num Lock is on.

A combo is one set of modifiers plus exactly one key; multi-key
chords like `cmd+j+k` are not supported — use layers. KiwiDesk
binds the physical key, so switching input sources changes what
the caps print, not which key fires.

A key sequence — a leader chord, then one key after another — is
recorded in Shortcuts ▸ Personal ▸ Key sequences, or written with
[`define_sequence`](lua-reference.md#define_sequence).

A combo can also be a modifier tapped alone, `cmd+cmd` or `rcmd`
([Modifiers and Keys](lua-reference.md#modifiers-and-keys)).

sections.heading: Actions
parts:
### Actions

- **macOS Desktop rows** sit in their own **macOS Desktops**
  section, one per Desktop you have, on every screen: Go to
  Desktop ships bound, and the moves, under **Move windows to a
  macOS Desktop**, ship unbound. They appear only where macOS
  exposes the window-management bridge
  ([macOS Desktops](#macos-desktops-mission-control)). A bound
  row whose Desktop leaves with its screen stays in place,
  dimmed, and works again when the screen is back; a Desktop
  shortcut for an absent Desktop does nothing, while a Space
  shortcut for an absent Space still works: it recreates the
  Space and switches to it. Each row sends the window to the Desktop and nothing
  more; naming the Space it lands in is a Lua/CLI argument,
  `move_to_desktop(3, "mail")` ([Lua
  reference](lua-reference.md#move_to_desktop)).
- **Resize** — a window outside tiling (floated by you, or in a
  Floating space) resizes its own frame in any layout. Held, a
  resize shortcut glides: the first press is one step; after
  your Mac's key-repeat delay the window resizes smoothly, faster
  over the next couple of seconds, scaled to your resize step.
  A floating window grows around its centre;
  an edge against the screen edge or a bar stays put and the
  whole step goes to the other side. Floats are held clear of a
  bar and the screen edge by the focus ring's width.
- **Applications** — *Open or Focus* focuses a running app's
  window or launches the app, and pressing again cycles its
  windows; which window each press reaches is in
  [`focus_or_spawn`](lua-reference.md#focus_or_spawn). Add the
  same app twice to bind one shortcut per behaviour.

A floating window's resize and move shortcuts run under a bar on
the bottom or a side to the screen's edge; only a bar on the top
edge stops them.

The verb behind *Open or Focus* is now `focus_or_spawn`, formerly
`pull_or_spawn`; shortcuts made here are updated for you.

A window that fills its whole screen — a slide show, a
borderless-fullscreen game or player — is not held clear of the
bars: it stays where its app put it, and both bars hide while it
is in front ([limitations](accepted-limitations.md)).

sections.heading: Import & Adopt
parts:
### Import & Adopt

If `init.lua` holds custom keybindings, **Import from
init.lua…** (Shortcuts ▸ Built-in ▸ Default shortcuts) reads them for
review before you Save; each binding must be an inline
`function() … end` on one line. **Adopt into the GUI** imports
the whole file's managed settings and keeps your custom Lua live.

Import and Adopt bring in one key per action: a key is left out
when its action already has one, on the Shortcuts page or earlier
in `init.lua` — a Space keeps its own digit where it has one — and
that row names each key left out.

sections.heading: Shortcut Layers
parts:
### Shortcut Layers

The **+** beside the layer chips defines a layer: a name, an
optional icon, and bindings that shadow the base
shortcuts while it is active. Every layer gets its own `⌃⌥K`
row. Switch layers with `KiwiDesk.switch_layer` ([Lua
reference](lua-reference.md)).

Each binding's **Applies to** says which profiles use it: **All
profiles**, or the profiles ticked. **Remove from** one profile
turns a shared shortcut off there and keeps it everywhere else,
and a profile can put a shared shortcut on another key of its
own. Ticking a profile that uses the key for something else
gives the key to this shortcut there.

A key sequence's **Applies to** is on its first key's row and
covers the whole sequence. Where a sequence and a shortcut would
share one key in a profile, that profile cannot be ticked: the key
is never taken over.

A new layer also carries the `⌃⌥,` Open Settings row.

sections.heading: macOS Desktops (Mission Control)
parts:
## macOS Desktops (Mission Control) **Profiles ▸ Profiles per macOS Desktop** lists the Desktops on your **main screen** by their Mission Control number. How Desktops are numbered is in [Spaces & Desktops](spaces-and-desktops.md#how-desktops-are-numbered). A Desktop you bound that is not on your main screen carries a **not on main screen** badge and cannot fire until a screen change makes it the main screen's; a Desktop that is not there at all carries **not present** ([Accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md)). A binding stays on the Desktop you gave it when Mission Control renumbers — [A binding follows its Desktop, not its number](spaces-and-desktops.md#a-binding-follows-its-desktop-not-its-number). Under a row, the screen its Desktop is on — for a *not present* row, the screen it was last seen on. With profiles saved for more than one screen count, the card groups its rows by count, and a pick in a group binds a profile for that count alone ([a binding fires only for its profile's screen count](spaces-and-desktops.md#the-main-screen-chooses-the-profile)). A bound name no saved profile carries sits in a last *Couldn't load* group; None clears it. **A binding fires when its Desktop becomes current on your main screen** (the one with the menu bar) and it holds a profile saved for your screen count ([Which Profile Loads](#which-profile-loads)). With "Displays have separate Spaces" on, macOS's default, each screen switches on its own: a swipe on the main screen switches profiles, a swipe on a secondary never does. A Save while editing a stored profile keeps a binding change too. ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Your main screen switches
to a macOS Desktop"] --> B{"A profile bound
to this Desktop
for these screens?"} B -->|"Yes"| A["That profile activates —
its layout, gaps, and rules"] B -->|"No binding, or
not for these screens"| K["The current profile
stays active"] P["You pick a profile
by shortcut or menu"] --> A ``` A hand-written config declares bindings in `init.lua` with `bind_profile_to_desktop`. Each Desktop remembers which space it was on, on every screen, and your main screen's Desktops remember which window you had focused. A window that takes more than a few seconds to come back keeps whatever macOS focused ([Accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md)). Where macOS exposes its window-management bridge (present on macOS 26.6.1, checked 2026-08-18), KiwiDesk can also **drive** Desktops: `focus_desktop(n)`, `move_to_desktop(n)` and `move_to_desktop_and_follow(n)` ([Lua reference](lua-reference.md#focus_desktop)). Where it is absent the commands do nothing and log why; KiwiDesk never asks you to turn SIP off.

sections.heading: Getting Help
parts:
## Getting Help

For Lua configuration, see [lua-reference.md](lua-reference.md);
for integration recipes (sketchybar, external commands, …),
[recipes](recipes/index.md); for the CLI, [cli.md](cli.md).

To check your current state in raw form:
```
kiwidesk get_state
kiwidesk get_profile_status
```

To reload your config after editing `init.lua` by hand:
```
kiwidesk reload_config
```

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
parts:
## Troubleshooting

**Accessibility permission missing?**  
Window management pauses: the menu bar icon shows a warning
triangle and the quick menu's **Window Management Paused…** row
reopens the permission tour. Add KiwiDesk under System Settings ›
Privacy & Security › Accessibility; management resumes on its
own.

**Permission granted, but nothing is tiled?**  
Granting Accessibility does not start tiling on its own: the
first time, press **Start Tiling** — in the permission tour, the
quick menu or the banner at the top of Settings.

**Settings window won't open, or KiwiDesk seems stuck?**  
Run `kiwidesk service restart` in a terminal, or quit and reopen
KiwiDesk. Launching KiwiDesk while a copy is already running
never starts a second one: the second launch brings the running
instance forward and exits with `already running`.

**Windows come back in the wrong spaces after a restart or wake?**  
**General ▸ Files & Reset ▸ Saved window arrangement ▸ Discard**
clears the remembered arrangement without changing settings.
**All settings ▸ Reset…** below it is the last resort: it deletes every
profile, your spaces, layouts and keybindings and reseeds the
defaults, keeping `init.lua`, your palettes, the display language,
the login item and onboarding; the old files go to the Trash.

**Reporting a bug?**  
**General ▸ Files & Reset ▸ Log**: pick a time range and press
**Export…** to save KiwiDesk's log for it to a file. Make the
problem happen again first: the range counts back from now, and
"since KiwiDesk started" means this run. The file names the apps
and windows KiwiDesk managed, so glance through it before
attaching it. The terminal form is in the [CLI
reference](cli.md#exporting-the-log).

**Report a problem**, at the foot of Home and of the Simple page,
opens a GitHub bug report with your KiwiDesk and macOS versions,
screen count and Desktop mode filled in. The exported log also
lists the settings you changed.

**Shortcut not working?**  
Check Shortcuts for a ⚠️ marker ([Conflict
Detection](#conflict-detection)). If you hand-edited, run
`kiwidesk reload_config`.

**Typo in init.lua?**  
A misspelled function name (`scroll.set_width` for
`scroll.set_slot_size`) does not abort the config: the call is
skipped with a did-you-mean hint and the rest still runs. Every
typo is listed under menu bar › Config Issues….

**Windows aren't tiling?**  
Ensure the space's layout is not Floating and the app is not in
float_rules. On a hand-written config, make sure `init.lua`
exists and the app is managing tiling (check the banner).

**Profile not loading after a screen change?**  
See [Which Profile Loads](#which-profile-loads): a new hardware
combination uses the built-in Standard until you Save on it.

pages.title: Spaces & Desktops
pages.description: How your screens, macOS's Desktops, KiwiDesk's profiles and KiwiDesk's Spaces fit together — and which of them owns what.

sections.heading: Spaces & Desktops
parts:
# Spaces & Desktops

Two systems are stacked here, and they use two different words.

- **Desktops** are **macOS's**. Mission Control labels them
  "Desktop 1", "Desktop 2", …; you swipe or press Ctrl+arrow
  between them, and macOS decides which windows live on which.
- **Spaces** are **KiwiDesk's**. A Space is a named group of
  windows with a layout of its own — `focus_space("mail")`, the
  Space Bar, the Spaces list in Settings.

Neither is built out of the other. macOS decides which windows
exist for you right now; KiwiDesk arranges the ones it can see
and keeps its own Spaces on top.

sections.heading: The picture
parts:
## The picture ```mermaid flowchart TD S["Screen
(the main one has the menu bar)"] --> D["macOS Desktop
Mission Control's Desktop 2"] D -->|"main screen only,
and only where you bound one"| P["Profile
one at a time, for the whole desk"] P --> SP["Spaces
KiwiDesk's — one list per profile"] SP -->|"pinned, or placed for you"| S D -.->|"remembers the Space
it last showed"| SP ``` Four facts: a profile owns Spaces, Spaces are placed on screens, a Desktop can *choose* a profile, and a Desktop *remembers* a Space.

sections.heading: Spaces belong to a profile, and sit on screens
parts:
## Spaces belong to a profile, and sit on screens

The Space list is part of the **profile**, with its layout
modes, gaps, borders and rules. Whenever a different profile
becomes live — loaded by you, or arriving on its own from a
Desktop binding or a screen change — its Space list becomes the
authority. A Space's name is what makes it that Space: when both
profiles have a `1`, it stays on screen and takes the new
profile's settings. Re-applying the profile that is already
live changes nothing, so a screen reconnect is harmless.

**Switching holds the Spaces it does not name.** When a
different profile or a built-in Standard becomes live, each Space
it does not have, and that still has windows in it, is **held**
for the profile you left instead of being dropped — whether its
screen was unplugged or is still there. A window the new profile
has had before goes back to the Space it had it in, so a held
Space keeps only windows that profile has never seen, and one
left empty goes away.

**Unplugging a screen holds its Spaces.** When unplugging a
screen makes a different profile live, each Space that was on
that screen and still has windows in it is carried onto a
remaining screen instead of being dropped. Where the new profile
has a Space of its name, it takes the next number past the
highest one in use, so a held `3` beside
your own `1`–`5` becomes `6`, and a held `Mail` beside your own
`Mail` becomes a number too. A held Space moves to a new number
again whenever a profile that loads uses its current one.

Where KiwiDesk manages your config, a Space missing its go-to,
move or move-and-follow digit shortcut gets it for its own number —
a held `6` gets `⌃⌥6` — if that key is still free. Any other Space
takes the digit of its place among the first ten, unless a
numbered Space owns that digit. A Space never gets a second
digit shortcut for the same thing, and reordering your Spaces never
changes them.

Held Spaces keep the order they had: when a screen's Spaces are
held, a numbered Space after a renumbered one is renumbered after
it too, so the Space Bar and the digit shortcuts list them in the
order the screen had them. A later renumber keeps the Space Bar in
that order.

The Space Bar draws a two-screen marker after a held Space's
identifier, and VoiceOver reads the profile it was held from, the
screen it came from, its old name when it was renumbered, and that
it is not saved: saving a profile never includes a held Space. A
Space held from a built-in Standard names only its screen.

A Space you make on the fly — **New Space** on a Space's
right-click menu, `create_space`, or `focus_space` and
`move_to_space` naming a Space that does not exist — is
**temporary**. It wears an hourglass marker, lasts through a
restart, a reload and a Settings Save, and goes away when its
last window leaves it. No save writes it into the profile until
you choose **Add Space ‹n› to this profile** in Settings ▸
Spaces, or save the profile under a name with `save_profile`.
Switch to another profile while it holds windows and it is held
like any other Space, and comes back temporary; an empty one goes
away on the switch.

An empty temporary Space also goes away once you have switched to
it and then left it with nothing in it, so a Space shortcut that
made one by mistake leaves nothing behind. Temporary Spaces sit
in the Space Bar in number order.

Plug the screen back in and a held Space goes back to it with
everything in it, windows opened while it was held included, when
what comes back is the profile (or built-in Standard) it left and
that has a Space of the held one's original name. Otherwise it
moves back onto its screen and stays held.

A held Space goes away once no window is left in it; a window on
another Desktop, or hidden with its app, still counts. Loading a
profile does not end a hold, and neither does a Desktop binding:
it ends when the profile or Standard it left comes back and has
a Space of its original name, when it empties, or when you reset
every setting. `delete_space` moves its windows to the fallback
Space (`set_fallback_space`), which empties it.

Held Spaces come back when KiwiDesk quits and reopens, updates or
crashes — a window hidden, on another Desktop or still opening
included — and go home at once, as above, if their screen is back
by then. A restart of the Mac ends them, since a held Space names
its windows by ids a restart retires and no restore re-keys a
hold. A window of a hidden app goes home with its
held Space too, and comes back there when you show the app.

Every Space sits on a screen. In Settings the **Screens**
section is a picture of your desk: drag a Space chip onto the
screen it belongs to, or leave it outlined and KiwiDesk places
it for you. From Lua the same pin is
`pin_space_to_display("mail", 2)`.

Each screen shows **one** of its Spaces at a time — with two
screens, two Spaces are on show at once. The Spaces no screen is
showing are parked (see [Parking is not a Desktop
move](#parking-is-not-a-desktop-move)).

sections.heading: Every Desktop keeps its own Space, and its own windows
parts: ## Every Desktop keeps its own Space, and its own windows Every Desktop remembers which Space it was on. Switch away and back and you land on the same Space, with the same windows in the same order and the same one focused — as long as they come back promptly ([accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md) has the case where they do not). Where KiwiDesk owns your config and can give a Desktop an identity of its own, that memory survives quitting KiwiDesk; a hand-written `init.lua` setup keeps it for the session only. That memory is kept on this Mac alone, in `~/Library/Application Support/KiwiDesk/machine.json`. **Your windows stay with their Desktop.** A Space holds whatever of its windows are on the Desktop you are looking at. Switch Desktop and the same Space shows you that Desktop's windows instead — nothing is moved, and nothing is lost. A Desktop you have never visited takes a Space no other Desktop is **showing or remembers**; when every Space is spoken for it takes the first. With **Displays have separate Spaces** on, each screen switches Desktops on its own, and each moves only its own Space — swiping the external screen leaves the built-in one alone.

sections.heading: A binding gives a Desktop a different set of Spaces
parts:
## A binding gives a Desktop a different set of Spaces

Bind a profile to a Desktop — the **Profiles per macOS Desktop**
card in Settings, or `bind_profile_to_desktop(2, "Creator
Studio")` in Lua — and activating that Desktop loads that
profile, with its Spaces, layouts and settings. A binding
changes *which Spaces exist at all*: two Desktops bound to
different profiles offer you different lists, while two bound to
the same profile offer the same list and still keep their own
windows in it.

**Desktops without a binding keep whatever profile is active.**

sections.heading: The main screen chooses the profile
parts:
## The main screen chooses the profile

KiwiDesk runs **one** profile across the whole desk, so a
binding fires when its Desktop becomes current on your **main**
screen — the one with the menu bar. A swipe on a secondary
screen re-tiles the windows that arrived with it and moves that
screen onto its own Desktop's Space, but never selects a profile.
With a single screen, the main screen's Desktop is simply *the*
Desktop.

The profile it loads applies to every screen, so a second screen
can change Space too, even though its Desktop did not. A Space
both profiles have stays on screen; for one that still has windows
and that the new profile lacks, see [Switching holds the Spaces it
does not name](#spaces-belong-to-a-profile-and-sit-on-screens).

A Desktop you bound that is not on your main screen keeps its
row in the card, with a *not on main screen* badge; the binding
goes live again if a screen change makes that Desktop your main
screen's.

**A binding fires only for its profile's screen count.** A
Desktop holds a profile per screen count, so the same Desktop
can load a one-screen profile undocked and a two-screen one
docked: the profile saved for as many screens as are connected
fires, and the others wait until that many are. A Desktop bound
only to a one-screen profile stands aside on two, and KiwiDesk
picks by your screens ([Which Profile
Loads](user-guide.md#which-profile-loads)).

**A binding can also be for one screen setup.** Within a screen
count, a Desktop can hold a profile for each particular set of
screens you name, beside the one for all its other setups: with
exactly those screens connected, that set's profile loads; any
other setup of the count loads the one for all setups. Either
loads over a profile saved for exactly those screens.

sections.heading: How Desktops are numbered
parts: ## How Desktops are numbered With "Displays have separate Spaces" on and more than one screen, Mission Control numbers every Desktop in one count across your screens, the screen it lists first counted first: with six Desktops on the built-in screen and two on a second one, the second screen's read Desktop 7 and Desktop 8. A command or a binding takes that number: [`focus_desktop`](lua-reference.md#focus_desktop), `move_to_desktop`, `bind_profile_to_desktop`, and the **Go to Desktop N** shortcuts, as macOS's own "Switch to Desktop N" does. KiwiDesk shows that same number: KiwiHub's window switcher, the Desktop switch plate and the Desktop rows in Settings. A KiwiHub row for a window on another screen names that screen too — `Work · DELL U2723 · Desktop 7` — and the plate's dots still show the Desktops of the screen that switched. With more than one screen, Settings ▸ Shortcuts and KiwiHub's Shortcuts side name the screen each Desktop row reaches right now. A Settings row for a Desktop that is not present keeps the number it was last seen at.

sections.heading: A binding follows its Desktop, not its number
parts:
## A binding follows its Desktop, not its number

Desktops are numbered by **position**: add a Desktop
before a bound one, delete one, drag them around in Mission
Control, plug a screen in or unplug it, and everything after the
change is renumbered.

A binding is not stored against that number. KiwiDesk writes a
small private identifier into each Desktop's own settings the
first time it sees it, and files the binding under **that**. A
Desktop keeps its profile when the numbers shift, the Desktop
that inherits its old number does not inherit its profile, and
the card's rows re-label themselves to the new numbers.

Deleting the Desktop deletes the identifier with it. That
binding shows a *not present* badge and does nothing until you
point it somewhere else — it is never fired for a different
Desktop.

**Unplugging a screen:** the first Desktop of the unplugged
screen merges into the one you are on and is gone, and the rest
move over to the remaining screen at new numbers. Their
identifiers travel with them, so their bindings keep working.
The merged one goes quiet; plugging the screen back in restores
it, identifier and all, and its binding comes back with it.

On a Mac where KiwiDesk cannot write the identifier, bindings
key by the Desktop's number — the behaviour above minus
the protection.

A binding follows its **profile** the same way: it names the
profile by an identifier the profile file keeps, so renaming the
profile — on this Mac or on another one syncing your config
folder — keeps the binding. Delete the profile and the binding
moves under *Missing profiles* in the card; a new profile under
the old name does not take it over. A binding written in
`init.lua` names its profile on every load and follows the name.

sections.heading: "Displays have separate Spaces" decides the nesting
parts: ## "Displays have separate Spaces" decides the nesting This macOS switch (System Settings ▸ Desktop & Dock) changes which of *screen* and *Desktop* is the outer level, and KiwiDesk follows it either way: | The macOS setting | The shape | What it means here | |---|---|---| | **On** (macOS's default) | Screen → Desktop → Space | Each screen has its own Desktops and switches them on its own. A binding applies only on your main screen's Desktops. | | **Off** | Desktop → Screen → Space | One Desktop set spans every screen, so all screens switch together and every Desktop is bindable. |

sections.heading: Parking is not a Desktop move
parts:
## Parking is not a Desktop move

When a Space is not being shown on any screen, KiwiDesk **parks**
its windows: it moves them into a bottom corner of their own
screen, leaving a hair of each at the edge, and moves them back
when their Space is shown again. The same park holds the windows
a Stack, Track, Grid or BSP layout cannot fit, which wait off
screen until they scroll in, and, under
`monocle.set_hide_style("park")`, the windows Monocle is not
showing.

**A parked window has not gone anywhere.** It is still on the
same macOS Desktop, still in the same KiwiDesk Space, still
listed in `get_state`. Parking is how a Space is hidden; it is
never how a window changes Desktop.

The only things that move a window between Desktops are macOS
itself and the two verbs that ask it to: `move_to_desktop` and
`move_to_desktop_and_follow`. A window
sent to another Desktop leaves KiwiDesk's view and rejoins its
Space when that Desktop is next shown — a tiled window on another
screen, the Space that screen shows then — or the Space you named,
when you named one. It is reported gone with `reason: vanished`,
the same value a plain Desktop swipe produces.

A window on a hidden Desktop can be moved too, by naming its id from
`get_state`. With *Displays have separate Spaces* off, naming a Space
on another screen moves it there in the same command; the
[Lua reference](lua-reference.md#move_to_desktop) has the limits.

KiwiDesk keeps knowing it is there, but does not draw it. The
Space Bar shows the Desktop you are looking at, so a window on
another Desktop leaves the bar, and *Hide empty Spaces* hides a
Space holding only such windows. *Open or Focus* still finds it:
it switches to that Desktop and gives the window the focus.

sections.heading: With more than one screen
parts: ### With more than one screen KiwiDesk parks in the bottom-right corner of the window's own screen, and in the bottom-left corner when a screen sits to the right and none to the left. A screen counts as beside it when any part of it lies level with this screen. A parked window's top sits about 48 pt above the bottom of the screen's usable area (above a bottom Dock), a strip 1 pt wide shows, and the rest hangs down and out past that corner. Keep the corner KiwiDesk picks clear, with no screen beside it or below it; otherwise its parked windows show on that screen. A screen between two taller screens parks bottom-right, where the right-hand screen reaches below it. Raising the right-hand screen in System Settings ▸ Displays until its bottom sits more than about 48 pt above that corner clears it; raising the left-hand one changes nothing while both sides still have a screen. Parking on another screen's free corner is not an option ([Accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md)). AeroSpace's [proper monitor arrangement guide](https://nikitabobko.github.io/AeroSpace/guide#proper-monitor-arrangement) shows the same rule with more arrangements.

sections.heading: Every profile keeps its own arrangement
parts:
## Every profile keeps its own arrangement

Two profiles can each define a Space called `1` — or `Work` —
and it is one Space, which wears the settings of the profile that
is live. Where your windows go is each profile's own: KiwiDesk files
which Space each window was in under the profile you are leaving
and puts them back when you return. Give two Spaces different
names to keep them apart.

The full rules are in the [Lua reference](lua-reference.md)
▸ *Space Reconciliation*.

pages.title: CLI & IPC Reference
pages.description: Every command, the event stream, and the raw socket protocol.

sections.heading: CLI & IPC Reference
parts:
# CLI & IPC Reference

One binary is both the app and the CLI:

```sh
kiwidesk                      # run the window manager
kiwidesk <command> [args...]  # send a command to the app
kiwidesk help                 # local usage
kiwidesk --version            # local version (no app needed)
kiwidesk list_commands        # every command, grouped
kiwidesk help <name>          # one command's arguments
```

> The Homebrew cask and the Nix package put it on your `PATH` as
> lower-case `kiwidesk`, which every example here uses. A source build
> produces `.build/release/KiwiDesk` instead — same commands, so
> substitute that path for `kiwidesk` throughout. The capitalized
> `KiwiDesk` elsewhere on this page is the Lua global, the config
> directory, or the product name.

**Installed from the `.dmg`?** The app bundle carries the same
executable; the cask only links it onto your `PATH`. Do that once
yourself:

```sh
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/bin
sudo ln -sf /Applications/KiwiDesk.app/Contents/MacOS/KiwiDesk \
  /usr/local/bin/kiwidesk
```

The `mkdir` is there because `/usr/local/bin` may not exist on a
Mac that has never had Homebrew. Link, never copy: a copy fails
its signature check.

A directory you own works without `sudo` as long as your shell
already searches it; `~/.local/bin` is **not** on the macOS
default `PATH`, so it needs adding first.

Commands are sent over a UNIX domain socket at
`~/Library/Application Support/KiwiDesk/KiwiDesk.sock`.

Exit code is 0 on success, 1 on error; data goes to stdout, the
error message — and, on some successes, a note — to stderr.

Data on stdout is JSON with its object keys **sorted**, indented
when stdout is a terminal and compact — one line — when it is
piped or redirected. `subscribe` is unaffected either way: its
stream is newline-delimited JSON, one event per line, whatever
stdout is.

sections.heading: Version
parts:
## Version

```sh
kiwidesk --version   # or -v; works without the app running
```

Prints `<semantic version> (<short commit>)`, e.g. `0.1.0
(abc1234)`, or just the semantic version when the commit is
unknown: only a release build knows its commit, so a build you
make yourself prints the bare version. The same information is
available over IPC/Lua as the `version` command — see the table
below.

sections.heading: Discovering Commands
parts:
## Discovering Commands

```sh
kiwidesk list_commands              # every command, grouped
kiwidesk help scroll.set_anchor     # one command in full
kiwidesk list_commands --json       # the same, machine-readable
```

Both work **without the app running**: the listing describes the
API the binary was built with, carries no app state, and asks
nothing over the socket.

`list_commands` prints one block per group: the `KiwiDesk` table
first (the commands a keybinding usually names), then each layout
and bar namespace. Every line carries the command's arguments and
a one-line summary:

```
scroll
  set_anchor <anchor>                Sets where the focused …
  set_orientation <orientation>      Sets whether columns scroll …
  set_slot_size_override <space> <size>   Overrides the slot …
```

Required arguments are in `<angle brackets>`, optional ones in
`[square brackets]`. A command the CLI cannot reach is marked:
`(lua only)` for the entry points that live on the Lua table
alone (`bind`, `on`, `exec`, …), `(cli only)` for the commands
a config never calls, such as `subscribe`.

Naming one command prints its full signature, including the legal
values of an enum argument and the Swift type they come from:

```
$ kiwidesk help scroll.set_anchor
scroll.set_anchor <anchor>

  Sets where the focused window comes to rest in the viewport.

arguments:
  anchor        choice
                  center | start | end | follow
                  (ScrollingParams.Anchor)

  lua: scroll.set_anchor(anchor)
  cli: kiwidesk scroll.set_anchor <anchor>
```

Those values are **read from the decoder that accepts them**, so
the listing cannot fall behind the code.

A misspelled name fails with a suggestion and exit code 1:

```
$ kiwidesk help focsu
error: unknown command: focsu (did you mean focus?)
```

Unlike the did-you-mean hint on an unknown *command*, this one
will point at a Lua-only name.

**Text or JSON.** A terminal gets the text above; a pipe or a
redirect gets JSON. `--json` forces JSON either way. An
unrecognised option is an error, not a silent no-op.

`list_commands` returns `{"commands": <count>, "groups": [...]}`,
each group carrying one object per command — `name`,
`qualified_name`, `group`, `command`, `channel`, `summary`,
`aliases`, and an `arguments` array whose enum entries add
`values`.

Each command object also carries `destructive`: `true` for a
command that cannot be undone
([Using KiwiDesk from AI Apps](#using-kiwidesk-from-ai-apps)).

Each command object carries `kind`: `action` for a command that
does something, `setting` for one that changes a value, `query`
for one that only answers. `--kind action`, `--kind setting` or
`--kind query` keeps only that kind, in text or JSON:

```sh
kiwidesk list_commands --kind action
```

`--kind` lists; with a command name it is an error. The
[Actions](commands.md) page lists every action a key can run.

The Swift type an enum's values were read from is **not** a JSON
field; it appears in the terminal rendering only. `values` is
what answers "what may I send".

Bare `kiwidesk help` (and `--help` / `-h`) still prints the short
usage block. Add a name, or `--json`, to get the API instead.

sections.heading: Shell Completion
parts:
## Shell Completion

`kiwidesk completion zsh`, `bash` or `fish` prints a completion
script. It completes command names, an argument's legal values,
event names, and — while the app runs — Space ids, window ids,
profile names and look names. The script asks the binary for every
answer, so it never needs regenerating after an upgrade.

```sh
# zsh: add to ~/.zshrc, after compinit
source <(kiwidesk completion zsh)
# bash: add to ~/.bash_profile
eval "$(kiwidesk completion bash)"
# fish
kiwidesk completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/kiwidesk.fish
```

sections.heading: Using KiwiDesk from AI Apps
parts:
## Using KiwiDesk from AI Apps

`kiwidesk mcp` runs a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io)
server on stdin and stdout, so an AI app that launches local MCP
servers — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex — can drive
KiwiDesk. Point the app at the binary inside the bundle; most apps
take this entry, and one with its own config format takes the same
`command` and `args`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "kiwidesk": {
      "command": "/Applications/KiwiDesk.app/Contents/MacOS/KiwiDesk",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Settings ▸ AI ▸ Other AI apps ▸ **Copy Setup Prompt** puts a short
prompt carrying this entry, with the path of the copy you are
running, on the clipboard: paste it into the AI app, which adds
the server itself or walks you through it. The same page has
ready-made prompts that have the AI app ask you what you want, one
question at a time.

**Add…** in the Claude Desktop row of the same page builds a Claude
Desktop extension for the copy you are running and opens it in Claude
Desktop, which asks you to install it. The extension starts that
copy, so after moving KiwiDesk add it again.

In Claude Code, the KiwiDesk plugin adds the server and a skill
(`/kiwidesk:drive`) on how to change things live and keep them:

```sh
/plugin marketplace add KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk-Claude
/plugin install kiwidesk@kiwidesk
```

It finds KiwiDesk in `/Applications`, in `~/Applications` or as
`kiwidesk` on your `PATH`.

The server speaks MCP `2026-07-28` and, after an `initialize`,
`2025-11-25` and `2025-06-18`. It offers these tools:

| Tool | Does |
|---|---|
| `list_commands` | Every command the tools can send, filtered by name, group or summary, the destructive ones marked |
| `help` | One command's arguments, as `kiwidesk help <name> --json` returns them |
| `get_state` | `get_state`'s answer |
| `run` | One command that can be undone |
| `run_batch` | Up to 100 commands in order, stopping at the first failure |
| `run_destructive` | One command that cannot be undone |
| `keep` | Makes this session's setting changes permanent |
| `looks` | The `look.*` verbs as one tool: list, inspect, wear and save looks |
| `app_rules` | The `app_rule.*` verbs as one tool: list app rules, and set or remove which Space an app opens in and which windows float |
| `diagnose_window` | Why a window floats, tiles or opens where it does: `explain_window` for a window, `explain_app` for an app whose window KiwiDesk does not manage |
| `kiwivision` | The `kiwivision.*` verbs as one tool: read what KiwiVision shows, turn it or a lens on and off, change its settings, and define or delete a lens |

`list_commands` and `help` answer without the app; the others
need it running. A command `list_commands --json` marks
`destructive` goes only through `run_destructive`, and `run` and
`run_batch` refuse it. `run_destructive` carries MCP's destructive
hint, which an AI app that honours it turns into a question to you
before the command runs. A shortcut verb saves at once, so `run`
tells the AI app to show you the mapping and ask first. `subscribe` and the Lua-only verbs are
not offered.

The `list_commands` tool also takes `kind` (`action`, `setting` or
`query`), and each row it returns carries its `kind`.

Two more tools read the documentation the running copy of KiwiDesk
ships, without the network:

| Tool | Does |
|---|---|
| `docs_search` | Ranked sections for `query`: page, anchor, heading and a snippet. `section` narrows to a page or to `page#anchor`; `limit` is 1 to 20, 5 when omitted. An empty `query` lists the pages, their sections and the app version |
| `docs_get` | The exact text of the section `page` and `anchor` name, the page's opening without `anchor`; a long section comes in parts, picked with `part` |

They cover this page, the [Lua reference](lua-reference.md), the
[user guide](user-guide.md),
[Spaces and Desktops](spaces-and-desktops.md), the
[actions](commands.md), the
[accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md) and the
[recipes](recipes/index.md), and answer without the app. A figure
is returned as its description.

`help` and each `list_commands` row carry `lua`, the command's
`init.lua` call, and `docs`, the `page` and `anchor` of its Lua
reference section for `docs_get`. A command Lua cannot call has no
`lua`, and one no Lua reference heading names has no `docs`.
`kiwidesk help <name> --json` carries `lua` too.

An AI app opens the apps it needs with `run` and
`open_in_background`, which leaves your focus where it is
([`open_in_background`](lua-reference.md#open_in_background)).

An AI app reads Config Issues and the sync folder's status by
sending `get_config_status` through `run`. When `keep` cannot write
a change because a newer KiwiDesk wrote the file it goes to, it
says so (`newer_format`) instead of reporting a plain failed write.

`looks` takes an `action` — each `look.*` verb that can be undone —
and that verb's arguments by name; `look.delete` goes through
`run_destructive`. The AI page's **Make a new look** prompt offers to
match your wallpaper from a screenshot you give the AI app: KiwiDesk
never reads the wallpaper itself.

`app_rules` takes the same shape over the `app_rule.*` verbs. An app
is named by the `bundle_id` `get_state` lists for its windows.

`diagnose_window` takes exactly one of `window` (an id from
`get_state`'s `windows`) or `app` (a bundle id), and sends
`explain_window` or `explain_app`
([`explain_window`](lua-reference.md#explain_window)); `window` has
no focused-window default here.

`kiwivision` takes an `action`, as `looks` does, over every
`kiwivision.*` verb, `kiwivision.current` among them;
`define_lens` takes `table`, the lens as a JSON object string.
`keep` cannot write a KiwiVision change: Settings ▸ KiwiVision
keeps it, so change the setting, or define or delete the lens,
there.

A setting changed through MCP is live but not kept, and every
command result after the change tells the AI app so, with where
`keep` would write it: the live profile, or the shared look for a
look setting of a profile that wears it — a kept look setting
changes every profile wearing that look, and `keep` names them. An
app rule the live profile does not hold for itself is kept in the
shared rules, which every profile without its own rule for that app
follows, and removing one of those takes it from every profile
holding it; `keep` names every profile whose rule changed.
Say "keep" and `keep` writes those changes as they are now; a
change `init.lua` owns, one made while no saved profile is live, an
app-wide one, or one belonging to a Space that is not in the
profile is named but cannot be kept. A change a Settings Save
stored, or one set back to its saved value, needs no keep. A config
reload, a profile load, a built-in layout's apply or Settings that
puts another value there before the keep replaces it, and the AI
app is told. A command the binary does
not know is refused rather than sent. `get_state` hands the AI
app your window titles.

So do `diagnose_window` and `list_windows`, which the AI app can
send through `run`.

ChatGPT reaches only remote MCP servers, so it needs
[OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/secure-mcp-tunnels)
in front of `kiwidesk mcp`; KiwiDesk itself opens no network port.
With a tunnel created in your OpenAI Platform organization and a
runtime key in `CONTROL_PLANE_API_KEY`, OpenAI's `tunnel-client`
runs the server for it:

```sh
tunnel-client init --sample sample_mcp_stdio_local \
  --profile kiwidesk --tunnel-id <tunnel id> \
  --mcp-command "/Applications/KiwiDesk.app/Contents/MacOS/KiwiDesk mcp"
tunnel-client run --profile kiwidesk
```

Then add a connector in ChatGPT whose connection is that tunnel.

sections.heading: Drawing a Look's Preview
parts:
## Drawing a Look's Preview

`kiwidesk preview <look.json> <out.png>` draws an exported look
file as a 768 × 480 PNG: the picture its tile in Looks &
Animations shows, drawn larger and with the pocket standing on the
Space Bar's edge unless the look sets its own, over the default
settings on four Spaces in dark mode. It reads the file as Import…
does and needs no running app. Finder, Safari and Mail in the App
Bar take this Mac's own icons, unless the look draws App Font
symbols, so the PNG can differ between macOS versions. A font
family the Mac lacks draws as `"System"`, as on the bars
([`kiwishelf.set_font_family`](lua-reference.md#kiwishelfset_font_family)).

```sh
kiwidesk preview ~/Desktop/Dusk.json ~/Desktop/Dusk.png
```

sections.heading: Service Control
parts:
## Service Control

```sh
kiwidesk service start     # LaunchAgent: run at login,
                           # restart after crashes
kiwidesk service stop
kiwidesk service restart
kiwidesk service status    # loaded? running? pid?
```

`start` bootstraps the agent when it isn't loaded, and
**relaunches it when the job is loaded but idle** — the state a
quick-menu Quit leaves behind. It no-ops with `KiwiDesk service
is already running` only when a process is actually running. `stop` prints
`KiwiDesk service is not running` cleanly when nothing is
loaded. `restart` boots the job out and back in; when nothing
was loaded it reports `KiwiDesk service was not running —
started it`. `status` reports the loaded/running state and the
pid. A real `launchctl` failure exits non-zero; the ordinary
already-running / not-running cases exit 0. `start` while
KiwiDesk is already running loads the agent, whose `RunAtLoad`
spawns one supervised launch; it finds the instance lock held,
brings the running copy forward once — taking focus from your
terminal — and exits cleanly.

`start` and `restart` refuse a copy opened straight from
Downloads, which macOS runs from a temporary location that
changes each time it starts: move `KiwiDesk.app` to
`/Applications` and run them from there.

`restart` of a running service leaves your windows where they
are: the app is told first, spreads nothing out on its way down,
and the new process picks the windows up in place, sizes
included. It does so only when the program the service will start
is signed like the one running; otherwise, and on `stop`, the
windows are spread out per `quit.layout` as on any quit.

**This service is the only way to get crash supervision** (#1071),
and Settings offers no switch for it. Settings ▸ General's
**Start at login** is the `SMAppService` login item (visible in
System Settings ▸ Login Items) and nothing else — it never
touches this agent, and this agent never touches it.

Both launch at login. The single-instance lock keeps that to one
process, but only the launch that *wins* is supervised, so
running both makes supervision a coin flip (see
[Accepted limitations](accepted-limitations.md)). Run one: this
service if you want crash restart, the login item if you do not.
While the service is loaded, the Settings switch shows as on and
inert, saying so. `service status` adds a `login item:` line
reporting the login-item state, and `service start` prints a note
when the login item is *also* on, saying that two mechanisms will
start KiwiDesk and to run one. These strings are the login item's
only appearance in CLI output.

sections.heading: Exporting the Log
parts:
## Exporting the Log

KiwiDesk writes its diagnostic lines to the macOS unified log
under its own subsystem, at default level and with the text
public, so the shipped app's log is readable on any Mac with no
debug build and no extra permission. To attach it to a bug
report, export the last stretch to a file:

```sh
/usr/bin/log show --last 15m \
  --predicate 'subsystem == "com.kiwicanopy.kiwidesk"' \
  --style compact > ~/Desktop/kiwidesk-log.txt
```

Reach back to just before the problem happened — `--last 15m`,
`--last 2h`, or `--start "2026-09-02 09:40:00"` for an exact
window — and attach the whole file to the issue. Spell out
`/usr/bin/log`: a shell alias named `log` is common.

The file Settings exports also opens with the version, the
screen count and the settings changed from the defaults; this
command writes the log lines only.

To watch live while reproducing:

```sh
/usr/bin/log stream --predicate 'subsystem == "com.kiwicanopy.kiwidesk"' --style compact
```

`kiwidesk debug_log [message]` writes a marker line into this
same log — one before and one after a repro brackets it; it
exports nothing.

sections.heading: Checking the Private Fast Paths
parts:
## Checking the Private Fast Paths

KiwiDesk reaches some of macOS through private WindowServer
calls, each with a public fallback or, where macOS offers none, a
refusal. A new macOS can drop any of them without a crash, so
`self_test` asks the running app which ones still answer:

```sh
kiwidesk self_test          # a table on a terminal
kiwidesk self_test --json   # JSON, as a pipe also gets
```

Each path gets one verdict:

- `works` — it answered, and a second reading agreed.
- `answered` — it answered, and nothing else can read the same
  thing to check it: it is alive, no more.
- `resolved` — it is there, but the check never calls it: it
  writes, or calling it would take something KiwiDesk needs.
- `absent` — macOS no longer has it; the fallback runs.
- `failed` — it is there but answered nothing, or disagreed.
- `inconclusive` — it is there, with nothing to check it against
  (KiwiDesk showing no window, say).

The check only reads: it moves no window, switches no Desktop and
changes no setting. The JSON carries `macos`, a `counts` object by
verdict, and a `probes` array of `name`, `kind` (`symbol` or
`bridge_class`), `home`, `verdict` and `detail`. CLI only — Lua
cannot call it.

`kind` may also be `objc_method`: a private AppKit method
KiwiDesk answers on its own panels — `_hasActiveAppearance`,
which gives KiwiDesk's glass the bright edge of a focused window
(#2569). Its row reads `answered` while macOS still asks it and
`absent` once it stops, when that glass draws its plain look.

The exit code is 2 when any path `failed`, and 0 otherwise —
`absent`, `resolved` and `inconclusive` are findings, not
failures. 1 still means the command itself did not get through.

sections.heading: Commands
parts:
## Commands

A `set_*` command other than `set_default_profile` writes no file:
it changes the running value only.
[`save_profile`](lua-reference.md#save_profile-load_profile-delete_profile-set_default_profile)
keeps what it captures, and so does a Settings Save for a setting
the live profile stores; any other value lasts until a profile
load or a config reload sets it again, or until KiwiDesk quits.

`focus_space_previous`, `focus_space_next`, `focus_space_back`,
`focus_space_forward` and `set_space_history` step through the
Spaces by their order and by the ones you visited
([`focus_space_back`](lua-reference.md#focus_space_back--focus_space_forward)).
`set_desktop_cue` turns off the plate a Desktop switch shows
([`set_desktop_cue`](lua-reference.md#set_desktop_cue)).

`focus_display_last` goes to the screen you were on before, and
`focus_display` takes `left|right|up|down` to the nearest screen
that way, stopping at the edge; neither takes other arguments
([`focus_display_last`](lua-reference.md#focus_display_last--focus_display)).

`focus_space_last` toggles between the last two Spaces you visited
([`focus_space_last`](lua-reference.md#focus_space_last)).

`open_in_background` takes an app bundle id, and optionally a
Space id to put its windows in and a Desktop number to send them
to (`kiwidesk open_in_background com.apple.Music "" 2`), and opens
the app
without taking the focus: it launches it, or asks a running app
with no window for one, and does nothing when the app has a
window anywhere. When the app brings itself forward anyway,
KiwiDesk hands the focus back once
([`open_in_background`](lua-reference.md#open_in_background)).

`focus_app_window` takes `next|prev` and focuses the focused app's
next or previous window, on any Space, screen or Desktop, in the
order a repeat `focus_or_spawn` press walks; unlike macOS's own
**Move focus to next window**, it reaches past the current Space
([`focus_app_window`](lua-reference.md#focus_app_window)).

`focus_space_window` takes `next|prev` and focuses the Space's
next or previous window, along the row on Scrolling and Monocle
([`focus_space_window`](lua-reference.md#focus_space_window)).

`move_to_display_last` and `move_to_display` move the focused
window into the Space another screen shows, the screen
`focus_display_last` or `focus_display` would go to; their
`_and_follow` forms go with it. `move_to_display` and
`move_to_display_and_follow` take `left|right|up|down`; none of
the four takes a window id
([`move_to_display_last`](lua-reference.md#move_to_display_last--move_to_display)).

`set_space_transition` picks how an explicit Space switch shows itself, and
`set_space_slide_duration` paces the slide
([`set_space_transition`](lua-reference.md#set_space_transition)).

`set_space_scroll_transition` picks the same for the scroll Space
step, apart from every other Space switch
([`set_space_scroll_transition`](lua-reference.md#set_space_scroll_transition)).
