`animations.set_on_state_change` animates a window floating,
maximizing or going into the Pocket and out, the last as a brief
pocket
([`animations.set_on_state_change`](lua-reference.md#animationsset_on_state_change)).

`center_floating` follows it too.

`kiwishelf.set_pocket_edge top|bottom|left|right` (default
`bottom`) and `kiwishelf.set_pocket_position 0–100` (default `82`)
place the pocket
([`kiwishelf.set_pocket_edge`](lua-reference.md#kiwishelfset_pocket_edge)).

`kiwishelf.set_pocket_visibility always|auto|hidden` (default
`always`) sets when it shows, per profile
([`kiwishelf.set_pocket_visibility`](lua-reference.md#kiwishelfset_pocket_visibility)).
`pocket.set_capacity` fails naming it.

`kiwishelf.set_reading_contrast 1–4.5` (default `2.2`) sets the
contrast text keeps where the fill fades on KiwiHub, the plates
and the peek; `1` leaves the full fade
([`kiwishelf.set_reading_contrast`](lua-reference.md#kiwishelfset_reading_contrast)).

`set_mode_cue` turns off the plate `cycle_mode` shows
([`set_mode_cue`](lua-reference.md#set_mode_cue)).

`set_modifier_sides` takes `true|false` (default `false`) and
makes a shortcut written with a side, such as `rcmd+h`, keep it
([`set_modifier_sides`](lua-reference.md#set_modifier_sides)).

`take_over_hyper_remap` takes over a Hyper remap another tool
left in place when it is exactly the one KiwiDesk would write for
the chosen key ([`set_hyper_key`](lua-reference.md#set_hyper_key)).
KiwiDesk then removes it when it quits, and an app still listening
for F18 keeps hearing the key. CLI only — Lua cannot call it.

`export_setup <path>` writes the same backup file as **Export…** in
Settings, replacing a file already at that path, and `restore_setup
<path>` does what **Restore…** does: the same refusals, the replaced
files in the Trash, the reload, and unsaved edits in an open
Settings window dropped
([Backups](user-guide.md#moving-to-another-mac-backups)).
`init.lua` is opt-in on both ends: `--include-init-lua` carries it,
and `--init-lua` replaces this Mac's with the backup's where the
backup carries one; the reply's `init_lua` says what happened. The
`kiwidesk` CLI resolves a relative path against your current
directory; any other caller passes an absolute one. CLI only — Lua
cannot call them.

`get_config_status` returns the Config Issues and the sync
folder's status
([`get_config_status`](lua-reference.md#get_config_status)).

`get_settings [pointer] [space]` reads the live settings back, by
the same ids `keep_settings` takes
([`get_settings`](lua-reference.md#get_settings)):

```bash
kiwidesk get_settings /settings/layout/stack/stack_position
kiwidesk get_settings /settings/layout/stack/stack_position 3
```

`look.list`, `look.current`, `look.apply <name>`, `look.save
<name>` and `look.delete <name>` reach the look library
([Looks](lua-reference.md#looks)). `look.apply` wears a look
without writing it.

`shortcut.list`, `shortcut.set <chord> <command> [argument…]` and
`shortcut.remove <chord>` read and write the saved shortcuts; a
write saves at once ([Shortcut verbs](lua-reference.md#shortcut-verbs)).

`shortcut.remove_sequence <leader>` removes a whole key sequence
([`shortcut.remove_sequence`](lua-reference.md#shortcutremove_sequence)).

`shortcut.set_sequence_key <leader> <path> <command> [argument…]`,
`shortcut.name_sequence_key <leader> <path> <name> [symbol]` and
`shortcut.remove_sequence_key <leader> <path>` build a key sequence
one key at a time, a path's keys comma-separated
([`shortcut.set_sequence_key`](lua-reference.md#shortcutset_sequence_key)):

```bash
kiwidesk shortcut.set_sequence_key ctrl+alt+space w,h focus left
kiwidesk shortcut.name_sequence_key ctrl+alt+space w Windows macwindow
kiwidesk shortcut.remove_sequence_key ctrl+alt+space w,h
```

`shortcut.list_groups` lists the shortcut groups a binding's `group`
can name: the built-in tokens and the groups your shortcuts make
([`shortcut.list_groups`](lua-reference.md#shortcutlist_groups)).

`app_rule.list`, `app_rule.set_space <app> <space>`,
`app_rule.remove_space <app>`, `app_rule.set_float <app> [title]`
and `app_rule.remove_float <app> [title]` change the app rules live
([App rule verbs](lua-reference.md#app-rule-verbs)).

`explain_window [window]` says why a window floats or tiles and
what would change it; `explain_app <bundle_id>` says what KiwiDesk
knows of an app whose window it does not list
([`explain_window`](lua-reference.md#explain_window)).

`list_windows [space]` returns every window's frame, screen and
visibility ([`list_windows`](lua-reference.md#list_windows)), and
`focus_window <window>` focuses one by its id
([`focus_window`](lua-reference.md#focus_window)). Pick one window
with `jq`:

```bash
kiwidesk list_windows | jq '.[] | select(.focused)'
```

Each `list_windows` entry, the `explain_window` answer and each
window `explain_app` lists carry the window's `title`, as
`get_state` has it:

```bash
kiwidesk list_windows | jq -r '.[] | "\(.id) \(.title)"'
```

`swap <window> [window]` swaps the focused window with the one an
id names, or two named windows, across Spaces and screens too, and
`swap <direction> <window>` swaps a named window with its neighbour
([`swap`](lua-reference.md#swap)); `swap_here <window>` brings
one into your slot instead ([`swap_here`](lua-reference.md#swap_here)).

`kiwivision.toggle [lens]`, `kiwivision.current`, the
`kiwivision.set_*` verbs, `kiwivision.define_lens <table>` and
`kiwivision.delete_lens <name>` reach KiwiVision and its lenses
([KiwiVision](lua-reference.md#kiwivision)). `kiwivision.current`
says whether KiwiVision is on, which lens is on, its settings and
every lens with why it cannot turn on.

The defaults of `set_space_slide_duration`,
`animations.set_expand_duration` and `animations.set_reveal_duration`
are the Medium speed's
([Animation Cascade](lua-reference.md#animation-cascade)).

`animations.set_on_reveal` is new; see
[animations.set_on_reveal](lua-reference.md#animationsset_on_reveal).

`toggle_maximized` also takes `height|width`, then an optional share
from 0.1 to 1 and `center|in_place`: the window fills that axis at a
share of the other. `maximize.set_share <height|width> <share>
[shape]` and `maximize.set_anchor <center|in_place> [shape]` set what
a press without them takes on a screen of that shape, or on every
shape (`laptop|widescreen|ultrawide|super_ultrawide|portrait`;
[`toggle_maximized`](lua-reference.md#toggle_maximized)).

`maximize.set_follow_focus true|false` (default `false`) makes a new
Maximize move with focus instead of ending
([`maximize.set_follow_focus`](lua-reference.md#maximizeset_follow_focus)).

`maximize.set_share_override <space> <height|width> [share]` and
`maximize.set_anchor_override <space> [center|in_place]` set one
Space's own values over its screen shape's; leaving the value out
clears it
([`maximize.set_share_override`](lua-reference.md#maximizeset_share_override)).

`toggle_maximized` takes a floating window too, whole or along one
axis, and puts it back at the frame it had
([`toggle_maximized`](lua-reference.md#toggle_maximized)).

`monocle.set_maximize_windows true|false` (default `false`) makes
every Monocle window fill the screen with no gaps while the bars read
Hidden
([`monocle.set_maximize_windows`](lua-reference.md#monocleset_maximize_windows)).

`toggle_tiling [space]` turns a Space's tiling off and back on, and
`set_tiling <true|false> [space]` sets it; the windows stay where
they are while it is off. `set_tiling_start_global <true|false>`,
`tiling.set_start <true|false|null> [space]`,
`tiling.set_off_hides_borders <true|false>` and
`tiling.set_off_hides_bars <true|false>` set where Spaces start and
what a Space with tiling off hides
([`toggle_tiling`](lua-reference.md#toggle_tiling)).

`center_floating` moves the focused floating window to the middle of
its screen at its size
([`center_floating`](lua-reference.md#center_floating)).
`move_floating` moves it by a delta in points and a held key glides
([`move_floating`](lua-reference.md#move_floating)).

`pocket_app` takes an app bundle id: the app's own pocket window
out or away, or a new window of the app opened there
([`pocket_app`](lua-reference.md#pocket_app)).
`toggle_pocket_window` takes an optional window id, marking or
unmarking that window instead of the focused one.

`stack.toggle_stack_position [space]` moves a space's stack zone
to the opposite side (left ↔ right, top ↔ bottom) on the macOS
Desktop its screen shows now, the focused space when no id is
given. The flip lasts for the session and is no setting; what ends
it, and the `stack_position` that `get_state` reports, are in the
[Lua reference](lua-reference.md#stacktoggle_stack_position).

`gesture.bind <input> <keys> <action>` binds a mouse or trackpad
input held with keys — `drag`, `hover_move`, `wheel`, `swipe2`,
`tap4` and the rest of the
[Gesture inputs](lua-reference.md#gesture-inputs) — to a family
(`focus|walk|swap|display|track|space`), `move|resize` or Lua, and
`gesture.unbind <input> <keys>` turns one off, a default included;
`""` holds no keys
([`gesture.bind`](lua-reference.md#gesturebind)). The CLI passes
every argument as a string, so a table of directions is Lua's
alone. `scroll_gesture.set_pan`, `scroll_gesture.set_space_step`,
`modifier_drag.set_move`, `modifier_drag.set_resize` and
`trackpad_gesture.bind` are retired and fail naming
`gesture.bind`.

`get_state`'s window objects carry `pocket`: `"pocketed"` or
`"out"` for the [pocket](lua-reference.md#pocket)'s window, `null`
for every other.

`set_focus_wrap` takes `off`, `this_screen` or `all_screens`
(default `all_screens`): what `focus <direction>` does at the
last window that way in every layout — stop, wrap within the
screen, or continue onto the next screen
([Lua reference](lua-reference.md#set_focus_wrap)). It replaces
`scroll.set_wrap_focus`, `monocle.set_wrap_focus` and
`track.set_wrap_focus`, which now fail naming it. It also decides
whether `focus_space_previous` / `focus_space_next` wrap
([Lua reference](lua-reference.md#focus_space_previous--focus_space_next)).

`set_min_window_size`'s layout is `stack`, `grid`, `track`,
`bsp`, `scrolling` or `floating`, and without one it sets every
layout ([Lua reference](lua-reference.md#set_min_window_size)).
The starter setup seeds every layout from the main screen's
width instead of the 300 × 300 default.
`set_min_window_size_override` gives one Space a value that
replaces its layout's
([Lua reference](lua-reference.md#set_min_window_size_override)).

Grid: `grid.set_column_weight` and `grid.set_row_weight` take a
track number (from 1) and a positive weight, `1` being an equal
share; each has a `_override` sibling taking a space id first
([Lua reference](lua-reference.md#gridset_column_weight)).

`set_space_cue`, `animations.set_on_space_change` and
`animations.set_space_change` are refused, naming
`set_space_transition`; `animations.set_space_change_duration` is
refused, naming `set_space_slide_duration`; and
`set_space_switch_liquid_glass` is refused, since the Space
slide's plates follow KiwiHub's glass.

`stack.set_overflow_style`, `track.set_overflow_style` and their
`_override` siblings are refused, since a Stack zone or Track
track scrolls the windows that do not fit
([When windows no longer fit](lua-reference.md#when-windows-no-longer-fit)).

`animations.set_on_monocle_focus` and
`animations.set_monocle_flip_duration` are refused, since a
Monocle focus change is a raise and plays no flip.

`mouse.set_hover_focus` takes `true|false` (default `false`):
focus and raise the window the pointer comes to rest on.
`mouse.set_hover_focus_delay` takes milliseconds, `0` or more
(default `200`): how long the pointer rests first.

`focus_or_spawn` was `pull_or_spawn`; the old name is refused,
naming the new one.

`cycle_mode` (System) takes `prev` or `next` (default) and
moves the focused Space to the next layout in its cycle list;
`set_mode_cycle` sets that list. See
[cycle_mode](lua-reference.md#cycle_mode).

`kiwihub.show` takes `windows`, `shortcuts` or `view` and opens
KiwiHub on that side, so a launcher reaches it without a shortcut;
any other side is refused, naming the sides it takes. See
[kiwihub.show](lua-reference.md#kiwihubshow).

It also takes `desktops`, the Desktop overview.

`kiwihub.show_last_app` opens the window switcher on the app of
the window you used last. See
[kiwihub.show_last_app](lua-reference.md#kiwihubshow_last_app).

`kiwihub.set_key` takes a built-in KiwiHub key (`up`, `down`,
`page_up`, `page_down`, `left`, `right`) and a combo, and makes the
combo a second key for it while KiwiHub is open; no combo clears it.
See [kiwihub.set_key](lua-reference.md#kiwihubset_key).

It also takes `open_space`, `leave_space`, `pick_up` and
`follow`, the Desktop overview's own keys.

`gather` (Launch) takes an app bundle id and moves every window of
that app into the Space you are on, from other macOS Desktops too
where the Desktop bridge is present; it never launches the app, and
an app with nothing to move answers with an error. See
[gather](lua-reference.md#gather).

`move_here` (Launch) takes an app bundle id and optionally a piece
of window title, and moves that app's most recently focused window
not yet here into the Space you are on and focuses it — a
minimized one only once no open one is left; an app with no window
is opened. See [move_here](lua-reference.md#move_here).

`move_to_space`, `move_to_space_and_follow`, `make_floating`,
`make_tiled` and `toggle_floating` take an optional last
argument, a window `id` from `get_state`: they then act on that
window rather than the focused one, and refuse an id no managed
window carries (`kiwidesk make_floating 4711`).

`move_to_desktop` and `move_to_desktop_and_follow` take the same
window `id`, after the space id. Ahead of an id, an empty string
leaves the space out: `kiwidesk move_to_desktop 3 "" 4711`. The id
may be one `get_state` lists under `away_windows`. Neither moves a
full-screen window or a pocket window, named or focused. A named Space
has [limits with *Displays have separate Spaces* off](lua-reference.md#move_to_desktop).

`new_window` and `close_window` take the same optional window
`id`. `new_window` presses that window's app's **File ▸ New
Window**; `close_window` presses the window's close button. Both
reach another app through Accessibility, so `success` means the
press was asked for: an app with no such item, or a window with no
close button, is refused by a pill on screen, not in the reply —
see [Opening and Closing Windows](lua-reference.md#opening-and-closing-windows).

The `scroll_gesture.*` commands set the scroll gestures; see
[Gestures](lua-reference.md#gestures).

`scroll_gesture.set_natural_scrolling` takes `system`, the default,
which follows macOS's own Natural scrolling
([`scroll_gesture.set_natural_scrolling`](lua-reference.md#scroll_gestureset_natural_scrolling)).

`animations.set_on_expand` and `animations.set_expand_duration` set
the KiwiShelf expand on a Space switch, and
`animations.set_on_reveal` and `animations.set_reveal_duration` a
hidden bar's reveal; see
[animations.set_on_expand](lua-reference.md#animationsset_on_expand).

Both durations refuse `0` and below with `a duration must be above
0; …`, naming the `set_on_*` verb that turns the motion off.

`animations.set_on_shelf` and `animations.set_shelf_duration` are
retired and fail naming their replacements.

`animations.set_reduce_motion` (true|false) is the Off of Settings'
speed preset: motion drops in every profile and the lengths are
kept; it changes the running value only
([animations.set_reduce_motion](lua-reference.md#animationsset_reduce_motion)).

`animations.set_on_peek` (true|false, default true) turns the bars'
peeks instant; see
[animations.set_on_peek](lua-reference.md#animationsset_on_peek).

`make_auto` is retired: it fails with `make_auto was retired —
use make_tiled`, and `make_tiled` does its job. `make_tiled`, and
`toggle_floating` towards tiled, fail on a window that detection
or a float rule floats
([`make_tiled`](lua-reference.md#make_tiled)).

A float rule's window is the exception
([`make_tiled`](lua-reference.md#make_tiled)).

`set_float_placement` replaces `set_float_nudge`: a saved setting
that had the nudge off becomes `keep`, and a call to
`set_float_nudge` fails naming its replacement.

`drag.set_corner_radius` fails naming `border.set_corner_style`.

The drag markers' look is fixed: for the ghost and the drop zone
alike, `_border`, `_border_color`, `_border_alignment`,
`_border_width`, `_fill` and `_fill_color` fail with a message
starting `<verb> was retired: the drag markers' look is fixed`,
and the ghost is off for a fresh setup.

`bind_profile_to_desktop` files one profile per screen count on a
Desktop, for all screen setups: a second profile of another count
adds beside the first, the same count replaces it.

Screen fingerprints after the profile, as `list_monitors` prints
them, scope the binding to that one screen setup ([Lua
reference](lua-reference.md#bind_profile_to_desktop)).

¹ placement: `first\|last\|before_focused\|after_focused`

`reset_layout_sizing` clears what `resize` accumulated on the
active space — or the space named, or every space for `all` —
the session layer and the stack and track weights — so it
lands on what its profile authored (an override's size field
stays; the global only where nothing was authored), and leaves
structure alone
([Lua reference](lua-reference.md#reset_layout_sizing)).

A named space, or the active one, resets on the Desktop its screen
shows; `all` resets every Desktop. It also clears the length a
grow along a run kept.

Every layout global has a per-space `_override` twin (e.g.
`bsp.set_ratio_h_override`, `scroll.set_slot_size_override`) that
takes a leading `space id, value` and shadows the global for that
space only.

`resize` adapts to the active layout and is per-axis (#56). A
floating focused window resizes itself directly in any mode
(width for `x`, height for `y`, floored at `min_window_size`),
splitting the delta between both edges and pinning one that is
already against the screen edge or a bar (#1091). "Floating" is
the effective float (#1184): the window's own flag, or any window
in a floating-layout space, which places nothing.

That floor is Floating's `min_window_size` on the axis
resized, whatever layout the window's space uses.

A floating window's `resize` and `move_floating` run to the screen's
visible edge; a bar on the top edge stops them, a bottom or side bar
does not (#3163).

A focused window in native full screen is refused ahead of every layout,
whatever its float state, with `the focused window is
fullscreen` (#1298): nothing is written and no neighbour moves;
the pill and sound rule below apply to it as to the monocle
reply.
For tiled windows: in BSP, `x` moves the side-by-side split
ratio and `y` the stacked one, independently, each in the
direction that grows the *focused* window's region (#122). In
stack (#67, #222), the split axis (`x` for a left/right stack
zone, `y` for top/bottom) moves the master/stack split in the
direction that grows the *focused* window; the focused zone's
own axis grows that window's share of its zone (session-scoped
weights, reset on relaunch). An axis matching neither fails with
the cue, so a master zone lined up *along* the split axis has no
reachable per-window shares (accepted — see
[design decisions](design-decisions.md)). Scrolling resizes the
slot along its own scroll axis for either `x` or `y`. In a track
space the axis across the tracks resizes the focused window's
track, the axis along them its share within the track (#128;
session-scoped weights too). Monocle replies "not supported" —
that failure flashes a pill on the focused window
whatever issued it, and adds the system alert sound when
`set_refusal_sound` is on (default off) and a hotkey was what
fired: a CLI or IPC caller reads the error reply and never hears
one.

In grid (#763), `x` moves the edge the focused cell shares with
the next column (the previous one for the last column) and `y`
the same for rows, writing session-scoped column and row
weights.

Along a run's scroll direction a grow pushes its neighbour into
the run instead of stopping at its minimum
([Lua reference](lua-reference.md#resize)).

sections.heading: Deleting a Space
parts:
### Deleting a Space

`delete_space` succeeds whether or not the removal lasts.

`kiwidesk delete_space 5 profile` also removes the Space from
the live profile's file, and `kiwidesk create_space 7 profile`
adds one there; the scope is the command line's confirmation.
Both refuse a Space `init.lua` or a built-in layout declares,
naming it. A Space made any other way is temporary — see
[`create_space`](lua-reference.md#create_space).

When the space is still declared somewhere, the response says
where:

```json
{"status": "success",
 "data": {"declared_in": ["profile:Work", "init.lua"]}}
```

`declared_in` names every source that re-creates the space on the
next config load — what each means is under
[`delete_space`](lua-reference.md#delete_space) — and is absent
when none does. The JSON goes to stdout as always; the CLI adds
one line per source on stderr, so stdout carries nothing new:

```
removed from the live layout but still in saved profile "Work" — delete it with scope profile to remove it there too
still composed by the built-in "Developer" standard — save a profile to make this durable
still created by init.lua — remove the call that creates it
```

sections.heading: Applying Ignore Rules
parts:
### Applying Ignore Rules

`ignore_rules` is declarative config, not a session command. Edit
`ignore_rules = { "bundle.id" }` in `init.lua`, then
apply it with:

```sh
kiwidesk reload_config
```

For GUI-managed setups, put the array at the root `ignore_rules`
key in `gui.json` and reload the same way. Matching apps
disappear from KiwiDesk state and emit no window events. Removing
an id and reloading makes its windows manageable again.

Those declarations are the global base. A profile JSON may carry a
sparse `ignore_rules` object: `true` adds an id and `null` removes an
inherited one while that profile is active. `load_profile` applies the
resolved rules immediately over either a Lua- or GUI-owned base.

sections.heading: Event Stream
parts:
## Event Stream

External tools subscribe over the same socket:

```sh
kiwidesk subscribe                          # all events
kiwidesk subscribe space_change layout_change
```

Each event is one JSON line:

```json
{"event": "space_change",
 "data": {"space_id": "3", "mode": "bsp",
          "window_count": 4}}
```

Events: `space_change`, `layout_change`, `focus_change`,
`monitor_change`, `desktop_change`, `window_created`,
`window_destroyed`, `window_moved_to_space`, `layer_change`.

Give no arguments and you get every event; give arguments and
the filter is honoured exactly. An argument that names no event
is dropped, and the subscription still succeeds — so the
confirmation line lists what was dropped:

```json
{"status": "success", "data": {"unknown": ["space_chnage"]}}
```

A non-string argument is dropped the same way and appears there
as `<non-string>`. The same names, truncated after the first few,
go to the application log (viewable in Console.app).

Subscribe to nothing *but* unrecognised names and the stream
stays silent: an empty filter is not the same request as no
filter.

The stream ends when the app quits. Add `--reconnect` to keep it
across a quit and relaunch: it waits for the app, subscribes again
with the same names, and notes on stderr that events in between
were missed. Each reconnection prints the confirmation line again.

```sh
kiwidesk subscribe --reconnect space_change
```

A stream whose reader goes away — `kiwidesk subscribe | head -1`
once `head` has its line — ends with exit code 1, with or without
`--reconnect`. Any command whose app quits before the request is
sent fails with `sendFailed` and exit code 1.

Every window event carries `bundle_id` — the stable identity
key (the one app rules and `focus_or_spawn` match on) — next to
the locale-dependent display `app` name. It is JSON `null` for
unbundled processes; the Lua callback receives it as the
trailing positional argument, `""` when unknown.

`focus_change` data carries `window_id`, `app`, `bundle_id`,
**and** `title` — but the Lua callback receives only
`window_id, app, bundle_id` positionally, so the window title
is available on the socket stream but not to a Lua handler:

```json
{"event": "focus_change",
 "data": {"window_id": 4711, "app": "Ghostty",
          "bundle_id": "com.mitchellh.ghostty",
          "title": "~/src — zsh"}}
```

The window lifecycle events fire even when focus does not
change:

```json
{"event": "window_created",
 "data": {"window_id": 4711, "app": "Ghostty",
          "space_id": "2", "reason": "new",
          "bundle_id": "com.mitchellh.ghostty"}}
{"event": "window_destroyed",
 "data": {"window_id": 4711, "app": "Ghostty",
          "space_id": "2", "reason": "closed",
          "bundle_id": "com.mitchellh.ghostty",
          "desktop": null}}
```

`window_created` carries the space the window was placed in
(`app_rules` included); `window_destroyed` carries the space
the window disappeared from — its own space, even when that
space is not active.

These events track the *visible window set*, not app
lifecycle; the `reason` field says why the set changed:

- `window_created` — `new` (a genuinely new window),
  `returned` (back from another macOS Desktop, from an app
  that was unhidden, or from a session restore), `restored`
  (deminiaturized).
- `window_destroyed` — `closed` (a real close), `minimized`
  (only minimized; it will come back as `restored`),
  `hidden` (its app was hidden, with ⌘H or by hiding itself
  as its last window closed, and the window comes back as
  `returned` — or KiwiDesk stopped managing a window, an app's
  shadow window it had tracked),
  `vanished` (the window is on a
  macOS Desktop no screen is showing; it returns as
  `returned`). A `vanished` payload also carries `desktop`,
  the number of the Desktop holding the window, counted across
  every screen ([which count](spaces-and-desktops.md#how-desktops-are-numbered)), where the Desktop can be read; every other reason —
  and a Mac without SkyLight — sends `null`.

`window_created` also reports `existing`: a window that was
already open when KiwiDesk began managing it — every window found
when KiwiDesk starts, and, where macOS reports windows opening, a
window it adopts later that macOS never reported opening, such as
one it lost track of and finds again:

```json
{"event": "window_created",
 "data": {"window_id": 4702, "app": "Ghostty",
          "space_id": "2", "reason": "existing",
          "bundle_id": "com.mitchellh.ghostty"}}
```

`restored` wins over `returned`, which wins over `existing`; `new`
is everything else, KiwiDesk's own windows included. A pocketed
window that comes back after its app was hidden, or after KiwiDesk
restarted, is `returned`. Where KiwiDesk has to wait for macOS to
report the window opening, the event can follow the window's
`focus_change` by up to half a second; it always comes before that
window's `window_destroyed`. Where macOS reports windows opening,
a window re-shown after a `closed` destroy with no new window
behind it is `existing`, and so is a window a Desktop switch
reveals that KiwiDesk never placed. More reasons may be added, so
match the ones your consumer handles.

A window re-shown after a `closed` destroy — an app whose close
hides the window and shows the same one again — comes back as
`new` and is placed like one; `returned` is a Desktop return, an
unhide or a session restore.

A macOS Desktop switch thus fires a burst of `vanished`
destroys and a burst of `returned` creates — filter on
`reason` to ignore them. The reason is read off the
WindowServer: a window it still hosts on an unshown Desktop is
`vanished`, one it hosts nowhere is `closed`, whenever the
destroy lands. A window closed *while its Desktop is off-screen*
is reported `closed` when KiwiDesk next reads the Desktops — at
the next Desktop switch, or within about five seconds while any
window is away — so a consumer sees two destroys for that
window, `vanished` then `closed`, and refreshing on
`desktop_change` remains the safe pattern.

A `move_to_desktop_and_follow` that switches Desktop reports its
window `vanished` whatever the WindowServer hosts it on, where it
answers. `desktop` names the Desktop you sent it to, which may
already be on screen when the event fires.

`window_moved_to_space` fires when a window is explicitly
moved to another space (`move_to_space`,
with or without follow, or a drag onto another screen — the
live crossing emits as the membership moves, so a drag pulled
back before release emits once per crossing). A
`move_to_desktop` onto a Desktop that lives on **another
screen** emits it too: the window joins the space that screen
shows
([#1010](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1010)).
`move_to_desktop` with a **named Space** emits it as well when
that Desktop is the one its screen is already showing —
`to_space_id` is the Space you named. When the Desktop is hidden
there is no `window_moved_to_space` at all: the window is
reported `vanished` and comes back with `window_created`,
`reason: returned`, already in the named Space
([#1150](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1150)).

A window already on a hidden Desktop was reported `vanished` when it
left, so a move emits nothing until it reaches a Desktop on screen,
where it comes back with `window_created`, `reason: returned`.

Bulk reassignments (profile load, session restore) stay silent:

```json
{"event": "window_moved_to_space",
 "data": {"window_id": 4711, "app": "Spotify",
          "from_space_id": "1", "to_space_id": "3",
          "bundle_id": "com.spotify.client"}}
```

`desktop_change` fires when the visible Desktop changes on any
screen — a swipe, Mission Control, or a `focus_desktop` /
`move_to_desktop_and_follow` command; its data carries the 1-based
Desktop number now current on the screen that switched, counted
across every screen ([which count](spaces-and-desktops.md#how-desktops-are-numbered)), that
screen's positional number (`monitor`: 1 is the main screen,
secondaries follow left to right — the same 1-based positional
numbering a screen argument takes), and the active profile:

```json
{"event": "desktop_change",
 "data": {"desktop": 2, "monitor": 1,
          "profile": "Creator Studio"}}
```

`desktop_change` fires once KiwiDesk has read the arriving
Desktop's windows, after that switch's `vanished` and `returned`
bursts, so a state query sent on it sees them — save an app slow
to answer, whose windows follow within a few seconds
([#2347](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2347)).
Switches in quick succession deliver their events in order, after
the last one's windows are read.

With "Displays have separate Spaces" on, each screen switches
Desktops on its own, so watch `monitor` to tell them apart:
only a switch on the main screen (`monitor: 1`) selects a
profile. A secondary screen's swipe reports its Desktop and
moves that screen onto the Space its arriving Desktop should
show — which emits `space_change` too when that screen is the
one holding the active Space. With the
option off, or with a single screen, `monitor` is always 1.

`layer_change` fires when the active keyboard layer changes —
a `switch_layer` call, a config reload returning you to
`default`, a profile switch — and never when a switch names the
layer already active. It carries the previous and the new layer
names, `default` included:

```json
{"event": "layer_change",
 "data": {"from_layer": "default", "to_layer": "resize"}}
```

sections.heading: Running a Command per Event
parts:
### Running a Command per Event

`watch` runs a command once per event:

```sh
kiwidesk watch space_change -- sketchybar --trigger kiwi_space
kiwidesk watch -- sh -c 'echo "$KIWIDESK_EVENT" >> ~/events.log'
```

Event names go before `--`, as with `subscribe` (none means every
event), and a name the app does not know is reported on stderr; the
command and its arguments go after it and run without
a shell, so wrap shell syntax in `sh -c`. Each run gets the event's
JSON line on stdin, and these variables:

- `KIWIDESK_EVENT` — the event name.
- `KIWIDESK_DATA` — the event's `data` object as JSON.
- `KIWIDESK_<KEY>` for each top-level string, number or boolean
  in `data`, upper-cased: `KIWIDESK_SPACE_ID`, `KIWIDESK_WINDOW_ID`.

Runs happen one at a time, in event order; events that arrive
during a run wait for it. A command that exits non-zero is reported
on stderr and the watch continues. The watch reconnects across a
relaunch, as `subscribe --reconnect` does, and runs until stopped.

sections.heading: Raw IPC Protocol
parts:
## Raw IPC Protocol

Anything that can write to a UNIX socket can drive KiwiDesk —
newline-delimited JSON, one request per line:

```sh
printf '{"command":"set_mode","args":["1","grid"]}\n' \
    | nc -U ~/Library/Application\ Support/KiwiDesk/KiwiDesk.sock
```

Response:

```json
{"status": "success"}
{"status": "error", "error": "unknown command: ..."}
```

Unknown commands come back with a did-you-mean suggestion when
a close match exists.

A request may add `"report_changes": true` — `kiwidesk mcp` does —
and the response then carries a `changes` object: the live
`profile`, and the setting leaves the command changed under
`touched`, each an `id` (a JSON Pointer such as
`/settings/border/width`, `/space_modes/2` or
`/app_wide/refusal/sound`, `/app_rules/com.spotify.client`), an
`owner` (`profile`, `shared_look`, `shared_rules`, `init_lua` or
`none`), its live `value`, whether that is the
`stored` one, and a `not_keepable` reason where no keep can write
it. Ids sent as `"keep_watch": [...]` come back judged the same way
under `watched`. `keep_settings` writes those ids as they are live
and answers which ones it `kept`, which it could not
(`not_keepable`), the live `profile`, the profiles wearing a kept
shared look (`followers`) and the profiles whose rule a kept rule
changed (`rule_profiles`):

```sh
kiwidesk keep_settings /settings/border/width
```

`revert_settings` is its twin: it puts those ids back to the value
the live profile or its shared look stores, applied live, and
answers which ones it `reverted` and which it could not
(`not_revertable`, each an `id` with its `reason`: `not_a_setting`,
`not_keepable` or `not_applied`). It takes settings leaves only; a Space's
layout and the rules are left as they are live.

pages.title: Actions
pages.description: The actions KiwiDesk can run from a key.

sections.heading: Actions
parts:
# Actions

Each action below can be bound to a key with `bind`. The link opens its arguments in the [Lua reference](lua-reference.md). Settings and queries are listed by `kiwidesk list_commands --kind setting` and `--kind query` ([CLI & IPC](cli.md#discovering-commands)).

sections.heading: KiwiDesk
parts:
## KiwiDesk

| Action | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`focus`](lua-reference.md#focus) | Moves keyboard focus to the neighboring window. |
| [`swap`](lua-reference.md#swap) | Swaps the focused or named window with a neighbor; ids in place of direction swap two windows. |
| [`swap_here`](lua-reference.md#swap_here) | Brings the window an id names into your slot and focuses it; yours takes its place. |
| [`focus_window`](lua-reference.md#focus_window) | Focuses a window by id, switching to its Space where another Space holds it. |
| [`focus_space`](lua-reference.md#focus_space) | Switches to a Space, hiding the current Space's windows. |
| [`focus_space_back`](lua-reference.md#focus_space_back--focus_space_forward) | Goes back to the Space shown before, along the history space_history names. |
| [`focus_space_forward`](lua-reference.md#focus_space_back--focus_space_forward) | Goes forward again along the Space history, after focus_space_back. |
| [`focus_space_last`](lua-reference.md#focus_space_last) | Goes to the Space you were on before, like Cmd-Tab for Spaces; repeated, it toggles between two. |
| [`focus_space_previous`](lua-reference.md#focus_space_previous--focus_space_next) | Switches to the previous Space in the focused screen's order, stopping at the first. |
| [`focus_space_next`](lua-reference.md#focus_space_previous--focus_space_next) | Switches to the next Space in the focused screen's order, stopping at the last. |
| [`focus_display_last`](lua-reference.md#focus_display_last--focus_display) | Goes to the screen you were on before, like Cmd-Tab for screens. |
| [`focus_display`](lua-reference.md#focus_display_last--focus_display) | Goes to the nearest screen in a direction, stopping at the last. |
| [`move_to_space`](lua-reference.md#move_to_space) | Moves the focused window, or the one a window id names, to a Space without following it. |
| [`move_to_space_and_follow`](lua-reference.md#move_to_space_and_follow) | Moves the focused window, or the one a window id names, to a Space and switches to it. |
| [`move_to_display_last`](lua-reference.md#move_to_display_last--move_to_display) | Moves the focused window to the screen you were on before, without following it. |
| [`move_to_display_last_and_follow`](lua-reference.md#move_to_display_last_and_follow--move_to_display_and_follow) | Moves the focused window to the screen you were on before and follows it. |
| [`move_to_display`](lua-reference.md#move_to_display_last--move_to_display) | Moves the focused window to the nearest screen in a direction, without following it. |
| [`move_to_display_and_follow`](lua-reference.md#move_to_display_last_and_follow--move_to_display_and_follow) | Moves the focused window to the nearest screen in a direction and follows it. |
| [`focus_desktop`](lua-reference.md#focus_desktop) | Switches to a macOS Desktop, exactly as a swipe would. |
| [`move_to_desktop`](lua-reference.md#move_to_desktop) | Moves the focused or named window to a macOS Desktop, and into a Space when one is named. |
| [`move_to_desktop_and_follow`](lua-reference.md#move_to_desktop_and_follow) | Moves the focused or named window to a macOS Desktop, into a Space if named, and follows it. |
| [`move_space_to_display`](lua-reference.md#move_space_to_display) | Moves a Space to another screen, named by number, fingerprint or name, and shows it there. |
| [`create_space`](lua-reference.md#create_space) | Makes a Space; temporary unless scope is profile, which may take the optional mode's place. |
| [`delete_space`](lua-reference.md#delete_space) | Removes a Space after rehoming its windows; scope profile removes it from the profile too. |
| [`make_floating`](lua-reference.md#make_floating) | Marks the focused window, or the one a window id names, as floating above the tiles. |
| [`make_tiled`](lua-reference.md#make_tiled) | Tiles the focused or named window, a float rule's too; refused where detection floats it. |
| [`toggle_floating`](lua-reference.md#toggle_floating) | Flips the focused or named window between floating and tiled, refused as make_tiled is. |
| [`new_window`](lua-reference.md#new_window) | Asks the focused or named window's app for a new window; success means asked. |

| [`pocket`](lua-reference.md#pocket) | Pockets or takes out the next pocket window, or pockets the window an id names. |
| [`toggle_pocket_window`](lua-reference.md#toggle_pocket_window) | Marks the focused or named window as the pocket window, floating it, or unmarks it, tiling it. |

| [`center_floating`](lua-reference.md#center_floating) | Moves the focused floating window to the middle of its screen, clear of the bars, at its size. |

| [`focus_or_spawn`](lua-reference.md#focus_or_spawn) | Focuses an app's window, or launches a new instance. |

| [`open_in_background`](lua-reference.md#open_in_background) | Opens an app without taking focus, in a Space or on a Desktop you name, or where you are. |

pages.title: Accepted Limitations
pages.description: Behaviors that are bugs by design — each with its architectural root and, where planned, the real fix.

sections.heading: Accepted limitations
parts:
# Accepted limitations

Some behaviors are *bugs by design* — accepted consequences of a
settled architectural trade, not defects to fix — and each row
below names the trade, its architectural root and the real fix
where one is planned. OS-blocked-by-SIP items are a separate
class — see
[Blocked by macOS (SIP)](design-decisions.md#blocked-by-macos-sip).

| Behavior | Why it's accepted | Architectural root | Escape hatch / planned fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| A window [tiled over a float rule](lua-reference.md#make_tiled) floats by the rule again after an in-place restart (an update's Install and Relaunch, `kiwidesk service restart`) when its app lists it only after the restart's replay. | The Tile lives as long as the window, and the restart carries it only for windows already tracked when the replay runs; floating again is the safe direction, since the rule still names the window. | The Tile is session state carried on the in-place capture (`WindowSession.tiledOverRule`) and taken back by `adoptTilesOverRule` at the restore ([#2975](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2975)). | Tile the window again. |
| Swapping which bar a shared edge shows while the first is still leaving (four fifths of `animations.reveal_duration`) — hiding one bar and showing the other on the same edge in quick succession — makes the arriving bar join the leaving one — opening out of it, as a bar joining a shown shelf does — instead of sliding in from the screen edge. | The reveal slides the shelf's whole content as one layer inside one still panel, which is what keeps it smooth on the glass ([Design Decisions ▸ App Bar](design-decisions.md#app-bar), *A shelf can hide*); two bars on one edge therefore cannot travel separately. | `ShelfOverlay` plays one reveal motion on its content, and a show during a retract takes the shelf back as a join ([#2500](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2500), closed as not planned; `ShelfRevealSwapTests` pins the end state). | None planned — a per-bar slide was weighed and not planned (#2500): on a Plain shelf both bars share one plate, so sliding them separately would split that plate in two mid-flight and fuse it again at the end, showing two separate bars for the swap — what the fused shelf exists to avoid — and a motion right under Boxed alone is no fix. The shelf ends on the arriving bar alone either way. |
| On a synced config folder, a save can replace a file the sync client is still writing, if KiwiDesk reads it half-written; the broken copy is kept only on the Mac that saved. | One policy for a file no reader can decode: overwrite it after keeping a copy, rather than block every later save to it ([#2324](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2324), ruling 13). | `CorruptFile.keepBeforeOverwrite`, which every store's write door takes after its newer-format refusal (`CorruptFilePolicyTests`); the copy lives in `~/Library/Application Support/KiwiDesk/migration-backups/`, which does not sync. | Restore from `migration-backups/<path>.corrupt` on the Mac that saved, or from the sync client's version history. |
| Deleting a macOS Desktop leaves its profile binding **dormant**: the row stays, labelled with the number the Desktop was last seen at and badged *not present*, and does nothing until you re-point it. The one Desktop macOS destroys when you unplug a screen comes back, binding and all, when the screen returns. | A binding is filed under a private identifier KiwiDesk stamps into each Desktop's own settings, and the only guess for re-attaching a record whose stamp is gone is the Mission Control number — the silent wrong-Desktop behaviour it replaced ([a Desktop is its stamp, not its number](design-decisions.md#profiles)). | `DesktopKey.identity` keys `profile_bindings`; a record whose Desktop no reading can name is held, not pruned, since an unplugged screen's Desktops come back with their stamps ([#1147](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1147), `DesktopBindingIdentityTests`). | Pick the profile again on that row in **Profiles per macOS Desktop**, or clear it. On a Mac where the stamp cannot be written, bindings key by the Mission Control number and behave as they did before. |

| A sticky window with **Keep sticky windows visible across Desktops** on that is closed within a few seconds *after* a Desktop switch keeps its tile for a few reconcile beats — bounded — before KiwiDesk drops it. | For a beat after a switch a carried sticky window is absent from every reading KiwiDesk has — its AX element dies as it leaves the visible Space, on a native app before KiwiDesk hears of the switch and on an Electron app about two seconds after, and the compositor has not drawn it on the arriving Desktop yet — so it is indistinguishable from a window that was just closed, and refusing the removal briefly is what keeps a carried window's slot, sticky scope and reach pin through the switch ([sticky reach](design-decisions.md#sticky-reach-spans-macos-desktops-1145)). | The removal-distrust gate's carried arm (`EventLoop.carriedWindows`, [#1145](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1145)) refuses a carried window's vanish census-blind on the [#1157](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1157) episode's recheck budget, each refusal arming the follow-up reconcile that converges a true close (`CarriedRemovalTests` pins the bound); the reach-departure arm (`EventLoop.reachAwaitsCarry`, [#1215](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1215)) refuses a gesture departure's vanish the same way while the WindowServer still hosts the window on the Desktop you just left and KiwiDesk has not yet heard of the switch (`ReachDepartureRemovalTests`). | Wait it out — the rechecks drop the tile within a second or two; focusing the app reconciles it sooner. A sticky window closed in the fraction of a second *before* KiwiDesk hears of a switch waits out the same rechecks. A switch KiwiDesk itself dispatches promises the carry ahead of the OS ([#1213](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1213)); on a *gesture* switch (a swipe, Ctrl+arrow, Mission Control) the window is carried like any other ([#1215](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1215)). |
| A window closed **while in native fullscreen** (⌘W on the last tab of a fullscreen browser window, say) keeps its tile for a beat or two after macOS drops back to the Desktop — bounded — before KiwiDesk drops it and hands focus on. | Some apps (Zen, and Firefox behind it) order the real window out for the fullscreen transition's beat on both ends — absent from the app's Accessibility window list *and* from the on-screen census while the compositor still hosts it — so a vanish of a window last read in fullscreen, whatever its app, or one the compositor hosts on a fullscreen Space, is refused briefly, and a window that really closed while fullscreen looks the same at that moment ([#1272](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1272)). | The removal-distrust gate's fullscreen arm (`EventLoop.fullscreenRemovalArmIsOpen`, [#1272](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1272)) refuses the vanish census-blind on the [#1157](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1157) episode's recheck budget; `FullscreenRemovalTests` pins the bound. | Wait it out — the rechecks drop the tile within a second or two; focusing another app reconciles it sooner. |
| A Space named on `move_to_desktop` for a **hidden** Desktop is dropped, silently, if the window has not left within about five seconds — a slow app, or a move the bridge accepted and never applied — and the window then rejoins the Space it left. | The name is a debt paid at the window's departure, and an unbounded one would attach to a close minutes later ([a Desktop move's explicit Space is paid at the departure](design-decisions.md#a-desktop-moves-explicit-space-is-paid-at-the-departure-1150)). | `PendingSpaceAssignment`, bounded at `FollowFocusIntent.drainWindow` like the follow's own debt ([#1150](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1150), [#1007](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1007); `PendingSpaceAssignmentTests`). | `move_to_space` once that Desktop is shown, or `move_to_desktop_and_follow`, which takes you there with the window. |
| Returning to a macOS Desktop whose previously focused window takes **more than about five seconds** to come back — or never does, because it was closed from another Desktop — restores the space but not that focus: whatever macOS itself brought forward keeps it, and KiwiDesk's own post-switch refocus stands down. Until you next leave that Desktop with a window focused, each return holds the same stale entry for the same few seconds. | The remembered focus is a debt paid at the window's own arrival, an unbounded debt would fire minutes later at a switch it was never about, and paying it to some *other* window would be the first-in-row jump the fix removed ([a Desktop switch is not a close](design-decisions.md#a-desktop-switch-is-not-a-close-1207)). | `DesktopMemory.returnFocus` is a second `FollowFocusIntent`, bounded like the follow's at `drainWindow` ([#1007](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1007), [#1207](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1207)); the create fold pays it and `desktopSettle` stands down while it is owed (`DesktopFocusPaymentTests`). | Focus the window yourself; the next departure from that Desktop records the fresh focus and the return is right again. |

| In a **Track** space set to *focused track*, with Desktops bound to different profiles that share a Space name, a column can gain an extra divider right after a Desktop switch — one track drawn as two — and it lasts until you next leave that Desktop. *Own track* — the default — is unaffected. | For a beat after a switch the departing Desktop's windows are still in the row beside the arriving ones, a departing track head hands its divider to whatever sits next to it, and a handed break is never handed on, so the stray divider is bounded to one stay ([#1387](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1387), owner ruling 2026-09-15). | `Space.handedBreaks` marks a handed break; the one hand-off door drops it when the holder leaves, and its head takes its own back on return (`ReturningSlotTrackFoldTests`); refusing the hand-off across Desktops would need the state fold to know which Desktop a window is on, which [#1230](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1230) rules it never stores. | Switch Desktops and back. Moving the window that holds the stray divider to a neighbouring track drops it too, merging the column behind it until its own head returns. Not measured on a device yet — file the log if it shows. |
| With **Displays have separate Spaces** on, a Desktop switch on a **secondary** screen (one without the menu bar) does not restore that Desktop's focused window: the first window to re-list may take the focus. The main screen's Desktops are the ones that remember. | The switch handler's secondary arm knows only *which* screen changed, and the binding authority is the main screen's ([#888](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/888); ruled a residue, not a scope, [#1207](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1207)); [#1230](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1230) moves that screen's Space from the same arm, so the residue is the focus alone. | `moveSwitchedDisplaySpaces` moves that screen's Space from the one reading `switchedDisplays` takes, but the #1207 focus debt is recorded at the focus REPORT against the native Space it was honored on and paid by the create fold when the owed window re-lists — neither of which the secondary arm reaches, since the debt is owed per Space while the arm moves a screen (`SecondaryDisplaySpaceTests`; [design decisions](design-decisions.md#a-desktop-switch-is-not-a-close-1207)). | Make the screen you switch Desktops on the main one (System Settings ▸ Displays, drag the menu bar), or turn *Displays have separate Spaces* off so every switch is the main screen's. |
| Every keyboard focus destination in Settings that is not a text field — the layout picker a space deletion lands on, the Screens page's space chips, buttons and pop-up menus generally — is unreachable unless **System Settings ▸ Keyboard ▸ Keyboard navigation** is on (off by default as observed on macOS 26.6.1, 2026-08-11). With it off, an assignment lands nowhere and focus falls to the search field at the top of the window. | What is missing is a system-wide user preference; routing focus to the nearest text field instead is the top-of-window outcome the rule forbids, and no test can see the difference, since a source needle proves a destination was named and never that focus arrived. | macOS decides which control classes may become first responder from `AppleKeyboardUIMode`; an app may read the user's choice but must not set it, and `@FocusState` assignments to a control the system refuses are dropped silently ([#678](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/678) Phase 4 pass 10; the obligation is in `.claude/rules/gui.md` ▸ The keyboard path). | Turn Keyboard navigation on — every documented keyboard path then works. The user guide says so in [Using Settings from the Keyboard](user-guide.md#using-settings-from-the-keyboard); VoiceOver users need nothing, its cursor being independent of the setting. |

| With **VoiceOver on**, opening a Settings **drawer** while the VoiceOver cursor sits on some *other* element — a row near the top of the page, the drawer further down — makes VoiceOver scroll that element back into view and read it out again; keyboard focus was not seen to move, and nothing is lost, but the page has scrolled away from what was just opened. Whether any *other* layout change in Settings does the same is **unmeasured** — [#989](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/989)'s question. | The behaviour is VoiceOver's own cursor handling over a focus model that is the platform's — there is no repro with VoiceOver off, removing the drawer's expansion animation changed nothing ([#988](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/pull/988)), other applications were heard re-announcing on a state change the same way (device session 2026-08-25, macOS 26.6.2) — and forcing keyboard focus onto a clicked button is refused because the north star binds behaviour to the platform (the same reasoning that keeps the focus ring the platform's, #833). | SwiftUI on macOS does not give a `Button` or a `Menu` keyboard focus when it is clicked (device session 2026-08-28, macOS 26.6.2, Full Keyboard Access ON; observed on the drawer's own header button and on Layout Defaults' anchor menu), so the VoiceOver cursor stays parked where focus last was; revealing the drawer rebuilds the accessibility element list under the window — which no arrangement of `SettingsDisclosureStyle` avoids — and VoiceOver answers a changed tree by re-resolving the element under its cursor. KiwiDesk sets keyboard focus at most once per navigation — the content pane, on a push the platform would itself have moved focus for (`SettingsView`, [#996](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/996), [#991](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/991)) — and a CLICKED navigation states no destination at all ([#961](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/961), [#989](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/989)). | Move the VoiceOver cursor to the drawer with VoiceOver's own commands and open it from there, so the cursor and the change are in the same place, rather than clicking with the mouse while the cursor is parked elsewhere. Stated as the shape of the repro, not as a measured workaround: what was observed was the cursor on a row at the top and a click at the bottom, and the cursor-on-the-drawer case has not been tried. |
| Within the first **~12 s after starting VoiceOver** while a KiwiDesk window (Settings) is focused, one **clickless** cross-app focus change (cmd-tab, app-driven) is returned once — focus comes back to the KiwiDesk window. A **click** is always honored and clears the return; focus coming back to KiwiDesk on its own clears it too, and it fires at most once per VoiceOver start. | When the accessibility control process VoiceOver starts yields, macOS re-activates the most recent *regular* app — KiwiDesk is an accessory (menu bar) app, so activation lands on the previous app 3–8 s later — and that handoff is indistinguishable at OS level from a deliberate clickless focus in the same window ([#958](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/958)). | `KiwiCore+AccessibilityReturn.swift` owns the one-shot debt, armed only when an accessibility system process takes the ignored-panel flag while a window of KiwiDesk's own pid is focused; the click escape, fulfilment, expiry and one-shot are pinned by `AccessibilityReturnTests`. | Click the window you want — a click always wins — or wait out the grace; a returned cmd-tab needs one more press. |
| An app owning no normal (layer-0) window at all — on any Desktop, on any space — when KiwiDesk boots has its Accessibility tree materialized up to ~1 s late, plus the startup sweep's own duration for the last app in its queue: its windows can appear and get tiled a beat after apps the boot scan warmed eagerly. Chromium/Electron apps that are slow to show their first window are the affected class; an app whose windows are merely on another Desktop, on another space, or minimized is warmed eagerly. | The AX warmup is the slowest part of boot (Electron/WebKit answer lazily, 100–300 ms each), and paying it for every windowless helper made time-to-managed scale with apps *running*, not windows *showing*. | The boot scan warms only apps the WindowServer reports as owning a normal window (`AXHelper.pidsWithNormalWindows`); everything else keeps its observer and waits for the next reconcile — at latest the startup sweep, which begins 1 s after boot and is itself chunked ([#801](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/801)); an app the sweep's budget defers waits for the post-pass drain on top — whose warm-on-reconcile promise `StartupWarmupSkipTests` pins ([#662](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/662)). | None planned — the ceiling is the sweep's schedule plus its length, and an app that shows a window sooner is warmed by the reconcile its own activation triggers. |

| An app whose boot work exceeded the 500 ms per-app budget has its windows tiled after its pass, not in the first arrangement — a beat later, and one turn per deferred app, so the second slow app on a session waits behind the first. The affected class is an app whose AX calls block: the measured case cost 5011 ms by itself. The full reasoning is [Design Decisions ▸ Boot](design-decisions.md#boot-the-wait-is-narrated-never-hidden). | One app's AX work cannot be divided, so deferring is the only bound available from inside a blocking call, and the alternative is every other app on the desk waiting for that one — the whole ~10 s boot the chunking exists to end. | A chunked pass raises a per-app budget consulted between blocking AX calls (`EventLoop.openAppBudget`); past it the app's remaining work is dropped, its name logged, and a post-boot drain reconciles it unbudgeted, one per turn (`BootAppBudgetTests`, [#803](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/803)). | None planned — the deferral completes on its own, and activating the app heals it sooner still. The boot log names the app and its eventual cost, which is what a report needs. |
| When KiwiDesk boots, the window-rule re-check that the matched profile's apply would run is postponed to a pass beginning ~1 s after boot — **plus that pass's own duration**, since it is chunked. Where the profile's rules differ from the ones already installed, a window the profile floats is tiled by the boot's first arrangement and floats a beat later; where they resolve to what is already installed, the postponement still applies to the rest of that pass — a window only the later pass discovers returns to its Space but not to its captured slot. A switch to a Desktop bound to another profile postpones the same re-check to the switch's own pass, which applies once its window lists are read — within 0.4 s, and for an app slower to answer when its list arrives: the switch's first arrangement places a window under the outgoing profile's verdicts, and that pass re-places it ([#2347](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2347)). | A second full `reconcileAll` inside boot, unchunked and unbudgeted, pays one AX-unresponsive app's cost a second time — a measured 10.3 s `scan` figure against a 4.9 s scan ([#836](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/836)) — and a visible re-settle in a narrow case is cheaper than a frozen menu bar in every heavy one. | `reconcileAll` is never cut short (accessibility.md — the per-app budget is raised for a queued step, never for a pass), and a float verdict is stored per window at reconcile time (`recheckFloat`), not read from the rules at retile, so the rule write alone cannot re-classify. `setResolvedWindowRules` skips only where a pass it can defer TO is already queued — boot until its tail arms the startup sweep, with `drainDeferredBootApps` covering an app the scan gave up on (`defersWindowRuleReconcileToSweep`), `loadConfig` mid-write, which runs one itself on the way out (`defersWindowRuleReconcile`), and a bound Desktop switch's apply, whose switch requests one right after its handler (`defersRuleSweepToSwitchPass`; `DesktopBindingRuleSweepTests` pins its arm, `DesktopSwitchRuleSweepSeamTests` the pass that follows) — the bound argued once on `mayReconcileWindowRulesNow`; `BootWindowRuleReconcileTests` pins the four arms, `StartupSweepWiringTests` the tail still arming the sweep, `BootDeferralWiringTests` the flag's own four writes. | None planned — the ceiling is the sweep's schedule plus its length, the same band as the windowless-app warmup skip above. Switching profiles by hand after boot re-checks immediately. |
| A **shortcut** pressed while the menu-bar mark is dimmed acts on the windows scanned **so far**: it may tile a partial desk, which the first full arrangement then corrects. The CLI cannot reach this — the socket only starts in the boot tail, so a command sent mid-scan fails to connect. | Hotkeys are armed with the config, before the scan, and a bound key is not a surface that can be greyed the way the quick menu greys its two incomplete-state rows ([#801](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/801); queuing is ruled out in [Design Decisions ▸ Boot](design-decisions.md#boot-the-wait-is-narrated-never-hidden)). | Boot defers event-driven retiles per pass chunk and runs one arrangement in its tail (`defersEventRetiles`, `KiwiCore+Boot`); a command dispatched mid-scan retiles the state that exists at that moment. | Wait for the mark to return to full strength — that is the ready signal ([#802](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/802)) — or re-issue the command, which then acts on the whole desk. |

| Learning an app's size bound costs **one visible probe pass** ([#677](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/677)): on a window's first encounter with a refused size, the retile animates toward the full slot — the focus ring rides out and snaps back once. Otherwise it recurs only when the ledger loses the entry: an invalidation (a genuine resize; a gone window — destroyed or hidden — instead parks its believed entry in a pid-checked tombstone for 30 s, so an AX flap or an unhide re-tiles straight to the learned size without re-dancing, [#1049](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1049)), an eviction (more distinct asks per axis than the ledger's cap — sized past every real producer), or a **settled** compliance that contradicts the entry (the grid-snap edge, deliberately traded for never pinning a window at a size its app stopped insisting on — a transient compliance the app itself revokes clears nothing). |
