A window an app opens **in the background** (`open -g`, a login
item, a helper) takes KiwiDesk's focus ring only when it lands in
a Space with no focused window, so the ring and your keys can still
part there. A Space with no focus takes the first window to arrive
so that switching to it has somewhere to land
([#3152](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/3152)).
Click the window you are typing in to bring the ring back.

Within **10 seconds of an
[`open_in_background`](lua-reference.md#open_in_background)**, one
switch to that app by keyboard (⌘Tab, Spotlight) is handed back to
the window you were in, because macOS reports an app that brings
itself forward the same way it reports a switch you made
([#3141](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/3141)). A
click on the app or its Dock icon always wins, and the hand-back
happens once per app. Press the switch again, or click.

While **Secure Input** is on (a password field, Terminal's Secure
Keyboard Entry), macOS hides key presses from KiwiDesk, so a key
typed between two taps of a modifier cannot end the count: ⌘, a
letter, then ⌘ again can fire a `cmd+cmd` shortcut. No fix is planned
([#1872](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1872)).

The same hiding reaches a
[key sequence](lua-reference.md#define_sequence): a leader written
as a combo does nothing, and keys typed while a sequence is open
reach the front app, a sequence opened by a modifier-tap leader
included. Leave the field first. No fix is planned
([#1871](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1871)).

With **Displays have separate Spaces** off, a `move_to_desktop` that
sends a window to another screen answers before the window moves,
since the move waits for its frame to be written first. If the app
takes longer than about 150 ms, the window moves anyway, may show on
its old screen for a moment, and can land in the Space its screen
shows instead of the one named. If the window was re-created in that
moment, it does not move at all, though the command said it did. Both
leave a line in the log. Move it again
([#3048](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/3048)). No fix
is planned.

A second `move_floating` landing before the app reports the first
re-asks the same frame instead of adding to it, so it is swallowed.
This is the rapid-resize row above with its one difference: `resize`
has a spring to measure from where animation is on, and a move writes
instantly, so a press always measures from the reported frame. Holding
the key is exact. A Space switch inside that lag files the frame from
before the move, as it does for a drag or a `resize`
([#2972](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2972)). Press
again if a burst comes up short. No fix is planned.

A ⌃⌘ or ⌃⌥ press of a
[`move` or `resize` grab](lua-reference.md#gesture-actions) over anything
KiwiDesk cannot move there — the desktop, the Dock, the menu bar, a
bar, a window in full screen or on a Space nobody shows — does
nothing, and the app under the pointer never gets the click. The
pointer tap decides from the event alone, since every pointer event
on the Mac waits on it, and the window under the pointer is looked up
after the press is already swallowed
([#2447](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2447)). Let a
key go and click again. A fix would hand the tap the managed windows'
frames, or post the press again where no window takes it.

A Space switch while `center_floating` is still moving a window can
lose the centring: the switch files the frame the window has reached,
as it does for a window `make_floating` is placing
([#3007](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/3007)). Press
it again on the way back. No fix is planned.

With "Displays have separate Spaces" off and a second screen reaching
past a screen's bottom or right edge, a window near that edge jumps up to
about 32 pt and back on a small resize, unless a neighbouring screen
sits beside the window's whole length there and no third screen reaches
past that edge. macOS refuses the size otherwise, and a refused size leaves the window stuck
([#2966](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2966)). No escape
is planned beyond arranging the screens or turning that setting on.

A window whose close KiwiDesk judges late, most often one closing with
no animation, can keep its tile for under a second. It reads like the
first moment of native full screen, where macOS holds the window on no
Desktop for about half a second, so KiwiDesk waits and the window keeps
its slot (macOS 27.2, separate Spaces off, 2026-11-06,
[#2935](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2935)). No escape
is planned: the wait ends by itself.

An app that keeps one axis or its ratio can show half a resize step
for a moment when a floating window's keyboard resize grows it at a
screen's right or bottom edge, or off every screen. macOS clamps a size write there until
the origin moves, so only the move tells a clamp from a refusal
([#2981](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2981)). No
escape is planned.

A floating window whose app fixes one axis, or which sits at its own
maximum, can show its ring growing past the window on repeated resize
presses or a hold, until the screen's edge stops it, where a press says
"No room left to grow". macOS reports its size as settable, and a short answer alone
looks the same as a cell grid or a late app
([#2994](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2994)). No
escape is planned.

A reload drops the length a grow along a run kept as well, so the
windows it pushed come back once they fit
([#2709](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2709)).

A cross-screen float delivery is sent at most twice: when macOS
re-clamps the window both times, it stays where it was clamped,
and KiwiDesk stops re-sending it
([#2881](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2881)).
Move or drag it to place it.

In a Scrolling row, a focus step or closing the focused window can
show the wrong window of an edge pile for the length of its slide,
until the restack at the end of it
([#2985](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2985)).
Moving a window out of the Space, closing a window that does not hold
the focus, hiding an app, a window arriving, moving the focus from a
float onto the row or changing the slot size or anchor can leave it
there until the row next moves, and a pile showing only a strip can
show a window other than the next one. KiwiDesk keeps only the windows
that show in order, since raising every buried window took longer than
the time a restack is given. A float you focus while the row settles
has the other floats raised once it comes to rest.

After KiwiDesk restarts, the windows waiting on another macOS
Desktop come back to their Space in the order they left, but a
sticky window that stayed in that Space can land between them
rather than where it sat, and a Track column whose head was on
that Desktop can lose its divider until you next leave it. A
restart keeps each Space's waiting windows as a list, so it knows
their order but not their places beside the windows that stayed
or which of them headed a track
([#2907](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2907),
`PendingSlotCarryTests`). Switch Desktops and back, or move the
sticky window back by hand.

The stale-bound row and the probe-pass row above say a genuine
resize forgets what was learned about a window. That holds for a
resize the app makes itself, such as System Settings switching
panes. A resize you make by hand now keeps every learned limit
its new size does not contradict: dragging a window larger keeps
its learned minimum, and only a drag below a minimum or above a
maximum clears that limit
([#2706](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2706)).
So the stale-bound row's hand-resize remedy clears a stale
limit only when the drag goes past it; re-applying the layout
still clears it either way.

A window an app closes by itself **while the screen is locked**
keeps its tile until you unlock, then drops within one heal
tick. Under the lock neither the Accessibility list nor the
on-screen census can be trusted: a display waking behind the
lock drops every window from the census for a moment, and
trusting that would close every window and bring each back as
new at the unlock. So no close is taken from an app's window
list while the session is locked, and the apps refused are
reconciled at the unlock and on the heal ticks after it
([#2538](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2538)).
Nobody sees the desk while it is locked, so nothing is needed.

A snapshot written in **another login session** is discarded at launch too, so after a logout and login without a restart KiwiDesk starts as it does after a restart of the Mac, rather than replaying window ids the new session may reuse ([#1385](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1385)). That covers the Spaces as well as the windows: the active Space, a Space's layout changed from a shortcut or the CLI without saving, and held and temporary Spaces all come back as after a restart, while your saved profiles and settings are untouched.

The first launch after updating onto this version **other than through KiwiDesk's own updater** — replacing the app by hand, for one — starts fresh once in the same way: the older version's quit wrote an arrangement without the login-session mark, which is discarded by design. An update installed by KiwiDesk's own updater keeps the arrangement.

After a restart of the Mac, or a logout and login, KiwiDesk matches the windows macOS reopens to the arrangement it saved when the restart or logout began — or at a Quit of KiwiDesk up to 10 minutes before it — by app and title rather than by window id ([#1385](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1385)); the [Quit & Restart](lua-reference.md#quit--restart) section says how. What the match cannot do is listed here. An app's windows that share one title go back to that app's Spaces in no particular order. A window that reopens with a changed title, or one more than its app had, lands as a new window, and one placed after launch joins its Space where a new window would rather than in its old slot. Held and temporary Spaces, and the Spaces a profile that is not loaded remembers, do not come back. And if a window was hidden, minimized or left with its Desktop in the 30 seconds before the restart began, KiwiDesk cannot tell macOS's quitting from your own work, so it keeps the arrangement as it stood when the restart reached it — after macOS had already closed some of the apps. A logout you cancel and then a Quit of KiwiDesk within two minutes of it still counts as the logout: the next restart puts that arrangement back. Switching profiles, or a Desktop or screen change that switches them, in the first two minutes after launch stops the matching for the windows still to come.

The focused-window shortcut row above has one exception: `focus` itself runs through the activation race when it is KiwiDesk's own raise toward the focused window — a raise pending a scrolling pan or issued a moment ago, while the managed app it left is still in front ([#1812](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1812)). Every other focused verb still waits for the foreground.

The Layout menu subtitle row above has a remedy on every macOS: KiwiHub's view picker (`⌃⌥L`) names the layout of the Space under the pointer and adds "not saved to profile" while it drifts.

Keeping a sync folder in step ([#2324](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2324); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md#following-a-sync-folder-mirrors-it-one-sides-change-at-a-time)) copies one file at a time. A Save that writes several files can reach the other Mac a file at a time, so for about a second that Mac may show part of the change. A profile whose name contains "conflict" is taken for a sync app's conflict copy and does not sync. Deleting `gui.json` or `init.lua` does not delete it on the other Macs: KiwiDesk writes a starter file back on its next load, and that file syncs. A list both Macs edited — the app rules, say — is one Yours / Theirs row for the whole list in the sheet at Save, so the pick keeps one Mac's entries and drops the other's. Loading a profile or deleting a Space writes that Mac's Space list into `gui.json`, which the other Macs read only at their next launch, before a profile applies.

An App Bar item reads KiwiDesk's own layout, not what the screen draws ([#2234](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2234)). A window KiwiDesk does not manage — a picture-in-picture video, another app's panel — covering a tile leaves the tile's item lit, a float covering a tile does too by ruling, and two unfocused floats that overlap both read lit, since only the focused window is known to be on top. Asking the WindowServer what is drawn would see all of it, at the price of a round trip on every bar refresh, which stalls under GPU load ([#1925](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1925)).


The sticky-window row above covers the *gesture* switch too: a
sticky window whose app drops its Accessibility element before
KiwiDesk hears of a swipe is carried onto the arriving Desktop
with its slot, sticky scope and reach pin kept
([#1215](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1215)),
rather than staying on the Desktop you left until you return.

When you leave a macOS Desktop with a sticky window focused and
come back, that window takes the focus back once the switch has
settled, even though macOS first restores the focus to the last
window that stayed on that Desktop
([#1564](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1564)).
A click on another window during the switch keeps your choice.

A window you closed and then reopened — an app whose close hides the window and whose reopen shows the same one again, Telegram's main window for one — comes back like a new window: to the Space its app rule names, else the Space you are on, taking the focus there in every layout, rather than to the Space you closed it in with the slot it had there ([#1414](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1414), [#1561](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1561); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md)); the [#1161](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1161) row's bounce no longer reaches it. What remains: an app that re-shows a closed window on its own, with nothing you did behind it, takes the focus once, where you are.

On macOS 27 the focus that a menu-bar reveal moves to the previous app comes back: while the previous app's bar is revealed the Settings window looks inactive, and once the pointer leaves the edge — or KiwiDesk's menu-bar menu closes — KiwiDesk returns the focus to it once ([#1532](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1532), [#2224](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2224); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md)). A click in the menu bar keeps the return; another window taking the focus meanwhile, or a shortcut that moves the focus, is honored instead.

The rejection in the row above has a second form. Issued while the Space KiwiDesk shows is **empty** — after `move_to_desktop` and a `focus_desktop` to that Desktop ([Lua reference ▸ move_to_desktop](lua-reference.md#move_to_desktop)) — a focused-window shortcut is rejected, and the refusal names it: `the active Space 2 is empty; the focused window (Finder) is in Space 1 — focus_space 1 first`, which the log carries too ([#1336](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1336); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md#an-empty-active-space-refuses-by-name-1336)). What remains: the verb acts only on the Space you are on, so the window that `get_state` marks focused in another Space is parked, not focused, until `focus_space` brings its Space back.

Dragging a **stack** window's edge along its zone's own axis — a height drag beside a left or right stack, a width drag beside a top or bottom one — moves the dragged window's share of its zone, as the keyboard `resize` does ([#941](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/941); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md#layout-and-resize-behavior)). What remains: a master zone lined up *along* the split has no cross-axis share to move, by the row above on masters' shares, so that drag snaps back.

**Grid** ([#763](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/763)):
a grid column or row is drawn at least as long as Grid's
`min_window_size` and the learned minimum of every window that
sits in it alone, taking the room from the other tracks by their
weights. So the split-layout row's "a Grid cell" means only a
cell that spans several tracks — the last cell of a short row
under `fill_empty_cells` — and KiwiDesk's own Settings window
widens its grid column like any other app.

A Grid's scrolling last track instead takes, across its scroll
axis, the largest learned minimum of every member, hidden ones
included, and its members lift no column or row along it
([When windows no longer fit](lua-reference.md#when-windows-no-longer-fit)).
BSP's scrolling line does the same across its axis, as far as
the window split off beside it keeps `min_window_size`
([#2542](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2542)),
so a window in it is one the split-layout row's "deeper BSP
split" leaves at its minimum on that axis only past that
point.

A Grid's column and row count, fixed or
[auto-sized](lua-reference.md#gridset_auto_size), also falls to
fit the largest learned minimum among the Space's windows, and
grows back when that window leaves
([#2687](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2687)).
So the Settings window row's three-column grid on a laptop
screen drops a column rather than overlapping a neighbour, once
the 720 pt floor is learned.

Opening an app whose [app rule](lua-reference.md#app_rules) sends its window to another space takes you there only when the app came forward **within about a second of a click or key press** with no window of its own showing — a launch, a reopen, an un-minimize — or through `focus_or_spawn` ([#1599](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1599); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md#opening-an-app-follows-its-window-into-its-rules-space-1599)). macOS reports that an app became active, never why, so the timing of your last press and whether the app showed a window stand in for the cause. What remains: an app a script opens other than through `focus_or_spawn` (`open -a`, say) leaves you where you are, and so does a first window that appears more than about ten seconds after the app comes forward. An app with no window showing that brings itself forward within a second of a press you made elsewhere takes you along as if you had opened it. Use `focus_space` to reach the window when you are left behind.

A slow cold start takes you there too: the press counts when the app's process started within about a second of it, even when the app then takes up to about fifteen seconds to come forward ([#2201](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2201)). What remains: a click or key press you make between the launch and the app coming forward takes that place, so the app leaves you where you are unless it comes forward within a second of that later press.

New Window, or an un-minimize from the window switcher, pressed in the moment after a macOS Desktop switch — before KiwiDesk has read the arriving Desktop's windows, under half a second — does not take you to the window's Space when that window arrives with the switch's own windows; it opens where its app rule files it ([#2347](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2347)). A window of the same app that the switch reveals cannot take you there instead either.

Picking a window that was already in native full screen on a Space
no screen showed as KiwiDesk started brings the app forward, until
its Space has been shown once
([#2939](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2939),
[#2949](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2949)).
macOS gives KiwiDesk no handle on a window whose full-screen Space is
not shown. Show the Space once from Mission Control or with a swipe;
from then on, picking it shows its Space.

Reopening an app whose last window you closed while the app kept running can take you to **another macOS Desktop**. Some apps — Microsoft Word for one — hide a closed window and show that same window again when you click the app in the Dock, and macOS switches to the Desktop that window was on before KiwiDesk hears of it (measured 2026-10-13). KiwiDesk does not switch you back: undoing a switch macOS has already made would move you between two Desktops on every reopen ([#1515](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1515)). An app you quit opens its next window on the Desktop you are on. macOS's own *When switching to an application, switch to a Space with open windows for the application* (System Settings ▸ Desktop & Dock ▸ Mission Control) governs that switch; whether turning it off keeps you on your Desktop for a re-shown window is not measured.

[`new_window`](lua-reference.md#new_window) takes you there too, whatever the app already shows. It finds the app's **File ▸ New Window** by its ⌘N or ⇧⌘N shortcut and a word for "window" in any language macOS ships, because apps expose no other name for that menu item ([#1518](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1518)). What remains: an app whose New Window has no such shortcut (Claude's "New Session in New Window") is refused with a pill even though it has the item.

A new window of a running app takes you there too when its app
rule sends it to a Space no screen is showing — ⌘N, File ▸ New,
or one the app opens on its own
([#2478](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2478)).
What remains: in the first 15 seconds after the app's process
starts, its new window takes you along only when a click or key
press came within a second before it, so a window macOS reopens
at login in the same second as an unrelated press takes you
along, and a window a just-launched app opens on its own stays
where the rule files it. A new window that appears before the
window of another app you just opened has arrived stays too.
KiwiDesk tells a new window from one it is only now adopting by
WindowServer's create notification; where that route is
unavailable, only opening the app takes you along. Use
`focus_space` to reach the window when you are left behind.

A popup an app opens while you are opening it moves to the app's
space with you
([#3189](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/3189)).
What remains: a popup that opens before the app comes forward
stays in the space it opened in, and so does every popup of an
open whose window showed before the app came forward. KiwiDesk
ties a popup to an open through the app coming forward, which
macOS reports after such a window.

The [`window_created`](lua-reference.md#events) event reads the
same notification to tell `new` from `existing`
([#2630](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2630)). An
app whose new windows WindowServer never reports opening has
each of them reported `existing`, half a second late. A window
you open with ⌘N may also have its `window_created` arrive up to
half a second after its `focus_change` (measured 8–10 ms for
TextEdit): KiwiDesk places and focuses the window at once, and only
the event waits for macOS to report the window opening. Listen to
`focus_change` when timing matters. An app too slow to finish
loading when KiwiDesk starts is read a few seconds later; a window
it opens in that time that macOS does not report through
Accessibility is reported `existing` and does not take you along.

Open or Focus asks a running app with **no window at all** for a new one, the way a Dock click does, and it judges "no window" from what it can see ([#1840](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1840)). A window on another Desktop counts only once KiwiDesk has seen it: on a Mac where the per-Desktop window list cannot be read none does, and anywhere else a window the app opened on a Desktop nobody has shown since does not, so the shortcut sends that reopen anyway. Whether the app then opens a second window beside the one on the other Desktop is the app's own reopen handling. Not observed; reasoned from the mechanism. Switch to the Desktop that holds the window to reach it instead.

With the **Space Bar off**, switching a Space between a layout that shows an App Bar (Monocle, Scrolling) and one that does not moves its windows by the bar strip's depth: [KiwiShelf](lua-reference.md#kiwishelf) reserves its edge only in a layout where a bar draws ([#1517](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1517); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md)). Reserving it in every layout instead would leave an empty strip on screen in every layout that draws nothing there. With the Space Bar on, the strip is reserved in every layout and no switch moves a window.

The same holds, with the Space Bar on, for an App Bar on an edge of its own: its edge is reserved only in the layouts that show it, so switching a Space between Monocle or Scrolling and a layout without an App Bar moves its windows by the App Bar's strip ([#1731](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1731); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md)). Put both bars on one edge and the switch moves nothing again.

Or set the bar not to reserve its strip at all
([`space_bar.set_reserve`](lua-reference.md#space_barset_reserve),
[`app_bar.set_reserve`](lua-reference.md#app_barset_reserve)): it
then draws over the windows and no switch moves one.

The light-`fill_color` glass row above also reaches surfaces that are not bars: the **sticky mark** on its default **Automatic** color, and a sticky color light enough to pin nothing, are unpinned glass too, as is the untinted drag drop zone. Over dark window content macOS may draw such a mark's glass dark while its glyph — the system label color under KiwiDesk's Appearance — stays dark. Not observed; reasoned from the mechanism ([#1621](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1621)). A dark `sticky.set_color` pins the glass dark with a light glyph; `sticky.set_liquid_glass(false)` returns the badge with its disc.

The **floating mark** is unpinned glass on the same terms, with
`floating.set_color` in place of the sticky color.

An update's **Install and Relaunch** leaves the windows in place without checking who signed the new version, unlike `kiwidesk service restart`, which checks ([#930](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/930)). Sparkle has already validated the update, and every KiwiDesk release is signed with the same Developer ID and notarized. If a future release ever changed that identity, macOS would drop the Accessibility permission across the update: the windows would stay where the old version left them, hidden spaces' windows parked off screen, until the permission is granted again and the next launch restores the arrangement.

An in-place restart brings back every size you set, but not what KiwiDesk **learned** about an app's own minimum or maximum size ([#930](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/930)). A layout that had adjusted to such an app — fewer tracks, a narrower column — may ask for the unadjusted frame once after the restart and settle back when the app refuses it again. A window whose app is still starting when the new process scans comes back as the new process finds it, so a window you had made sticky by hand in such an app may return without it.

**Held Spaces** — those a profile switch kept, with their windows, for the profile it left ([#1507](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1507)) — come back after KiwiDesk quits, restarts or crashes, but not after a restart of the Mac ([#1646](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1646)). A held Space names its windows by the ids they had before the restart, which a restart retires, and no restore re-keys a hold: they are placed as on any fresh start, and the held Space would have been empty anyway. A held Space whose windows were closed while KiwiDesk was down ends shortly after launch, once macOS confirms they are gone; on a Mac where KiwiDesk cannot ask macOS which windows exist, such a Space stays in the Space Bar, empty, until the next time KiwiDesk starts, or until you delete it with `delete_space` or reset every setting. With more than one screen, the restart brings back the Space in front of you on the screen that has focus; another screen may come back showing a different one of its Spaces.

A profile that is not loaded keeps the Spaces it remembers for its windows across a KiwiDesk quit, restart or crash, and loses them with a restart of the Mac ([#1802](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1802)). **General ▸ Files & Reset ▸ Saved window arrangement ▸ Discard** clears what every profile remembers.

A logout and login loses them too, as a restart of the Mac does ([#1385](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1385)).

The **Play a sound when an action is blocked** setting and the **windows per pile on quit** are app-wide, kept in `gui.json` and in no profile ([#1741](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1741); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md#spaces-profiles--config-ownership)). On the upgrade itself, and when restoring a backup written before that change, the first saved profile loaded lends its values and every other profile's are dropped. Set both on **General** if that profile was not the one whose values you wanted.

With a **Lua-owned** `init.lua`, neither value is read from a profile file any more: `init.lua` is where both are kept ([#1741](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1741)), and General's two rows are greyed. A setup that relied on a profile's own copy runs at the defaults until `init.lua` calls `set_refusal_sound` and `quit.set_grid_target_depth`.

The four **animation lengths** cross the same way ([#3237](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/3237)): on the update, the first saved profile loaded lends them and every other profile's are dropped, and no Settings row sets one of them alone — call `animations.set_duration`, `set_scroll_duration`, `set_expand_duration` or `set_reveal_duration` from `init.lua`. With a Lua-owned `init.lua` they run at the defaults until it sets them.

Settings sets how fast KiwiDesk animates only through **Animation speed**, whose Very Slow, Slow, Medium and Fast each write one table of six lengths ([#3238](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/3238), [#3254](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/3254); the tables are in the [Lua reference](lua-reference.md#animation-cascade)): the four above, the Space slide's and the KiwiVision fade's. Settings cannot make one motion faster or slower alone; a length of your own is `init.lua`'s, and the preset then shows no speed picked. The KiwiVision **Fade curve** stays in Settings and shapes a fade whose length Settings does not show.

A KiwiVision lens made in Settings fades at the plain KiwiVision length and curve ([#3246](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/3246); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md#spaces-profiles--config-ownership)). On the update, and when restoring an older backup, every lens stored in `gui.json` loses its own fade length and curve, and no Settings row sets them again. A lens's own fade is `init.lua`'s, through a [`kiwivision.define_lens`](lua-reference.md#kiwivisiondefine_lens) table, and one already set there stays while `init.lua` owns the setup; moving the setup to Settings drops it, and a lens edited in Settings drops a fade the CLI gave it for the session.

The **shared look** lives in `gui.json`, and a KiwiDesk from before profiles could share a look drops it when it saves that file — a second Mac syncing `~/.config/KiwiDesk` on an older version, say ([#1752](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1752); the ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md)). Back on this version, the first saved profile loaded lends the shared look again, and a profile that shared a different one keeps it as its own; nothing on screen changes. Set it to share again in **Looks & Animations ▸ Shared look** if it should.

A window with **no title-bar buttons and no accessibility content** that is the first window its app shows — a decoration-less terminal or game window, when the app has just launched — is managed up to three seconds late ([#1785](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1785)). An app's "shadow" window (Orion's "Orion Preview") is told from such a window by the buttoned window of its own process beside it, and at launch that sibling can list over a second after the shadow, so a lone shell waits for one before it tiles; an app already showing a managed window pays no wait, and no known app ships a real window of that shape. The escape is `float_rules`, which floats the window as soon as it is managed but cannot shorten the wait.

A window that fills its whole screen — a slide show, a borderless-fullscreen game — is left where its app put it and hides both bars while it is in front ([#1787](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1787)). KiwiDesk tells it from a window you maximise by its missing title bar, so a titled window whose app reports itself as untitled still reads as one when it fills its screen ([#1788](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1788)). The bars come back at the next focus change, so a window of an app KiwiDesk ignores stepping in front of a show leaves them hidden until then, and a screen-filling window KiwiDesk does not manage keeps them drawn over it.

With Space switches on Slide, a window of an app that is slow
to move — System Settings is the usual one — can land a moment
after the plates have faded, and under a heavily loaded GPU a
window can stay visible for an instant after the slide
([#1956](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1956)).
KiwiDesk sends each window its move at the press and holds the
arriving ones until the plates land, but when the app performs
the move is the app's.

The same holds with **Step between Spaces (mouse or trackpad)** on
Slide.

A Stack zone, a Track track — the overflow track included —, a
Grid's last track (#2541) or BSP's scrolling line
([#2542](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2542)),
whose windows do not all fit at their minimums, an app's own
learned minimum among them, shows only the windows that do
([When windows no longer fit](lua-reference.md#when-windows-no-longer-fit)).
Each hidden window waits off screen, parked at the screen's
bottom corner like the windows of a Space you are not on, so it
never shows in the zone whatever size its app insists on. A
window scrolling in appears in its slot at once rather than
sliding there, since focusing it raises it over its neighbour.
An app's own minimum is learned only after it refuses a size,
so the first time such a shown window is placed it may overhang
its slot for one pass, until the next pass shows fewer
windows. A tiled sticky window scrolls and hides like any
other, and its sticky mark is not drawn while it is hidden
([#2235](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2235)).
KiwiDesk cannot read another app's minimum size and learns it
from the sizes the app refuses
([#677](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/677)), and
a hidden window is one focus step away, so it needs no slot of
its own. BSP's line can start beside a fixed window, under
either strategy, and the overflow mark at that end sits
across the gap, covering a few points of that window: the mark
rides the line's edge window, and the gap is narrower than the
mark.

The focus ring disappears with the desktop when Mission Control
opens and comes back when it closes, in either draw order and
with or without glow
([#1917](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1917)). A
swipe let go before Mission Control opens leaves the ring drawn
until the swipe ends
([#1921](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1921)).

That is accepted for now: until Mission Control opens, the swipe
gives KiwiDesk no signal but the raw finger contacts on the
trackpad, which KiwiDesk reads only for its own gesture slots
([#1873](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/1873)),
never for the ring.

With KiwiVision on, the window you move the focus away from stays clear for a split second — about 40–60 ms — after you click or switch, until KiwiDesk hears that the focus moved ([#2103](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2103)). A floating window shows it most, since it sits on top. macOS reports a focus change through Accessibility only after the window has come forward.

When `init.lua` owns the shortcuts, the shortcuts panel (`⌃⌥K`) lists every chord it registered, but names each one only as well as its source spells it ([#2482](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2482)). An inline action KiwiDesk knows is listed by name, any other inline body as its raw Lua, and a binding to a named handler or a C function as **Lua function**. A body that reads a variable shows its value only where that value is a string, number or true/false the panel can spell exactly and the file never assigns the name; otherwise the row shows its raw Lua, since the value could not be shown as fact. The panel reads the bindings back once per load, right after `init.lua` runs, so a `bind` or `define_layer` that runs later, from an event hook, is not listed, and while a layer defined that way is active the panel shows the first layer it knows. The chords KiwiHub and the menus print beside an action read the same list, so they now show an `init.lua` chord too. Spelling the action inline — `function() KiwiDesk.focus("left") end` — names the row; Settings ▸ Shortcuts ▸ **Import from init.lua…** moves the shortcuts into the visual editor.

A `desc` names such a row too ([Describing a Shortcut](lua-reference.md#describing-a-shortcut)).

A window that an app lifts above the normal window level *after*
KiwiDesk tiled it stays tiled — a player's "float on top" toggle,
or an app that sets a window's level a moment after opening it —
until the window reopens or KiwiDesk restarts
([#2572](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2572)).
KiwiDesk judges the level once, when it adopts the window, because
Brave lifted its tiled main window to that level each time it came
forward with a site permission prompt open (2026-10-23), and
re-judging it floated and shrank the window on every lift. Float
the window yourself (`make_floating`, or **Float Window** in its
App Bar item's right-click menu) to float it at once; a Float rule
for the app applies once the level drops. While Brave holds its
window at that level, the window also covers any part of the Space
Bar or App Bar that overlaps it — a revealed shelf, a peek — since
the bars sit at the floating window level, below it; they show
again as soon as the prompt closes or Brave loses focus.

A window in the [pocket](lua-reference.md#pocket) cannot be taken
out, or put back, while its app is hidden: the `pocket` command
refuses
([#2446](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2446)). A
hidden app's windows leave KiwiDesk's tracking, and a window
KiwiDesk does not track cannot be moved. Show the app again —
`⌘-Tab`, a Dock click, its row in KiwiHub's window switcher — and
the pocket answers as before.

Where macOS does not expose the window-management bridge, the
pocket window is not carried across macOS Desktops: a window left
in the pocket on another Desktop can be taken out only from that
Desktop ([#2446](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2446)).
Moving a window between Desktops needs that bridge, the same one
sticky windows' Desktop reach needs; on a Mac that has it, the
pocket window comes along with every switch.

Switching to the app of a window you pocketed — `⌘-Tab`, a Dock
click — within a second of pocketing it leaves the focus on the
parked window instead of taking it out
([#2446](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2446)).
For that second KiwiDesk reads a focus report for the pocketed
window as the echo of pocketing it, which an app can still send,
and swallows it. Press `⌃⌥P` to take the window out.

The pocket's **Holds** setting moved onto each profile as the
Pocket row under KiwiShelf ▸ Show ▸ Each bar and Pocket
([#2978](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2978); the
ruling is in [design decisions](design-decisions.md#the-pocket-belongs-to-kiwishelf-2678)).
On the upgrade every saved profile takes a value from it, but a
built-in Standard — what KiwiDesk uses where no saved profile matches
your screens — has no saved file to take one, so it shows the pocket
Always. If Holds was One window, set Pocket to Hidden there and Save.
A profile that crossed from One window shows **Show** with nothing
selected until you choose one, since its Pocket row reads Hidden and
its bars do not. A setup `init.lua` owns has no saved profile to
cross either: one that never called `pocket.set_capacity` showed the
pocket only while it was used, and now shows it Always until
`init.lua` adds `kiwishelf.set_pocket_visibility("hidden")`. A
profile file that would not read at the upgrade keeps the old
setting waiting for its next read only until KiwiDesk next rewrites
its settings file, after which it shows the pocket Always.

An app's own Pocket key ([`pocket_app`](lua-reference.md#pocket_app))
forgets its window when KiwiDesk quits
([#2612](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2612)): the
quit files the window as the [pocket](lua-reference.md#pocket) files
every pocket window, and the next press of the key opens a fresh
window of the app. Which window a key owns is kept only for a
restart that comes straight back — an update, or `kiwidesk service
restart` — and never written to a profile, so nothing else can hand
it back.

An app whose File menu has no New Window, with its windows all on
another macOS Desktop, opens nothing on its Pocket key: the key
reopens the app, which only brings one of those windows forward, and
for about ten seconds a second press waits for a window that never
comes. The window count KiwiDesk reads sees only the Desktop shown.

A [stack flip](lua-reference.md#stacktoggle_stack_position) lasts
for the session and is filed under the macOS Desktop's own id
([#2771](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2771)), so a
restart of KiwiDesk, a quit and relaunch, and a screen replug that
makes macOS give a Desktop a new id each put the stack back on its
authored side. A screen plugged in since the last Desktop switch
refuses the flip until you switch Desktops once. To keep a side for
one Desktop, bind a profile with that side to it
([Design Decisions ▸ A stack flip belongs to one Desktop](design-decisions.md#a-stack-flip-belongs-to-one-desktop-2771)).

The sizes a [resize](lua-reference.md#resize) writes are filed
under the same Desktop id and the profile live there
([#2921](https://github.com/KiwiCanopy/KiwiDesk/issues/2921)): a
screen replug that makes macOS give a Desktop a new id returns that
Desktop's Spaces to the override, then the global value. On a
screen plugged in since the last Desktop switch, a resize writes one
set of sizes that every Desktop KiwiDesk cannot name shares; the
first Desktop switch on that screen leaves them behind, and the
Desktop shown uses the override, then the global value, until you
resize again.

pages.title: Recipes
pages.description: Integration patterns for KiwiDesk with tools like sketchybar, borders, and shell scripts.

sections.heading: Recipes
parts:
# Recipes

Real-world integration patterns for KiwiDesk. All recipes use
either Lua event callbacks or the CLI event stream — no plugins
required.

sections.heading: Integration approaches
parts:
## Integration approaches

**Lua hooks** (in `init.lua`): Subscribe to events within the
KiwiDesk Lua VM and trigger side effects directly. This is the
fastest path: no subprocess overhead, stateless, fire-and-forget.
Use this for tools that accept external command invocation
(sketchybar `--trigger`, borders `active_color=...`).

**CLI event stream** (shell scripts, other processes): Use
`kiwidesk subscribe <events...>` to receive newline-delimited
JSON from a separate terminal session or script. Query state
on-demand with `kiwidesk get_state` and `kiwidesk list_monitors`.
Use this when you need durable polling, cross-process
communication, or your tool runs in a different sandbox (like
Hammerspoon).

sections.heading: External commands (KiwiDesk.exec)
parts:
## External commands (KiwiDesk.exec)

Commands run asynchronously in the background and never block
window management. They append `/opt/homebrew/bin` and
`/usr/local/bin` to the child's PATH so Homebrew tools resolve.
See the [Lua reference](../lua-reference.md) for the full
`KiwiDesk.exec` and `os.execute` API, including callback,
timeout, and output capture.

> **Binary path note:** installed through the Homebrew cask,
> KiwiDesk is on your PATH as plain `kiwidesk` — use that
> directly. If you built from source instead, it is not on PATH:
> use the absolute path to your built binary (e.g.,
> `~/path/to/KiwiDesk/.build/release/KiwiDesk`) or symlink it
> yourself. The recipes below keep the path in a variable like
> `KIWIDESK=kiwidesk` so either setup works.

sections.heading: Recipe pages
parts:
## Recipe pages

- [**SketchyBar**](sketchybar.md) — spaces widget with click
  to focus, window icons, layout-aware styling, and a theme picker
  that repaints KiwiDesk. The flagship integration.
- [**JankyBorders**](jankyborders.md) — layout-aware border
  colors via the `layout_change` event.
- [**Miscellaneous**](misc.md) — shell scripts, event stream
  queries, Hammerspoon, per-Desktop keybinds.

pages.title: JankyBorders Integration
pages.description: Layout-aware window border colors based on the active layout mode.

sections.heading: JankyBorders
parts:
# JankyBorders

[JankyBorders](https://github.com/FelixKratz/JankyBorders)
(macOS window borders via [`borders`](https://github.com/FelixKratz/borders))
works standalone out of the box — it follows macOS focus
automatically.

For layout-aware border colors, subscribe to the `layout_change`
event and pass the mode name to `borders`:

```lua
KiwiDesk.on("layout_change", function(space_id, mode)
    local colors = {
        bsp       = "0xFFBD93F9",  -- purple
        stack     = "0xFF50FA7B",  -- green
        scrolling = "0xFF8BE9FD",  -- cyan
        monocle   = "0xFFFF79C6",  -- pink
        grid      = "0xFFFFB86C",  -- orange
        floating  = "0x00000000",  -- transparent
    }
    local c = colors[mode] or "0xFFFFFFFF"
    KiwiDesk.exec("borders active_color=" .. c)
end)
```

Install `borders` via Homebrew:

```sh
brew install felixkratz/formulae/borders
```

Color format is `0xAARRGGBB` (alpha + RGB). The example colors
are from [Dracula](https://draculatheme.com/) — adjust to your
theme.

pages.title: Miscellaneous Integrations
pages.description: Shell scripts, event streaming, Hammerspoon, and per-Desktop keybindings.

sections.heading: Miscellaneous Integrations
parts: # Miscellaneous Integrations

sections.heading: Shell scripts & event streaming
parts:
## Shell scripts & event streaming

Any process can subscribe to KiwiDesk events as newline-delimited
JSON:

```sh
KIWIDESK=kiwidesk   # or a source build's full path

"$KIWIDESK" subscribe space_change | while read -r line; do
    space=$(echo "$line" | jq -r '.data.space_id')
    echo "switched to space $space"
done
```

Query state on demand:

```sh
# List all spaces and their layout modes:
"$KIWIDESK" get_state | jq '.spaces[] | {id, mode}'

# List screens:
"$KIWIDESK" list_monitors | jq
```

The event stream is useful for durable external daemons, shell
functions, or tools that run in a different sandbox than
KiwiDesk. Each event has an `event` field (e.g.,
`"space_change"`) and a `data` object with fields matching the
Lua callback arguments
(e.g., `space_id`, `mode`).

sections.heading: Hammerspoon
parts:
## Hammerspoon

Drive KiwiDesk from Hammerspoon (or vice versa) through the CLI
(see the [recipes intro](index.md) for the binary path):

```lua
-- Absolute: Hammerspoon is a GUI app, so its os.execute inherits
-- launchd's minimal PATH without /opt/homebrew/bin. Swap in your
-- clone's path if you built from source.
local KIWIDESK = "/opt/homebrew/bin/kiwidesk"

hs.hotkey.bind({"cmd", "alt"}, "m", function()
    os.execute("'" .. KIWIDESK .. "' set_mode monocle")
end)
```

Or set up space switching via KiwiDesk:

```lua
hs.hotkey.bind({"cmd", "alt"}, "1", function()
    os.execute("'" .. KIWIDESK .. "' focus_space 1")
end)
```

**Tip:** KiwiDesk's own modal keybindings (see
[configuration](../lua-reference.md)) cover most Hammerspoon
window-management use cases natively, and they do not require
another daemon. If you are already running Hammerspoon for
other reasons, the CLI bridge above lets you invoke KiwiDesk
commands without duplicating logic.

sections.heading: Per-Desktop keybindings (hand-written configs)
parts:
## Per-Desktop keybindings (hand-written configs)

> **Native support exists now:** A profile can carry a sparse
> `"layers"` override that shadows individual base shortcuts.
> Combined with `bind_profile_to_desktop`, each Desktop
> gets its own layouts and its own keybinds with no Lua code.
> See *Config cascade* under
> [Keybindings](../lua-reference.md). This recipe remains for
> hand-written (non-GUI-managed) configs, where Lua owns all
> keybindings.

For a hand-written config, combine shortcut layers with the
`desktop_change` event. Only the active layer's bindings
fire, so build each Desktop's layer by merging shared binds with
per-Desktop overrides:

```lua
-- Shared binds, active in every layer:
local common = {
    ["cmd+alt+1"] = function()
        KiwiDesk.focus_space("1")
    end,
    ["cmd+alt+2"] = function()
        KiwiDesk.focus_space("2")
    end,
    ["cmd+alt+left"] = function()
        KiwiDesk.focus("left")
    end,
    ["cmd+alt+right"] = function()
        KiwiDesk.focus("right")
    end,
    -- ... other shared binds
}

-- Helper: merge common binds with per-layer overrides.
local function layer(overrides)
    local merged = {}
    for k, v in pairs(common) do
        merged[k] = v
    end
    for k, v in pairs(overrides) do
        merged[k] = v
    end
    return merged
end

-- Desktop 1: standard binds, no overrides.
KiwiDesk.define_layer("desk1", layer({}))

-- Desktop 2: override cmd+alt+m to enter the monocle layout.
KiwiDesk.define_layer("desk2", layer({
    ["cmd+alt+m"] = function()
        KiwiDesk.set_mode("monocle")
    end,
}))

-- Switch layer when the macOS Desktop changes. Only the main
-- screen's Desktop counts ("Displays have separate Spaces"
-- makes secondary screens report their own switches too):
KiwiDesk.on("desktop_change", function(n, monitor)
    if monitor ~= 1 then return end
    KiwiDesk.switch_layer(n == 2 and "desk2" or "desk1")
end)

-- Start on Desktop 1.
KiwiDesk.switch_layer("desk1")
```

Pair this with `bind_profile_to_desktop` (see
[configuration](../lua-reference.md)) and each Desktop gets
its own layouts *and* its own keybinds.

pages.title: SketchyBar Integration
pages.description: Build a spaces widget with KiwiDesk events, window icons, and click-to-focus.

sections.heading: SketchyBar
parts:
# SketchyBar

The flagship integration: a live spaces widget with click to
focus, window icons per space, and layout-aware styling.

sections.heading: How the bridge works
parts:
## How the bridge works

KiwiDesk never triggers sketchybar events itself. Instead, you
write a hook in your `init.lua` that listens to KiwiDesk events
and calls `sketchybar --trigger <custom-event>` via
`KiwiDesk.exec`. Your sketchybar items subscribe to that custom
event and update when it fires.

```
KiwiDesk event → init.lua hook → sketchybar --trigger custom-event
                                      ↓
                            sketchybar item script runs
                            (queries get_state, updates display)
```

This decouples the two processes: sketchybar's script runs in
its own Lua sandbox, outside the app watchdog and main-thread
restrictions.

> **Wedged daemon → runaway triggers.**
> `sketchybar --trigger` normally exits in milliseconds. If the
> sketchybar daemon is absent or wedged, the trigger blocks instead
> — and because these hooks fire on *every* KiwiDesk event,
> unbounded fire-and-forget would let thousands of stuck `--trigger`
> processes pile up (re-parented to launchd, some alive for hours),
> measurably loading the scheduler.
>
> `KiwiDesk.exec` bounds this automatically: each trigger gets a
> 30 s default `timeout` and identical in-flight commands are
> deduped, so even a permanently wedged daemon leaves **at most
> one** stuck child per distinct trigger, reaped every 30 s (see
> [`KiwiDesk.exec`](../lua-reference.md#kiwideskexec)). KiwiDesk
> also warns in its log once more than 20 children are outstanding.
>
> If you hit a pile-up from an older config (or a hard-wedged
> daemon), clear the clients and restart the daemon:
>
> ```sh
> pkill -f "sketchybar --trigger"    # clients only, not the daemon
> brew services restart sketchybar
> ```

sections.heading: Events you can subscribe to
parts:
## Events you can subscribe to

Every event below fires whenever KiwiDesk's state changes. Hook
any of them to keep sketchybar in sync:

| Event | Lua arguments | Fires when |
|---|---|---|
| `space_change` | `space_id`, `mode` | A KiwiDesk space switches |
| `layout_change` | `space_id`, `mode` | Layout mode changes on a space |
| `focus_change` | `window_id`, `app`, `bundle_id` | Focused window changes |
| `monitor_change` | `monitor_count` | Screens connect or disconnect |
| `desktop_change` | `desktop`, `monitor` | A macOS Desktop switches on some screen (`monitor` 1 is the main screen) |
| `window_created` | `window_id`, `app`, `space`, `reason`, `bundle_id` | A managed window appears ([reasons](../lua-reference.md#events)) |
| `window_destroyed` | `window_id`, `app`, `space`, `reason`, `bundle_id`, `desktop` | A managed window disappears (`closed`/`minimized`/`hidden`/`vanished`); `desktop` names the Desktop holding a `vanished` window, else `nil` |
| `window_moved_to_space` | `window_id`, `app`, `from`, `to`, `bundle_id` | See caveats |
| `layer_change` | `from`, `to` | The active keyboard layer changes (layer names, `default` included) |

**Caveats:**

- `window_created` and `window_destroyed` track the *visible
  window set*, not app lifecycle — deminiaturizing and macOS
  Desktop switches also fire them. Filter on the `reason`
  argument to ignore the artifacts (`vanished`/`returned`
  bursts on every Mission Control round-trip). A window closed
  while its Desktop was off-screen sends its corrective
  `closed` when KiwiDesk next reads the Desktops — at the next
  Desktop switch, or within about five seconds — so it fires
  two destroys, `vanished` then `closed`. Keep a
  `desktop_change` handler that re-queries state anyway: it is
  the shape that stays right whatever a consumer filters.
- `space` in Lua callbacks is always a string (the space id).
  A window on an unknown space receives `""` (empty string
  instead of nil, so the argument list doesn't truncate). In
  the CLI JSON event stream, the key is `space_id` and the
  value is `null` for unknown spaces.
- `window_moved_to_space` fires only on explicit
  `move_to_space` commands with a different target;
  bulk operations like profile loads stay silent.

sections.heading: Minimal recipe
parts:
## Minimal recipe

A simple space label + layout mode display:

```lua
KiwiDesk.on("space_change", function(space_id, mode)
    KiwiDesk.exec(
        "sketchybar --trigger kiwi_space_change "
        .. "SPACE=" .. space_id .. " MODE=" .. mode)
end)

KiwiDesk.on("focus_change", function(window_id, app)
    KiwiDesk.exec(
        "sketchybar --trigger kiwi_focus APP='"
        .. app .. "'")
end)

-- macOS Desktop indicator (the number focus_desktop takes). With
-- "Displays have separate Spaces" on, secondary screens report
-- their own switches too — filter on the main screen so the
-- indicator tracks the Desktop that selects profiles:
KiwiDesk.on("desktop_change", function(desktop, monitor)
    if monitor ~= 1 then return end
    KiwiDesk.exec(
        "sketchybar --trigger kiwi_desktop DESKTOP="
        .. desktop)
end)

-- Window icons stay fresh even when focus doesn't change.
-- Reason-filtered: Desktop-switch bursts (vanished/returned)
-- spawn no processes; the desktop_change handler above
-- already refreshes on the round-trip.
for _, event in ipairs({
    "window_created", "window_destroyed",
}) do
    KiwiDesk.on(event, function(id, app, space, reason)
        if reason == "vanished" or reason == "returned" then
            return
        end
        KiwiDesk.exec(
            "sketchybar --trigger kiwi_space_change")
    end)
end
KiwiDesk.on("window_moved_to_space", function()
    KiwiDesk.exec(
        "sketchybar --trigger kiwi_space_change")
end)
```

In your `sketchybarrc`:

```sh
sketchybar --add event kiwi_space_change
sketchybar --add item kiwi_space left
sketchybar --set kiwi_space \
    script="sketchybar --set kiwi_space \
      label=\"\$SPACE (\$MODE)\"" \
    --subscribe kiwi_space kiwi_space_change
```

sections.heading: Full spaces widget
parts:
## Full spaces widget

A complete, production-ready widget with window icons, click
to focus per space, and smart app icon display.

sections.heading: Architecture overview
parts:
### Architecture overview

The widget creates one item per space, pre-allocates window
icon slots beneath each, and polls state via
`kiwidesk get_state | jq` on every `kiwidesk_update` event. A
cold-start watchdog polls until the first successful read, then
goes event-driven.

sections.heading: SbarLua item script
parts:
### SbarLua item script

Add this to your sketchybar config in a new file (e.g.,
`items/kiwidesk_spaces.lua`) and require it in your main
config:

```lua
-- =============================================================
-- KIWIDESK SPACES WIDGET
-- =============================================================
-- SbarLua handle. This script uses `SBAR` throughout; alias it
-- to whatever your config uses (the SbarLua default global is
-- `sbar`):
local SBAR = require("sketchybar")

-- Binary path: absolute, like JQ below. sketchybar is spawned by
-- launchd with a minimal PATH that usually lacks
-- /opt/homebrew/bin, so a bare "kiwidesk" would not resolve here
-- even though the cask installs it there. Point this at your
-- clone instead if you built from source.
local KIWIDESK = "/opt/homebrew/bin/kiwidesk"
local JQ = "/opt/homebrew/bin/jq"

-- Optional: load an icon map (app name → icon character).
-- This example uses sketchybar-app-font. Define it yourself
-- or comment out if you have your own icon scheme.
-- local icon_map = require("helpers.icon_map")

local function kiwidesk_cmd(args)
    return "'" .. KIWIDESK .. "' " .. args
end

-- =============================================================
-- STATE & ITEM CREATION
-- =============================================================
local spaces_store = {}
local space_item_list = {}
local has_data = false
local space_names = { "1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6" }
local current_focused_space = "1"

for _, space_key in ipairs(space_names) do
    local space = SBAR.add("item", "space." .. space_key, {
        position = "left",
        icon = { string = space_key },
        label = { drawing = false },
        drawing = true,
    })

    table.insert(space_item_list, space.name)

    local win_items = {}
    spaces_store[space_key] = {
        item = space,
        win_items = win_items,
    }

    local function on_click()
        os.execute(
            kiwidesk_cmd(
              "focus_space " .. space_key)
        )
    end

    space:subscribe("mouse.clicked", on_click)

    -- Pre-allocate 5 window item slots per space
    for i = 1, 5 do
        local win_item = SBAR.add(
            "item",
            "space." .. space_key .. ".win." .. i,
            {
                position = "left",
                icon = { drawing = false },
                label = {
                    string = "",
                    font = {
                        family = "sketchybar-app-font",
                        style = "Regular",
                        size = 14.0,
                    },
                    padding_left = 2,
                    padding_right = 2,
                },
                drawing = false,
            }
        )

        table.insert(space_item_list, win_item.name)
        table.insert(win_items, win_item)

        win_item:subscribe("mouse.clicked", on_click)
    end
end

-- =============================================================
-- UPDATE: QUERY STATE & REFRESH DISPLAY
-- =============================================================
local function update_spaces()
    local handle = io.popen(
        kiwidesk_cmd("get_state")
            .. " 2>/dev/null | " .. JQ .. " -r "
            .. "'.active_space, \"---SPACES---\", "
            .. "(.spaces[] | \"\\(.id):\\(.focused):"
            .. "\\(.windows | join(\",\"))\"), "
            .. "\"---WINDOWS---\", "
            .. "(.windows[] | \"\\(.id):\\(.app):"
            .. "\\(.floating)\")' 2>/dev/null"
    )
    if not handle then
        return
    end

    local active_space = handle:read("*l")
    if not active_space or active_space == "" then
        handle:close()
        return
    end

    local line = handle:read("*l")
    if line ~= "---SPACES---" then
        handle:close()
        return
    end

    has_data = true

    -- Parse spaces: id:focused_window:window1,window2,...
    local spaces = {}
    line = handle:read("*l")
    while line and line ~= "---WINDOWS---" do
        local id, focused_win, windows_str =
            line:match("([^:]+):([^:]*):(.*)")
        if id then
            local window_ids = {}
            if windows_str and windows_str ~= "" then
                for win_id in windows_str:gmatch("([^,]+)") do
                    table.insert(window_ids, tonumber(win_id))
                end
            end
            spaces[id] = {
                focused = tonumber(focused_win),
                windows = window_ids
            }
        end
        line = handle:read("*l")
    end

    -- Parse windows: id:app:floating
    local windows = {}
    line = handle:read("*l")
    while line do
        local id, app, floating =
            line:match("([^:]+):([^:]+):([^:]+)")
        if id and app then
            windows[tonumber(id)] = {
                app = app,
                floating = (floating == "true")
            }
        end
        line = handle:read("*l")
    end
    handle:close()

    current_focused_space = active_space

    -- Update each space and its window items
    for _, space_key in ipairs(space_names) do
        local w = spaces[space_key]
        local is_focused = (space_key == active_space)
        local space_data = spaces_store[space_key]

        if space_data then
            space_data.item:set({
                icon = {
                    color = is_focused and 0xffffffff
                        or 0xff888888
                }
            })

            local win_count = 0
            if w and w.windows and #w.windows > 0 then
                for _, win_id in ipairs(w.windows) do
                    local win = windows[win_id]
                    if win and win_count < 5 then
                        win_count = win_count + 1
                        local win_item =
                            space_data.win_items[win_count]

                        -- Use your icon_map here, or a plain
                        -- app abbreviation:
                        local icon = (win.app or ""):sub(1, 1)

                        local icon_color = is_focused
                            and 0xffffffff or 0xff888888
                        if is_focused and
                           w.focused == win_id then
                            icon_color = 0xff00ff00  -- green
                        end

                        win_item:set({
                            label = {
                                string = icon,
                                color = icon_color,
                            },
                            drawing = true,
                        })
                    end
                end
            end

            -- Hide unused window slots
            for i = win_count + 1, 5 do
                space_data.win_items[i]:set({
                    drawing = false
                })
            end
        end
    end
end

-- =============================================================
-- EVENT SUBSCRIPTION & COLD-START WATCHDOG
-- =============================================================
SBAR.add("event", "kiwidesk_update")

local event_item = SBAR.add("item", { drawing = false })
event_item:subscribe("kiwidesk_update", function()
    update_spaces()
end)

-- Initial update
update_spaces()

-- Self-heal: on a cold start (sketchybar loads before the
-- KiwiDesk socket is ready, e.g., a reload KiwiDesk triggers
-- while loading init.lua), the initial update fails silently.
-- Poll every 2 seconds until the first successful read, then
-- stop and go event-driven.
local watchdog = SBAR.add("item", {
    drawing = false,
    update_freq = 2
})
watchdog:subscribe("routine", function()
    if has_data then
        watchdog:set({ update_freq = 0 })
    else
        update_spaces()
    end
end)
```

sections.heading: Hooks in init.lua
parts:
### Hooks in init.lua

Wire up the events to trigger sketchybar updates:

```lua
-- Fire kiwidesk_update on all relevant events.
-- desktop_change stays in the list: a window closed while
-- its Desktop was off-screen is reported closed only when
-- KiwiDesk next reads the Desktops, so the Mission Control
-- round-trip re-queries rather than waiting (see the caveats
-- above).
for _, event in ipairs({
    "space_change",
    "layout_change",
    "focus_change",
    "desktop_change",
    "window_created",
    "window_destroyed",
    "window_moved_to_space",
}) do
    KiwiDesk.on(event, function()
        KiwiDesk.exec(
            "sketchybar --trigger kiwidesk_update"
        )
    end)
end
```

> **Keep your hooks in init.lua under GUI-managed settings**
>
> When the Settings app takes ownership of your config
> (adopting it into `gui.json`), only the *managed* parts of
> `init.lua` go inert — tiling settings, keybindings, window
> rules. `KiwiDesk.on(...)` event hooks are not managed: they
> keep running from `init.lua` on every reload, and `init.lua`
> stays the only place they can live. Don't delete your
> sketchybar hooks because "the GUI owns the config now" —
> that silently kills the bar.

sections.heading: Cold-start race condition
parts:
### Cold-start race condition

If sketchybar loads items conditionally (e.g., only when
KiwiDesk is running) and its item loader fires before
KiwiDesk's config process reaches the event loop, the initial
`update_spaces()` call in the item script will fail (the socket
isn't ready). Add a grace period to your loader:

```sh
sleep 1 && sketchybar --add item kiwidesk_spaces right
```

Or use the watchdog above, which polls until the first
successful read.

> **io.popen inside sketchybar's SbarLua**
>
> The sketchybar widget script runs in sketchybar's own Lua
> process, not inside KiwiDesk's. sketchybar bundles its own
> Lua (SbarLua), separate from KiwiDesk's embedded 5.5 VM, and
> it is a normal unrestricted runtime — so `io.popen` is fully
> available. Inside KiwiDesk's Lua VM, `io.popen` is disabled
> to prevent blocking the main thread — use `KiwiDesk.exec`
> with a callback instead (see [Lua
> reference](../lua-reference.md)).

sections.heading: Match the bar's theme
parts:
## Match the bar's theme

A theme picker in your bar can repaint KiwiDesk too: its colours
and the KiwiShelf font are CLI commands. One script holds the
themes, and a picker item runs it.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# ~/.config/sketchybar/kiwidesk-theme.sh <theme>   (chmod +x it)
k() { kiwidesk "$@" >/dev/null || echo "kiwidesk $1 failed" >&2; }

case "$1" in
  gruvbox)
    ring="#D79921"; accent="#D79921"; focus="#83A598"
    fill="#1E1E2EFA"; font="Charter" ;;
  blue)
    ring="#15BDF9"; accent="#15BDF9"; focus="#FF7F00"
    fill="#021254FA"; font="Avenir Next" ;;
  profile)
    # Back to the profile. These are KiwiDesk's shipped defaults:
    # replace them with your own profile's values.
    ring="#4A9816"; accent="#8DB354"; focus="#C2790A"
    fill="#14201CB3"; font="System" ;;
  *) exit 1 ;;
esac

k border.set_focused_color "$ring"
k kiwishelf.set_highlight_color "$accent"
k kiwishelf.set_active_item_color "$accent"
k space_bar.set_focused_item_color "$focus"
k kiwishelf.set_fill_color "$fill"
k kiwishelf.set_font_family "$font"
```

What to know:

- **The commands change the live look, and only until the next
  profile apply.** Loading a profile, a Desktop binding switching
  profiles, a screen-count change, `reload_config` and a KiwiDesk
  restart all put the profile's look back, which is why the
  script carries a `profile` entry. The reverse holds too:
  `save_profile` after a theme pick saves that theme into the
  profile.
- **With Liquid Glass on, the fill tints the glass**
  ([`kiwishelf.set_fill_color`](../lua-reference.md#kiwishelf-colours)).
  A bar's usual faint wash (`0x40` alpha) barely tints it; a
  theme's solid pill colour reads as tinted glass.
- **KiwiDesk takes a font's family name**
  ([`kiwishelf.set_font_family`](../lua-reference.md#kiwishelfset_font_family)).
  If the bar uses the same font, give sketchybar the family's real
  style name: Charter's regular face is `Roman` and Apple
  Chancery's only style is `Chancery`, and sketchybar falls back to
  the system font without a word on a style the family lacks.
